Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 47–50 (part 1 of 3):

(﴿And if not that they would be struck by a calamity for what their hands have put forth⁠⁠⁠⁠ —⁠ punishment for disbelief and other things⁠⁠⁠⁠ —⁠ and they would say, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger⁠⁠⁠⁠ —⁠ why not?⁠⁠⁠⁠ —⁠ so we could follow Your verses⁠⁠⁠⁠ —⁠ those sent with him⁠⁠⁠⁠ —⁠ and be among the believers"﴾ [al-Qasas 47]).
("Lawla" [if not / why not] here is repeated twice, and in each place it has a meaning different from the other place.)
The first: He said, ﴿And if not that they would be struck⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾. The pronoun refers to Quraysh, the people of Makkah. The verb "isabah" (to strike, to befall) means "nuzul" (to descend upon), i.e., a calamity descends upon them. The calamity here is meant as punishment because of their disbelief. "Lawla" here is a particle of prohibition due to existence (harf imtina' li-wujud), and "an" and what follows it are in the interpretation of a masdar serving as the subject, and the answer of "an" is omitted, as the author estimates it.
His saying, ﴿for what their hands have put forth⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾: "bi-ma" means "bi-sabab" (because of), and "ma" is a relative pronoun, i.e., because of that which their hands have put forth. By "their hands" is meant themselves, i.e., by what they sent forth, and the hand is used to express the self, because the hand is generally the instrument of work.
Know that there is a difference between attributing an action to the hand and attributing an action to the self by means of the hand. For example, the saying of the Exalted: ﴿of what Our hands have made, livestock⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [Ya-Sin 71], i.e., of what We made, i.e., of what We created; and the meaning is not that God created the livestock with His hand.
As for His saying: ﴿that which I created with My two hands⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [Sad 75], here He attributed the action to Himself, then made the hand an intermediary, which indicates that Adam was created by the hand of God.
Likewise, for example, if you say, "by what your hand has done," we say here: a person did the thing with his hand, is that so or not? He did it himself, but with his hand. But if you say, "by what your two hands have done" or "by what your two hands have sent forth," the meaning is: by what you did, whether you did it through the hand or the eye or the foot or the tongue. The point is that it is attributed to you; the action is attributed to the hand, not to the doer through the hand. So when it is attributed to the doer through the hand, the action belongs to him, but the hand is the direct agent of the action; and when the action is attributed to the hand, the meaning is the action of the person, whether by his hand or not by his hand.
So His saying, ﴿by what their hands have put forth⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, is it not like His saying, "by what they have put forth with their hands," or not?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Because the first means "by what they put forth," whether it was with the hand, or the foot, or the eye, or the ear, or the tongue.
And his saying, (﴿by what their hands have put forth⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ — of disbelief and other things): it is true that calamities only occur because of sins: ﴿And whatever misfortune strikes you is for what your hands have earned, and He pardons much⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-Shura 30]. And here He said, ﴿And if not that they would be struck by a calamity⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ because of their disbelief.
﴿So they say⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾: the "fa" is a conjunction particle, and "yaqulu" is conjoined to ﴿tusibahum⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾. That is: "so that they would say" — when? After the calamity or before it?
* Student: After it.
* Shaykh: After the calamity, ﴿so they say⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, arguing against God: ﴿Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger, so we would follow Your verses⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, meaning: why did You not send us a messenger before You struck us with punishment ﴿so we would follow Your verses and be among the believers⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾. And is this a proof for them or not?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes, a proof for them. If they were struck without a messenger being sent to them, that would be a proof, because God, the Exalted, says: ﴿messengers as bearers of good news and warners, so that people would have no argument against God after the messengers⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, and He says: ﴿And We would never punish until We send a messenger⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-Isra 15]. So were it not for this matter, that they would be struck for their disbelief and sins and then argue against their Lord that no messenger had been sent to them, what is the answer? Is the answer, "We would have punished them"? Or is the answer, "We did not send you to them"?
* Student: "We did not send you to them."
* Shaykh: Let us see. The author said: (The answer of "lawla" is omitted, and what follows it is a subject; that is, the predicate is omitted and known. The meaning: were it not for the striking that would result in their saying, or were it not for their saying that would result in it, We would have hastened the punishment upon them, and We would not have sent You to them as a messenger).
It seems the author made the answer composed of an affirmation and a negation. The affirmation is his saying, "We would have hastened the punishment upon them," and the negation is, "and We would not have sent You to them." Why? Because they mentioned two matters, since God mentioned two matters: the striking, and their saying, ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾. So the answer was also composed of two matters.
It is also permissible that the answer be composed of one of the two matters, i.e., "We would have punished them" or "We would not have sent You to them," since the meaning is complete without estimating both together. In this case, the "wa" in the author's words would mean "aw" (or).
I think the meaning of the verse is clear in general: were it not that these disbelievers deserve punishment because of their disbelief, and were it not that they would argue that no messenger was sent to them, We would have punished them without sending you, or We would not have sent you to them. So the sending of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is the establishment of proof against them, and a removal of what? Of their argument; a removal of their argument and a refutation of it. So it is as if the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, has now been sent to them before they are seized with punishment, and this requires that if they deny him, they deserve the punishment, because the argument they would use has been removed.
Now, we have the grammatical analysis, which I think we have understood from the author's words:
"Lawla" the first is conditional, and it is a particle of prohibition due to existence.
And "lawla" the second is hortative, meaning "hal" (why not).
And his saying, ﴿fa-yaqulu⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ is conjoined to his saying, ﴿an tusibahum⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾.
And his saying, ﴿fa-nattabi'a⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ is in the accusative by an implied "an" after the causal "fa" that falls in the answer of the hortative "lawla," is that right or not? It is in the accusative by an implied "an" after the causal "fa" that falls as an answer to the hortative "lawla."
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No. The hortative "lawla," "lawla" means "hal," yes, and it is hortative; and when the "fa" falls in its answer, the verb is put in the accusative by an implied "an."
Ibn Malik says:
"After the 'fa' of a answer to a negation or a demand, pure ones, 'an' is implied, and its concealment is obligatory in the accusative."
That is, "an" is put in the accusative after "fa" that falls in the answer to a pure demand or negation, and "its concealment" (i.e., its omission) is "obligatory" (hatm).
And I think it is present in a verse that students have memorized since childhood, where "an" is implied in the accusative in the answer, which is?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, that is an example; these are rules.
"Mur, wad'u, wanha, sal, wa'ridh li-haddihim, tamanna, warju, kadhalika al-nafyu qad kamula"
These are nine. When "fa" falls as an answer to one of them, it puts the following verb in the accusative by an implied "an." Did you memorize this before?
........................... "tamanna, warju, kadhalika al-nafy qad kamula"
* Student: It is not valid (...)?
* Shaykh: No, it is not valid, because the "fa" may be coordinating rather than causal.
Now, after these matters: "Mur" is an imperative, yes, as you say, "Descend to us, and we will honor you."
"Wad'u" is supplication to God, as the poet said:
"My Lord, grant me success, so that I do not deviate from the paths of those who strive toward the best path."
(Rabbi wafiqni fa-la a'dila: "My Lord, grant me success, so I may not deviate"), and you say: "My Lord, grant me success, so I may do righteous deeds."
"Wanha": ﴿And do not transgress therein⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, and what follows?
* Student: ﴿Lest My wrath descend upon you⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Lest My wrath descend upon you⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [Ta-Ha 81].
"Sal," ask, for interrogation: ﴿Do we have any intercessors who will intercede for us?⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-A'raf 53]; the verb is in the accusative by "an."
"Wa'ridh," the offer (al-'ard), as in the saying of the speaker: "Will you not descend to me so you may obtain good?" ("Will you not descend" is an offer, "so you may obtain good").
"Li-haddihim": this is urging (al-tahdid), from which this verse: ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger, so we would follow Your verses⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-Qasas 47].
"Tamanna": what is meant is wishing (al-tamanni), as you say: "Would that I had wealth, so I could give charity from it."
"Warju": hoping (al-raja'), the expression of hope, as in: ﴿Perhaps I may reach the means, the means to the heavens, and look upon the God of Moses⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [Ghafir 36–37]: "Perhaps I may reach, so I may look."
"Kadhalika al-nafy": negation is not prohibition, so you say: "Zayd has not studied, so he would teach you."
Yes, these are nine places; when "fa" falls after them, the verb is put in the accusative by an implied "an."
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: In negation.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: "Zayd has not studied, so he would teach you."
Now, He said: ﴿fa-nattabi'a āyātika⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-Qasas 47].
* Student: Is there prohibition in it (...)? Is there prohibition in it, in "wanha," is there prohibition in it?
* Shaykh: Is there prohibition in it?

* Shaykh: Yes, we gave an example of it with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not transgress therein, lest My wrath descend upon you⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [Ta-Ha 81].

"My Lord, grant me success, so I do not deviate..."
* Shaykh:
"My Lord, grant me success, so I do not deviate from the paths of those who strive toward the best path."
He said: (﴿fa-nattabi'a āyātika⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ — the one sent with it — ﴿and be among the believers⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾; and the answer of ﴿lawla⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-Qasas 47] is omitted).
The meaning: We have sent you, O Muhammad, as an establishment of proof against them and as mercy toward them, lest the punishment strike them without a messenger having reached them.
﴿Then when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?"⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-Qasas 48].
God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then when the truth came to them⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾. We mentioned earlier that "al-haqq" means the established thing, and that in contrast to commands it means justice, and in contrast to reports it means truth. The author said that what is meant here by "the truth" is "Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him." It seems he turned away from its apparent meaning because of His saying: ﴿why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾. But the correct view is that what is meant by "the truth" is the revelation that descended upon Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. This is why He said: ﴿when the truth came to them from Us⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, and "from Us" (indi) implies nearness and that it is from God, which cannot be understood as Muhammad himself, but rather it is the truth he brought. Likewise, this verse ﴿when the truth came to them from Us⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ in all the places of the Qur'an consistently refers to the revelation that descended upon Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him.
And His saying, ﴿why was he not given⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, meaning Muhammad who brought this truth. The meaning of the verse here is very clear and without strain. As for saying that the pronoun in ﴿why was he not given⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ supports that the truth is Muhammad, we say: there is no need for that, since the truth came, and the one who brought it is Muhammad; so it is known that His saying, ﴿why was he not given⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, means Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, who brought the truth, and Muhammad is not the truth itself. This is why "the Truth" is not among the names of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. Yes, he, peace and blessings be upon him, is truthful in what he brought of prophethood, but he brought the truth.
﴿Then when the truth came to them from Us, they said⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾: the pronoun refers to whom? It refers to those to whom the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, came.
("﴿They said, 'Why⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾' — why not?")
* Student: Hortative.
* Shaykh: Hortative, not conditional: why not "was given" — that is, was given — ﴿the like of what was given to Moses⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, meaning (of the signs), like what was given to Moses of signs. This answer has a difficulty if we take it as referring to Quraysh, because Quraysh, as is known, were an unlettered people who knew nothing of the messengers. How then would they argue with the story of Moses?
The exegetes answered that when the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent, Quraysh used to correspond with the Jews and say: a man has come to us claiming to be a prophet; what are the signs of prophets according to you? The Jews would inform them of the signs of prophets. This is why Quraysh opposed the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, with the signs that came to Moses.
It is possible that His saying, ﴿Then when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses before?"⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-Qasas 48] refers to the Jews, since the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent to them too. This possibility is supported by His saying: ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses before?⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-Qasas 48]. The rest of the discussion of the verse will come, God willing.

Now let us return to deriving the benefits.

The first benefit: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But when the truth came to them from Us, they said: Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?﴾ [al-Qasas 48]. It is known that this verse is a consequence of what came before: ﴿Otherwise, they would say: Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs?﴾ [al-Qasas 47].

* In it: a refutation of the claim of these people in their saying: ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs﴾, for the truth has come to them with the Messenger, and despite that they denied it, did they not? They denied it and said: ﴿Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?﴾
* In the verse: a refutation of those who said: ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs﴾.
* Among its benefits: that what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought is the truth. The truth means what is established, and with respect to reports it is truthfulness, and with respect to rulings it is justice.
* Among its benefits: that what opposes what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought is falsehood, due to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So what is there after the truth but error?﴾ [Yunus 32]. Thus every report that contains the denial of the report of Allah and His Messenger is a lie. For example, if someone says: man's origin is the ape, then he evolved and became a human, what do we say to him? It is a lie, because it opposes what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought. Yes. And if a person legislates laws that oppose the Sharia, we say: this is false and misguidance, because the truth is only in what the Sharia brought. Yes.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the explanation of the arrogance and obstinacy of these deniers of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), their arrogance and stubbornness, for they denied the truth after they had said: ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs﴾ [al-Qasas 47].
* And among the benefits of the verse: that the Quraysh had some information about the earlier messengers, since they said: ﴿Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?﴾ By what means did they obtain this knowledge?
* Student: Through the Jews.
* The Shaykh: Through the Jews, because when the Messenger (ﷺ) was sent, they sent to the Jews asking them about the reports of this man, and they wrote to them what they knew of his reports and what Moses had brought [[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il (611) from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them.]].
* Among the benefits of the verse: the establishment of the prophethood of Moses (peace be upon him), from their saying: ﴿the like of what was given to Moses﴾ [al-Qasas 48].
* Among its benefits: that Allah the Exalted gave Moses (peace be upon him) signs that human beings believe in when similar ones are shown. This is not specific to him, rather it applies to every messenger Allah sent: he must be given signs by which mankind is made to believe in the like of them, for people will not accept a man who says: I am a messenger of Allah to you, I command you to do such and such and forbid you from such and such, and leave what your fathers were upon of worshipping idols, and leave what your fathers were upon of forbidding the lawful, and so on. They will not accept except with signs that show his truthfulness and support him.
* Good. And also among them, among the benefits of the verse: the invalidation of the argument of these deniers, the invalidation of their argument: ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses before?﴾ [al-Qasas 48].
* And among its benefits also: that in the context of debate and argumentation, it is fitting to overwhelm the opponent by invalidating his statement with his own statement or his own action, that his statement is refuted by what has occurred from himself. Why? Because what has occurred from him cannot be denied by him, and if he denied it, it would not be accepted. So when we establish the proof against the opponent from his own action and speech, this is more effective in silencing him. ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses before?﴾
* And among them: that the nature of human beings is one, based on His saying: ﴿Did they not disbelieve﴾ [al-Qasas 48], where the pronoun refers to the kind of human being, because human nature is one.
* And among the benefits of the verse also: that it is also appropriate, during disputation or debate, to invalidate the opponent's statement by reality, that you refute the opponent's claim in a matter of fact, (...) in a matter of fact. For the signs that Moses brought and (...) these people denied them, did they not deny them?
* Student: They denied them.
* The Shaykh: They denied them. Mankind did not believe in them. So the criterion is not the type of signs, but the condition of the addressee. Otherwise the signs are established and clear, but ﴿Signs and warnings do not avail a people who will not believe﴾ [Yunus 101].
* And among them: that the people of falsehood give the people of truth derogatory nicknames to repel people from accepting them. From where is this taken?
* Student: ﴿Two sorcerers﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿They said: two sorcerers﴾, or ﴿sorcerers﴾, ﴿They said: two sorcerers who support each other﴾ [al-Qasas 48], or ﴿two sorcerers who support each other﴾. Whether they described what the messengers brought as sorcery or described the messengers themselves as sorcerers, the purpose of that is repulsion, repelling people from accepting what the messengers brought.

Good. Can we say that this principle is established for the followers of the messengers?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: By the evidence of His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed. And when they passed by them, they winked at one another. And when they returned to their families, they returned jesting. And when they saw them, they said: Indeed, these are misguided﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 29–32]. And Allah, blessed and exalted, has made for every prophet an enemy among the criminals. Is the enemy among the criminals an enemy of the prophet personally, or an enemy of him by his attribute?
* Student: By his attribute.
* The Shaykh: By his attribute. The evidence: Muhammad (ﷺ), before the message came to him, was among the Arabs the truthful and trustworthy one, and they regarded him as one of the best of the Banu Hashim and the most upright in justice. But when he brought the truth, what became of him? He became the treacherous liar. Clear? If these criminals opposed the messengers because of their attribute, then this hostility will extend to those who follow these messengers, because the meaning by which the enmity arose is also present in the followers of the messengers.
* Based on this, we can derive a benefit from it, which is: reassuring the followers of the messengers and strengthening them in the knowledge that they will receive the same derogatory nicknames and hostility that the messengers received. Yes. So they must meet that with patience, steadfastness and strength. Yes. Not that they become discouraged, but that they be as their predecessors were: ﴿So be patient as the steadfast of the messengers were patient, and do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them. It will be as if they had not remained but an hour of a day﴾ [al-Ahqaf 35].
* And also among the benefits of the verse: that cooperation, even in falsehood, has an effect. Is that not so? Cooperation even in falsehood has an effect and strengthens it. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿who support each other﴾ [al-Qasas 48]. So if cooperation in falsehood has an effect, then how much more so cooperation in truth.

Based on this, we ought, and this is the benefit that follows from it: we ought to cooperate with one another in the call to the truth that we are upon, and that none of us abandon another. Yes. This is in contrast to the condition of people today, for they are not cooperative in this regard. Even the people of truth and the people of the call, you find them not cooperating, because first, each one cares only for himself, and second, they may differ over a simple, partial matter of religion and become enemies over it. Yes. One of them may oppose the other over how to raise the hands at the opening takbir. This one says: you raise your hands to your ears, and that one says: you raise them to your shoulders. Then he says: you are misguided, and he says: you are misguided. Then what does this word produce? It produces hatred, malice and enmity.

I have related to you the story of two groups from the people of Africa, each group declaring the other to be unbelievers over a simple matter of religion. One group says: the Sunnah is that a person places his right hand over his left above his chest, and another group says: the Sunnah is that a person lets his hands hang at his sides. Each one says to the other: you are a disbelieving cursed one, because you have abandoned the Sunnah deliberately and intentionally, and whoever dislikes what Allah has sent down is a disbeliever. So there is great enmity. During the Hajj in these days in Mina, and by Allah, people from the brotherhood of the awareness campaign gather, they came to them and calmed them down and explained that this is not permissible, because this is harm to you, O people of truth, for if some of you declare others to be unbelievers, what will you become before the people of superstitions and the people of innovations? Yes. The one who declares another a disbeliever (...) is himself a disbeliever.

So we say: cooperation has a far-reaching effect. I think you know about the annulment of the document that the Quraysh wrote to boycott the Banu Hashim, how they annulled this document. No one among the people came and annulled it, he could not. But he went to so-and-so and said to him, reproaching him: the Banu Hashim are a people from among you, how are you content that you boycott them until they die of hunger? And he went to another, and a third, and a fourth, until they formed a group and went to this document in the Ka'bah and tore it up [[See the story of the assembly (al-saqifah) in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham (1/376).]]. So cooperation is the foundation of success, as the common people say. And look at the saying of the criminals: they say ﴿two sorcerers who support each other﴾ [al-Qasas 48].

Good. Secondly, among the benefits of the verse: the explanation of the arrogance of these people also in that they did not believe in both matters, and they said: ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in all of it﴾ [al-Qasas 48].

And also among them: what does placing the object first in His saying: ﴿we disbelieve in all of it﴾ indicate? Restriction (hasr), even though they disbelieved in it along with other things. But it has already been said that this restriction is intended to enrage the opponent, as if they are saying: even if we believed in everything, we would only disbelieve in these two. Otherwise it is known that they disbelieve in it and in other things. This is a benefit that few notice: that when a thing is not restricted to this thing but is restricted to it, there must be a purpose. The purpose here is to enrage, as if they are saying: even though we believe in everything, we are disbelievers in what you have brought: ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in all of it﴾.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Then bring a book from Allah that is more guided than both of them, and I will follow it, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Qasas 49].

In this verse, among the benefits: it is part of justice to descend to the level of the opponent to a point he accepts. For it is known that Allah, glorified and exalted, knows that they cannot bring what is demanded of them, or not? When He demanded of them that they bring a book more guided than the Torah and the Qur'an, and Allah knows that they will not bring it, or not? How can He say to the Messenger: ﴿Say: Bring﴾, when He knows it is impossible? This is from the aspect of descending to the opponent to the utmost of justice, as if He made him and his opponent one thing. He says: you bring a book more guided than the Torah and the Qur'an, and I commit to following it. If they do not come with it, then it means they must follow the Torah and the Qur'an, or not? They must do that. That is, since I commit to them that if you bring a book more guided than both, I will follow it, then you must follow what you have found.

So there is in it a descent to the opponent's level, and that this is part of the perfection of justice in debate.

And among the benefits of the verse also: overwhelming the opponent by challenge. If you read the end of Surah al-Tur, you will find in it something remarkable from debate, from His saying: ﴿So remind, for by the grace of your Lord you are not a soothsayer or a madman﴾ [al-Tur 29], up to His saying: ﴿until they meet their Day in which they will be struck senseless﴾ [al-Tur 45]. You will find many etiquettes of debate: ﴿Or do they have a ladder by which they listen?﴾ [al-Tur 38], if that is the case, ﴿then let their listener bring a clear authority﴾ [al-Tur 38]. ﴿Or do they say: he has fabricated it? Rather, they do not believe﴾ [al-Tur 33]. If that is the case, ﴿then let them produce a statement like it, if they are truthful﴾ [al-Tur 34]. So in debate, that is, Allah the Exalted, at the conclusion of the debate, makes the opponent silenced by a challenge to what he cannot do. Here they cannot bring the like of it, so the proof is established against them.

And among the benefits of the verse: that the Torah and the Qur'an are from Allah, so the Qur'an and the Torah are the speech of Allah. But the Qur'an was sent down as revelation, and the Torah was sent down in writing, which Allah wrote on tablets that He threw to Moses.

Among the benefits of the verse also: a person is not obliged to shift from what he is upon to another thing unless what is other is more guided (ahda). For me, for example, it is not obligatory to move from the school of the Hanbalis to the school of the Shafi'is until I see that it is more correct. For He said: "Following is not required except if what they have brought is more guided than it." As for if it is equal, then you do not oblige me, and I do not oblige you if it is equal. The obligation comes when? When what the opponent has brought is more guided than what I am upon. And this is a very important benefit: a person is not obliged to move from what he is upon of a path or school except to one that is more correct, better and more guided than it. As for when they are equal, he is not obliged, nor is he blamed either if he does not move. And likewise, if what is in the other is lower, then by way of greater priority he is not obliged.

So the levels now are three: either what you are called to is lower than what you are upon, or more guided, or equal. If it is more guided, what is the obligation? Following is required. If it is lower, following is prohibited. What remains is: if it is equal, is following required, prohibited, or is the person given a choice?

The scholars say in such a situation: the person is given a choice. They said: and if two scholars issue a legal ruling to him and neither of them is more weighty in his view, then he is given a choice to follow whichever of the two opinions he wishes. And perhaps the ruling of this question is derived from this verse, perhaps it is derived from this verse; because Allah only made following obligatory if it is more guided, and it is known that if it is lower, following is prohibited. So the equal remains neither on the side of prohibition nor on the side of obligation, and this is the level of choice.

Also among the benefits of the verse: the challenge may be by description just as it may be by action. "Then bring" [al-Qasas 49] is a challenge by doing what they are not able to bring. "If you are truthful" [al-Qasas 49] is a challenge by description: if you are among the truthful that what you are upon is true, then bring this; otherwise you are among the liars. And for this reason He said: "Follow it, if you are truthful" [al-Qasas 49].

Allah the Exalted said: "And if they do not respond to you, then know that they only follow their desires. And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people" [al-Qasas 50].

His saying: "And if they do not respond to you" means: if their response to you is nonexistent.

In it: permissibility of conditioning with a condition regarding what is certain to occur. Or did you not understand this?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Meaning, "And if they do not respond to you" — this is a matter certain to occur. Does the one who thinks suppose there is a possibility that they will respond?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: There is none; no one supposes it. So we say: permissibility of conditioning a thing that is certain with a condition, even if it is certain that it will not happen, and likewise even if it is certain that it will happen, for here the non-response is certain to happen without doubt, and yet it was conditioned. And in the hadith the Prophet ﷺ said: "And indeed we, if Allah wills, will be joining you" [(1)], saying it to the people of the graves. So it is known that this matter—?
* Student: Certain.
* The Shaykh: Certain, yes.

Also among its benefits: these deniers of the Messenger ﷺ have no proof except following their desires, due to His saying: "Then know that they only follow their desires" [al-Qasas 50]. And does that meaning mean: so do not argue with them? Because one who follows his desire is stubborn and obstinate; the one who follows his desire is obstinate, you cannot persuade him, as long as he does not seek the truth but wants only to defend himself and follow his desire. So I believe such a man cannot be debated; if you debate him, while he is a person of desire, there is no benefit.

So shall we say: it is derived from this verse that if it is known that the one being debated wants to follow his desire, there is no benefit in arguing with him, because it is a waste of time? Yes, we say so; because He said: "Then know that they only follow their desires," meaning: there is no benefit in arguing with them. So if you have made the truth clear to the person and manifested it by its textual, rational and sensory proofs, as far as the available proofs go, but he insists on remaining upon what he was upon, then know that he is following his desire, and one who follows desire is stubborn; he is not a person seeking guidance, and he cannot benefit.

And for this reason we say in such a situation: it is not obligatory upon a person to argue with him; rather he moves to something else, which is to punish him: "And do not argue with the People of the Book except in a way that is best, except those of them who have wronged" [al-Ankabut 46]. The obstinate person is other than one who wants to follow the truth but it has not become manifest to him; the obstinate has his own state. And Allah the Exalted said: "So remind, if the reminder benefits" [al-A'la 9], meaning: and if it does not benefit, then do not remind. And this has been discussed before: is this condition to have an implication (mafhum) or not?
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, (...) as long as you argued in front of people and the truth became clear, it does not mean that he speaks falsehood and you remain silent; because if you do not hear him speaking falsehood, people must know the truth and change this falsehood. But if you argued with him in front of people and the truth was made clear and he refused, you have nothing more; there is no benefit in arguing with him.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, in any case we do not say: argue in front of people; but sometimes the argument happens in front of people, you are with people in a gathering and research begins and discussion takes place. Do we say that you should remain silent and leave this man? No, you must resist with what you have. Yes. Likewise, if you hear him, for example, speaking in an assembly and establishing falsehood, you must speak the truth. Yes indeed.

Among the benefits of the verse: people differ in misguidance; that people differ in going astray, so they are not equal in misguidance, just as they are not equal in guidance, and not equal in error, and not equal in rectitude. Or no? Are people equal in these matters?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: No. For this reason He said: "And who is more astray than one who follows..." [al-Qasas 50]. In this is evidence that people vary in misguidance, but there is no one more astray than this one who followed his desire without guidance from Allah.

Also among the benefits of the verse: that desire may agree with guidance. From where do we take it?
* Student: "His desire without guidance."
* The Shaykh: "His desire without guidance from Allah" [al-Qasas 50]. As for one who follows his desire based on guidance from Allah, this is good: that his desire follows what the truth has brought; this is good. We have mentioned to you the hadith narrated from the Prophet ﷺ: "None of you believes until his desire is subordinate to what I have brought" [(2)]. So the conclusion is that the blameworthy desire is that which is not upon guidance.

Good. Also among the benefits of the verse: that the wrongdoer has exposed himself to being deprived of guidance; or if you wish, say: wrongdoing is a cause for the wrongdoer's deprivation of guidance; due to His saying: "Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people" [al-Qasas 50]. So the wrongdoer is the one who deprived himself of guidance.

(...)
As for His saying: "Indeed, Allah does not guide," the Qadariyya hold that a person can be guided by himself, and Allah the Blessed and Exalted has no authority over him at all, because they—may Allah protect us—are the Qadariyya. And what do they say concerning the decree of Allah?
* Student: That the matter is "unprecedented" (anf).
* The Shaykh: Yes, that the matter is unprecedented, meaning that Allah did not decree the actions of the servants, and I act and leave by my pure, absolute choice, and Allah has no will, no creation, nor anything in it. But "Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people" [al-Qasas 50] refutes them, just as it also refutes the Jahmiyya Jabriyya who say compulsion; because Allah the Exalted attributed these people—by their action—to wrongdoing, and if they were compelled to it, attributing wrongdoing to them would be wrong, and Allah the Blessed and Exalted does not wrong anyone.

So in the verse there is a refutation of the Qadariyya, and a refutation of whom? A refutation of the Jabriyya; and the Jabriyya are Jahmiyya; that is, the Jahmiyya's doctrine is compulsion, and among them are three "jeems," as Ibn al-Qayyim said in the Nuniyya: "The Jahmiyya have three jeems, all of them jeems of blame: what are they? Jabr (compulsion), Irja' (postponement), and the jeem of tajahhum." So they are Jabriyya, Murji'a, Jahmiyya. Yes, may Allah suffice you against the evil of the three jeems. Yes: the Jahmiyya, the Jabriyya and the Murji'a.

* In any case, in the noble verse there is a refutation of the two misguided groups: the Qadariyya and the Jabriyya. The Qadariyya deny Allah's decree regarding the actions of the servant, and the Jabriyya are the opposite.

"Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people."

* Also among the benefits of the verse: whoever seeks justice has exposed himself to guidance, because wrongdoing's opposite is justice, and the negation of guidance by the attribute of wrongdoing requires the affirmation of guidance by the attribute of justice. So whoever seeks justice is granted guidance; justice is a cause of guidance. Likewise, everyone who seeks good—though may Allah grant us success in seeking it—everyone who seeks good is granted it if the intention is sincere and the resolve is firm.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: They say: the person has an independent will in which Allah has no part; Allah has no part in it at all. (...)

<br>

[(1)] Related by Muslim (249/39) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.

[(2)] Related by Ibn Battah in al-Ibanah (279) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 47–50 (part 1 of 3):

(﴿And if not that they would be struck by a calamity for what their hands have put forth⁠⁠⁠⁠ —⁠ punishment for disbelief and other things⁠⁠⁠⁠ —⁠ and they would say, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger⁠⁠⁠⁠ —⁠ why not?⁠⁠⁠⁠ —⁠ so we could follow Your verses⁠⁠⁠⁠ —⁠ those sent with him⁠⁠⁠⁠ —⁠ and be among the believers"﴾ [al-Qasas 47]).
("Lawla" [if not / why not] here is repeated twice, and in each place it has a meaning different from the other place.)
The first: He said, ﴿And if not that they would be struck⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾. The pronoun refers to Quraysh, the people of Makkah. The verb "isabah" (to strike, to befall) means "nuzul" (to descend upon), i.e., a calamity descends upon them. The calamity here is meant as punishment because of their disbelief. "Lawla" here is a particle of prohibition due to existence (harf imtina' li-wujud), and "an" and what follows it are in the interpretation of a masdar serving as the subject, and the answer of "an" is omitted, as the author estimates it.
His saying, ﴿for what their hands have put forth⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾: "bi-ma" means "bi-sabab" (because of), and "ma" is a relative pronoun, i.e., because of that which their hands have put forth. By "their hands" is meant themselves, i.e., by what they sent forth, and the hand is used to express the self, because the hand is generally the instrument of work.
Know that there is a difference between attributing an action to the hand and attributing an action to the self by means of the hand. For example, the saying of the Exalted: ﴿of what Our hands have made, livestock⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [Ya-Sin 71], i.e., of what We made, i.e., of what We created; and the meaning is not that God created the livestock with His hand.
As for His saying: ﴿that which I created with My two hands⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [Sad 75], here He attributed the action to Himself, then made the hand an intermediary, which indicates that Adam was created by the hand of God.
Likewise, for example, if you say, "by what your hand has done," we say here: a person did the thing with his hand, is that so or not? He did it himself, but with his hand. But if you say, "by what your two hands have done" or "by what your two hands have sent forth," the meaning is: by what you did, whether you did it through the hand or the eye or the foot or the tongue. The point is that it is attributed to you; the action is attributed to the hand, not to the doer through the hand. So when it is attributed to the doer through the hand, the action belongs to him, but the hand is the direct agent of the action; and when the action is attributed to the hand, the meaning is the action of the person, whether by his hand or not by his hand.
So His saying, ﴿by what their hands have put forth⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, is it not like His saying, "by what they have put forth with their hands," or not?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Because the first means "by what they put forth," whether it was with the hand, or the foot, or the eye, or the ear, or the tongue.
And his saying, (﴿by what their hands have put forth⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ — of disbelief and other things): it is true that calamities only occur because of sins: ﴿And whatever misfortune strikes you is for what your hands have earned, and He pardons much⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-Shura 30]. And here He said, ﴿And if not that they would be struck by a calamity⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ because of their disbelief.
﴿So they say⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾: the "fa" is a conjunction particle, and "yaqulu" is conjoined to ﴿tusibahum⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾. That is: "so that they would say" — when? After the calamity or before it?
* Student: After it.
* Shaykh: After the calamity, ﴿so they say⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, arguing against God: ﴿Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger, so we would follow Your verses⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, meaning: why did You not send us a messenger before You struck us with punishment ﴿so we would follow Your verses and be among the believers⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾. And is this a proof for them or not?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes, a proof for them. If they were struck without a messenger being sent to them, that would be a proof, because God, the Exalted, says: ﴿messengers as bearers of good news and warners, so that people would have no argument against God after the messengers⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, and He says: ﴿And We would never punish until We send a messenger⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-Isra 15]. So were it not for this matter, that they would be struck for their disbelief and sins and then argue against their Lord that no messenger had been sent to them, what is the answer? Is the answer, "We would have punished them"? Or is the answer, "We did not send you to them"?
* Student: "We did not send you to them."
* Shaykh: Let us see. The author said: (The answer of "lawla" is omitted, and what follows it is a subject; that is, the predicate is omitted and known. The meaning: were it not for the striking that would result in their saying, or were it not for their saying that would result in it, We would have hastened the punishment upon them, and We would not have sent You to them as a messenger).
It seems the author made the answer composed of an affirmation and a negation. The affirmation is his saying, "We would have hastened the punishment upon them," and the negation is, "and We would not have sent You to them." Why? Because they mentioned two matters, since God mentioned two matters: the striking, and their saying, ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾. So the answer was also composed of two matters.
It is also permissible that the answer be composed of one of the two matters, i.e., "We would have punished them" or "We would not have sent You to them," since the meaning is complete without estimating both together. In this case, the "wa" in the author's words would mean "aw" (or).
I think the meaning of the verse is clear in general: were it not that these disbelievers deserve punishment because of their disbelief, and were it not that they would argue that no messenger was sent to them, We would have punished them without sending you, or We would not have sent you to them. So the sending of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is the establishment of proof against them, and a removal of what? Of their argument; a removal of their argument and a refutation of it. So it is as if the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, has now been sent to them before they are seized with punishment, and this requires that if they deny him, they deserve the punishment, because the argument they would use has been removed.
Now, we have the grammatical analysis, which I think we have understood from the author's words:
"Lawla" the first is conditional, and it is a particle of prohibition due to existence.
And "lawla" the second is hortative, meaning "hal" (why not).
And his saying, ﴿fa-yaqulu⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ is conjoined to his saying, ﴿an tusibahum⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾.
And his saying, ﴿fa-nattabi'a⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ is in the accusative by an implied "an" after the causal "fa" that falls in the answer of the hortative "lawla," is that right or not? It is in the accusative by an implied "an" after the causal "fa" that falls as an answer to the hortative "lawla."
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No. The hortative "lawla," "lawla" means "hal," yes, and it is hortative; and when the "fa" falls in its answer, the verb is put in the accusative by an implied "an."
Ibn Malik says:
"After the 'fa' of a answer to a negation or a demand, pure ones, 'an' is implied, and its concealment is obligatory in the accusative."
That is, "an" is put in the accusative after "fa" that falls in the answer to a pure demand or negation, and "its concealment" (i.e., its omission) is "obligatory" (hatm).
And I think it is present in a verse that students have memorized since childhood, where "an" is implied in the accusative in the answer, which is?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, that is an example; these are rules.
"Mur, wad'u, wanha, sal, wa'ridh li-haddihim, tamanna, warju, kadhalika al-nafyu qad kamula"
These are nine. When "fa" falls as an answer to one of them, it puts the following verb in the accusative by an implied "an." Did you memorize this before?
........................... "tamanna, warju, kadhalika al-nafy qad kamula"
* Student: It is not valid (...)?
* Shaykh: No, it is not valid, because the "fa" may be coordinating rather than causal.
Now, after these matters: "Mur" is an imperative, yes, as you say, "Descend to us, and we will honor you."
"Wad'u" is supplication to God, as the poet said:
"My Lord, grant me success, so that I do not deviate from the paths of those who strive toward the best path."
(Rabbi wafiqni fa-la a'dila: "My Lord, grant me success, so I may not deviate"), and you say: "My Lord, grant me success, so I may do righteous deeds."
"Wanha": ﴿And do not transgress therein⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, and what follows?
* Student: ﴿Lest My wrath descend upon you⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Lest My wrath descend upon you⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [Ta-Ha 81].
"Sal," ask, for interrogation: ﴿Do we have any intercessors who will intercede for us?⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-A'raf 53]; the verb is in the accusative by "an."
"Wa'ridh," the offer (al-'ard), as in the saying of the speaker: "Will you not descend to me so you may obtain good?" ("Will you not descend" is an offer, "so you may obtain good").
"Li-haddihim": this is urging (al-tahdid), from which this verse: ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger, so we would follow Your verses⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-Qasas 47].
"Tamanna": what is meant is wishing (al-tamanni), as you say: "Would that I had wealth, so I could give charity from it."
"Warju": hoping (al-raja'), the expression of hope, as in: ﴿Perhaps I may reach the means, the means to the heavens, and look upon the God of Moses⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [Ghafir 36–37]: "Perhaps I may reach, so I may look."
"Kadhalika al-nafy": negation is not prohibition, so you say: "Zayd has not studied, so he would teach you."
Yes, these are nine places; when "fa" falls after them, the verb is put in the accusative by an implied "an."

He said: (﴿fa-nattabi'a āyātika⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ — the one sent with it — ﴿and be among the believers⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾; and the answer of ﴿lawla⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-Qasas 47] is omitted).
The meaning: We have sent you, O Muhammad, as an establishment of proof against them and as mercy toward them, lest the punishment strike them without a messenger having reached them.
﴿Then when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?"⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-Qasas 48].
God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then when the truth came to them⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾. We mentioned earlier that "al-haqq" means the established thing, and that in contrast to commands it means justice, and in contrast to reports it means truth. The author said that what is meant here by "the truth" is "Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him." It seems he turned away from its apparent meaning because of His saying: ﴿why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾. But the correct view is that what is meant by "the truth" is the revelation that descended upon Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. This is why He said: ﴿when the truth came to them from Us⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, and "from Us" (indi) implies nearness and that it is from God, which cannot be understood as Muhammad himself, but rather it is the truth he brought. Likewise, this verse ﴿when the truth came to them from Us⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ in all the places of the Qur'an consistently refers to the revelation that descended upon Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him.
And His saying, ﴿why was he not given⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, meaning Muhammad who brought this truth. The meaning of the verse here is very clear and without strain. As for saying that the pronoun in ﴿why was he not given⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ supports that the truth is Muhammad, we say: there is no need for that, since the truth came, and the one who brought it is Muhammad; so it is known that His saying, ﴿why was he not given⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, means Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, who brought the truth, and Muhammad is not the truth itself. This is why "the Truth" is not among the names of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. Yes, he, peace and blessings be upon him, is truthful in what he brought of prophethood, but he brought the truth.
﴿Then when the truth came to them from Us, they said⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾: the pronoun refers to whom? It refers to those to whom the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, came.
("﴿They said, 'Why⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾' — why not?")
* Student: Hortative.
* Shaykh: Hortative, not conditional: why not "was given" — that is, was given — ﴿the like of what was given to Moses⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, meaning (of the signs), like what was given to Moses of signs. This answer has a difficulty if we take it as referring to Quraysh, because Quraysh, as is known, were an unlettered people who knew nothing of the messengers. How then would they argue with the story of Moses?
The exegetes answered that when the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent, Quraysh used to correspond with the Jews and say: a man has come to us claiming to be a prophet; what are the signs of prophets according to you? The Jews would inform them of the signs of prophets. This is why Quraysh opposed the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, with the signs that came to Moses.
It is possible that His saying, ﴿Then when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses before?"⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-Qasas 48] refers to the Jews, since the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent to them too. This possibility is supported by His saying: ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses before?⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-Qasas 48]. The rest of the discussion of the verse will come, God willing.
* Student: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do they not see that We created for them from what Our hands have made⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [Ya-Sin 71] (...) the created, and that the hand is the instrument of work.

(...) So its meaning is the particle of existence; it is similar to the conditional.

Now, God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses before?⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-Qasas 48]. Do you not say: ﴿they disbelieved in what was given⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾; the pronoun refers to whom?

So your suggestion that Muhammad's signs be like Moses's signs does not necessarily compel belief, because Moses's signs were disbelieved in.
His saying, ﴿they said, "Two sorceries⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾ [al-Qasas 48]: is there a second reading in it? ﴿They said, "Two sorceries"⁠⁠⁠⁠﴾, and what is the reading in it?

Now let us return to deriving the benefits.

The first benefit: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But when the truth came to them from Us, they said: Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?﴾ [al-Qasas 48]. It is known that this verse is a consequence of what came before: ﴿Otherwise, they would say: Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs?﴾ [al-Qasas 47].

* In it: a refutation of the claim of these people in their saying: ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs﴾, for the truth has come to them with the Messenger, and despite that they denied it, did they not? They denied it and said: ﴿Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?﴾
* In the verse: a refutation of those who said: ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs﴾.
* Among its benefits: that what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought is the truth. The truth means what is established, and with respect to reports it is truthfulness, and with respect to rulings it is justice.
* Among its benefits: that what opposes what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought is falsehood, due to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So what is there after the truth but error?﴾ [Yunus 32]. Thus every report that contains the denial of the report of Allah and His Messenger is a lie. For example, if someone says: man's origin is the ape, then he evolved and became a human, what do we say to him? It is a lie, because it opposes what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought. Yes. And if a person legislates laws that oppose the Sharia, we say: this is false and misguidance, because the truth is only in what the Sharia brought. Yes.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the explanation of the arrogance and obstinacy of these deniers of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), their arrogance and stubbornness, for they denied the truth after they had said: ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs﴾ [al-Qasas 47].
* And among the benefits of the verse: that the Quraysh had some information about the earlier messengers, since they said: ﴿Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?﴾ By what means did they obtain this knowledge?
* Student: Through the Jews.
* The Shaykh: Through the Jews, because when the Messenger (ﷺ) was sent, they sent to the Jews asking them about the reports of this man, and they wrote to them what they knew of his reports and what Moses had brought [[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il (611) from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them.]].
* Among the benefits of the verse: the establishment of the prophethood of Moses (peace be upon him), from their saying: ﴿the like of what was given to Moses﴾ [al-Qasas 48].
* Among its benefits: that Allah the Exalted gave Moses (peace be upon him) signs that human beings believe in when similar ones are shown. This is not specific to him, rather it applies to every messenger Allah sent: he must be given signs by which mankind is made to believe in the like of them, for people will not accept a man who says: I am a messenger of Allah to you, I command you to do such and such and forbid you from such and such, and leave what your fathers were upon of worshipping idols, and leave what your fathers were upon of forbidding the lawful, and so on. They will not accept except with signs that show his truthfulness and support him.
* Good. And also among them, among the benefits of the verse: the invalidation of the argument of these deniers, the invalidation of their argument: ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses before?﴾ [al-Qasas 48].
* And among its benefits also: that in the context of debate and argumentation, it is fitting to overwhelm the opponent by invalidating his statement with his own statement or his own action, that his statement is refuted by what has occurred from himself. Why? Because what has occurred from him cannot be denied by him, and if he denied it, it would not be accepted. So when we establish the proof against the opponent from his own action and speech, this is more effective in silencing him. ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses before?﴾
* And among them: that the nature of human beings is one, based on His saying: ﴿Did they not disbelieve﴾ [al-Qasas 48], where the pronoun refers to the kind of human being, because human nature is one.
* And among the benefits of the verse also: that it is also appropriate, during disputation or debate, to invalidate the opponent's statement by reality, that you refute the opponent's claim in a matter of fact, (...) in a matter of fact. For the signs that Moses brought and (...) these people denied them, did they not deny them?
* Student: They denied them.
* The Shaykh: They denied them. Mankind did not believe in them. So the criterion is not the type of signs, but the condition of the addressee. Otherwise the signs are established and clear, but ﴿Signs and warnings do not avail a people who will not believe﴾ [Yunus 101].
* And among them: that the people of falsehood give the people of truth derogatory nicknames to repel people from accepting them. From where is this taken?
* Student: ﴿Two sorcerers﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿They said: two sorcerers﴾, or ﴿sorcerers﴾, ﴿They said: two sorcerers who support each other﴾ [al-Qasas 48], or ﴿two sorcerers who support each other﴾. Whether they described what the messengers brought as sorcery or described the messengers themselves as sorcerers, the purpose of that is repulsion, repelling people from accepting what the messengers brought.

Good. Can we say that this principle is established for the followers of the messengers?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: By the evidence of His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed. And when they passed by them, they winked at one another. And when they returned to their families, they returned jesting. And when they saw them, they said: Indeed, these are misguided﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 29–32]. And Allah, blessed and exalted, has made for every prophet an enemy among the criminals. Is the enemy among the criminals an enemy of the prophet personally, or an enemy of him by his attribute?
* Student: By his attribute.
* The Shaykh: By his attribute. The evidence: Muhammad (ﷺ), before the message came to him, was among the Arabs the truthful and trustworthy one, and they regarded him as one of the best of the Banu Hashim and the most upright in justice. But when he brought the truth, what became of him? He became the treacherous liar. Clear? If these criminals opposed the messengers because of their attribute, then this hostility will extend to those who follow these messengers, because the meaning by which the enmity arose is also present in the followers of the messengers.
* Based on this, we can derive a benefit from it, which is: reassuring the followers of the messengers and strengthening them in the knowledge that they will receive the same derogatory nicknames and hostility that the messengers received. Yes. So they must meet that with patience, steadfastness and strength. Yes. Not that they become discouraged, but that they be as their predecessors were: ﴿So be patient as the steadfast of the messengers were patient, and do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them. It will be as if they had not remained but an hour of a day﴾ [al-Ahqaf 35].
* And also among the benefits of the verse: that cooperation, even in falsehood, has an effect. Is that not so? Cooperation even in falsehood has an effect and strengthens it. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿who support each other﴾ [al-Qasas 48]. So if cooperation in falsehood has an effect, then how much more so cooperation in truth.

Based on this, we ought, and this is the benefit that follows from it: we ought to cooperate with one another in the call to the truth that we are upon, and that none of us abandon another. Yes. This is in contrast to the condition of people today, for they are not cooperative in this regard. Even the people of truth and the people of the call, you find them not cooperating, because first, each one cares only for himself, and second, they may differ over a simple, partial matter of religion and become enemies over it. Yes. One of them may oppose the other over how to raise the hands at the opening takbir. This one says: you raise your hands to your ears, and that one says: you raise them to your shoulders. Then he says: you are misguided, and he says: you are misguided. Then what does this word produce? It produces hatred, malice and enmity.

I have related to you the story of two groups from the people of Africa, each group declaring the other to be unbelievers over a simple matter of religion. One group says: the Sunnah is that a person places his right hand over his left above his chest, and another group says: the Sunnah is that a person lets his hands hang at his sides. Each one says to the other: you are a disbelieving cursed one, because you have abandoned the Sunnah deliberately and intentionally, and whoever dislikes what Allah has sent down is a disbeliever. So there is great enmity. During the Hajj in these days in Mina, and by Allah, people from the brotherhood of the awareness campaign gather, they came to them and calmed them down and explained that this is not permissible, because this is harm to you, O people of truth, for if some of you declare others to be unbelievers, what will you become before the people of superstitions and the people of innovations? Yes. The one who declares another a disbeliever (...) is himself a disbeliever.

So we say: cooperation has a far-reaching effect. I think you know about the annulment of the document that the Quraysh wrote to boycott the Banu Hashim, how they annulled this document. No one among the people came and annulled it, he could not. But he went to so-and-so and said to him, reproaching him: the Banu Hashim are a people from among you, how are you content that you boycott them until they die of hunger? And he went to another, and a third, and a fourth, until they formed a group and went to this document in the Ka'bah and tore it up [[See the story of the assembly (al-saqifah) in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham (1/376).]]. So cooperation is the foundation of success, as the common people say. And look at the saying of the criminals: they say ﴿two sorcerers who support each other﴾ [al-Qasas 48].

Good. Secondly, among the benefits of the verse: the explanation of the arrogance of these people also in that they did not believe in both matters, and they said: ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in all of it﴾ [al-Qasas 48].

And also among them: what does placing the object first in His saying: ﴿we disbelieve in all of it﴾ indicate? Restriction (hasr), even though they disbelieved in it along with other things. But it has already been said that this restriction is intended to enrage the opponent, as if they are saying: even if we believed in everything, we would only disbelieve in these two. Otherwise it is known that they disbelieve in it and in other things. This is a benefit that few notice: that when a thing is not restricted to this thing but is restricted to it, there must be a purpose. The purpose here is to enrage, as if they are saying: even though we believe in everything, we are disbelievers in what you have brought: ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in all of it﴾.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Then bring a book from Allah that is more guided than both of them, and I will follow it, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Qasas 49].

In this verse, among the benefits: it is part of justice to descend to the level of the opponent to a point he accepts. For it is known that Allah, glorified and exalted, knows that they cannot bring what is demanded of them, or not? When He demanded of them that they bring a book more guided than the Torah and the Qur'an, and Allah knows that they will not bring it, or not? How can He say to the Messenger: ﴿Say: Bring﴾, when He knows it is impossible? This is from the aspect of descending to the opponent to the utmost of justice, as if He made him and his opponent one thing. He says: you bring a book more guided than the Torah and the Qur'an, and I commit to following it. If they do not come with it, then it means they must follow the Torah and the Qur'an, or not? They must do that. That is, since I commit to them that if you bring a book more guided than both, I will follow it, then you must follow what you have found.

So there is in it a descent to the opponent's level, and that this is part of the perfection of justice in debate.

And among the benefits of the verse also: overwhelming the opponent by challenge. If you read the end of Surah al-Tur, you will find in it something remarkable from debate, from His saying: ﴿So remind, for by the grace of your Lord you are not a soothsayer or a madman﴾ [al-Tur 29], up to His saying: ﴿until they meet their Day in which they will be struck senseless﴾ [al-Tur 45]. You will find many etiquettes of debate: ﴿Or do they have a ladder by which they listen?﴾ [al-Tur 38], if that is the case, ﴿then let their listener bring a clear authority﴾ [al-Tur 38]. ﴿Or do they say: he has fabricated it? Rather, they do not believe﴾ [al-Tur 33]. If that is the case, ﴿then let them produce a statement like it, if they are truthful﴾ [al-Tur 34]. So in debate, that is, Allah the Exalted, at the conclusion of the debate, makes the opponent silenced by a challenge to what he cannot do. Here they cannot bring the like of it, so the proof is established against them.

And among the benefits of the verse: that the Torah and the Qur'an are from Allah, so the Qur'an and the Torah are the speech of Allah. But the Qur'an was sent down as revelation, and the Torah was sent down in writing, which Allah wrote on tablets that He threw to Moses.

Among the benefits of the verse also: a person is not obliged to shift from what he is upon to another thing unless what is other is more guided (ahda). For me, for example, it is not obligatory to move from the school of the Hanbalis to the school of the Shafi'is until I see that it is more correct. For He said: "Following is not required except if what they have brought is more guided than it." As for if it is equal, then you do not oblige me, and I do not oblige you if it is equal. The obligation comes when? When what the opponent has brought is more guided than what I am upon. And this is a very important benefit: a person is not obliged to move from what he is upon of a path or school except to one that is more correct, better and more guided than it. As for when they are equal, he is not obliged, nor is he blamed either if he does not move. And likewise, if what is in the other is lower, then by way of greater priority he is not obliged.

So the levels now are three: either what you are called to is lower than what you are upon, or more guided, or equal. If it is more guided, what is the obligation? Following is required. If it is lower, following is prohibited. What remains is: if it is equal, is following required, prohibited, or is the person given a choice?

The scholars say in such a situation: the person is given a choice. They said: and if two scholars issue a legal ruling to him and neither of them is more weighty in his view, then he is given a choice to follow whichever of the two opinions he wishes. And perhaps the ruling of this question is derived from this verse, perhaps it is derived from this verse; because Allah only made following obligatory if it is more guided, and it is known that if it is lower, following is prohibited. So the equal remains neither on the side of prohibition nor on the side of obligation, and this is the level of choice.

Also among the benefits of the verse: the challenge may be by description just as it may be by action. "Then bring" [al-Qasas 49] is a challenge by doing what they are not able to bring. "If you are truthful" [al-Qasas 49] is a challenge by description: if you are among the truthful that what you are upon is true, then bring this; otherwise you are among the liars. And for this reason He said: "Follow it, if you are truthful" [al-Qasas 49].

Allah the Exalted said: "And if they do not respond to you, then know that they only follow their desires. And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people" [al-Qasas 50].

His saying: "And if they do not respond to you" means: if their response to you is nonexistent.

In it: permissibility of conditioning with a condition regarding what is certain to occur. Or did you not understand this?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Meaning, "And if they do not respond to you" — this is a matter certain to occur. Does the one who thinks suppose there is a possibility that they will respond?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: There is none; no one supposes it. So we say: permissibility of conditioning a thing that is certain with a condition, even if it is certain that it will not happen, and likewise even if it is certain that it will happen, for here the non-response is certain to happen without doubt, and yet it was conditioned. And in the hadith the Prophet ﷺ said: "And indeed we, if Allah wills, will be joining you" [(1)], saying it to the people of the graves. So it is known that this matter—?
* Student: Certain.
* The Shaykh: Certain, yes.

Also among its benefits: these deniers of the Messenger ﷺ have no proof except following their desires, due to His saying: "Then know that they only follow their desires" [al-Qasas 50]. And does that meaning mean: so do not argue with them? Because one who follows his desire is stubborn and obstinate; the one who follows his desire is obstinate, you cannot persuade him, as long as he does not seek the truth but wants only to defend himself and follow his desire. So I believe such a man cannot be debated; if you debate him, while he is a person of desire, there is no benefit.

So shall we say: it is derived from this verse that if it is known that the one being debated wants to follow his desire, there is no benefit in arguing with him, because it is a waste of time? Yes, we say so; because He said: "Then know that they only follow their desires," meaning: there is no benefit in arguing with them. So if you have made the truth clear to the person and manifested it by its textual, rational and sensory proofs, as far as the available proofs go, but he insists on remaining upon what he was upon, then know that he is following his desire, and one who follows desire is stubborn; he is not a person seeking guidance, and he cannot benefit.

And for this reason we say in such a situation: it is not obligatory upon a person to argue with him; rather he moves to something else, which is to punish him: "And do not argue with the People of the Book except in a way that is best, except those of them who have wronged" [al-Ankabut 46]. The obstinate person is other than one who wants to follow the truth but it has not become manifest to him; the obstinate has his own state. And Allah the Exalted said: "So remind, if the reminder benefits" [al-A'la 9], meaning: and if it does not benefit, then do not remind. And this has been discussed before: is this condition to have an implication (mafhum) or not?
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, (...) as long as you argued in front of people and the truth became clear, it does not mean that he speaks falsehood and you remain silent; because if you do not hear him speaking falsehood, people must know the truth and change this falsehood. But if you argued with him in front of people and the truth was made clear and he refused, you have nothing more; there is no benefit in arguing with him.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, in any case we do not say: argue in front of people; but sometimes the argument happens in front of people, you are with people in a gathering and research begins and discussion takes place. Do we say that you should remain silent and leave this man? No, you must resist with what you have. Yes. Likewise, if you hear him, for example, speaking in an assembly and establishing falsehood, you must speak the truth. Yes indeed.

Among the benefits of the verse: people differ in misguidance; that people differ in going astray, so they are not equal in misguidance, just as they are not equal in guidance, and not equal in error, and not equal in rectitude. Or no? Are people equal in these matters?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: No. For this reason He said: "And who is more astray than one who follows..." [al-Qasas 50]. In this is evidence that people vary in misguidance, but there is no one more astray than this one who followed his desire without guidance from Allah.

Also among the benefits of the verse: that desire may agree with guidance. From where do we take it?
* Student: "His desire without guidance."
* The Shaykh: "His desire without guidance from Allah" [al-Qasas 50]. As for one who follows his desire based on guidance from Allah, this is good: that his desire follows what the truth has brought; this is good. We have mentioned to you the hadith narrated from the Prophet ﷺ: "None of you believes until his desire is subordinate to what I have brought" [(2)]. So the conclusion is that the blameworthy desire is that which is not upon guidance.

Good. Also among the benefits of the verse: that the wrongdoer has exposed himself to being deprived of guidance; or if you wish, say: wrongdoing is a cause for the wrongdoer's deprivation of guidance; due to His saying: "Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people" [al-Qasas 50]. So the wrongdoer is the one who deprived himself of guidance.

(...)
As for His saying: "Indeed, Allah does not guide," the Qadariyya hold that a person can be guided by himself, and Allah the Blessed and Exalted has no authority over him at all, because they—may Allah protect us—are the Qadariyya. And what do they say concerning the decree of Allah?
* Student: That the matter is "unprecedented" (anf).
* The Shaykh: Yes, that the matter is unprecedented, meaning that Allah did not decree the actions of the servants, and I act and leave by my pure, absolute choice, and Allah has no will, no creation, nor anything in it. But "Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people" [al-Qasas 50] refutes them, just as it also refutes the Jahmiyya Jabriyya who say compulsion; because Allah the Exalted attributed these people—by their action—to wrongdoing, and if they were compelled to it, attributing wrongdoing to them would be wrong, and Allah the Blessed and Exalted does not wrong anyone.

So in the verse there is a refutation of the Qadariyya, and a refutation of whom? A refutation of the Jabriyya; and the Jabriyya are Jahmiyya; that is, the Jahmiyya's doctrine is compulsion, and among them are three "jeems," as Ibn al-Qayyim said in the Nuniyya: "The Jahmiyya have three jeems, all of them jeems of blame: what are they? Jabr (compulsion), Irja' (postponement), and the jeem of tajahhum." So they are Jabriyya, Murji'a, Jahmiyya. Yes, may Allah suffice you against the evil of the three jeems. Yes: the Jahmiyya, the Jabriyya and the Murji'a.

* In any case, in the noble verse there is a refutation of the two misguided groups: the Qadariyya and the Jabriyya. The Qadariyya deny Allah's decree regarding the actions of the servant, and the Jabriyya are the opposite.

"Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people."

* Also among the benefits of the verse: whoever seeks justice has exposed himself to guidance, because wrongdoing's opposite is justice, and the negation of guidance by the attribute of wrongdoing requires the affirmation of guidance by the attribute of justice. So whoever seeks justice is granted guidance; justice is a cause of guidance. Likewise, everyone who seeks good—though may Allah grant us success in seeking it—everyone who seeks good is granted it if the intention is sincere and the resolve is firm.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: They say: the person has an independent will in which Allah has no part; Allah has no part in it at all. (...)
