**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 28, verses 51–54 (part 3 of 4):**

* The Shaykh: For weakness. Repelling an evil deed with a good one is praiseworthy when it stems from strength. But if it stems from weakness, it is not praiseworthy. Suppose a highway robber comes to someone and says, "Come on, give me your clothes." He replies, "I'll give you my clothes and the stick I have on the camel!" What would happen then? Or suppose he says, "Come on, give me the camel's saddle," and he replies, "Wait, wait, let me take care of it for you so you don't get tired. I'll unload it and put it on your camel." Is this good or not?
* Student: No, it is not good.
* The Shaykh: It is not good. This is weakness. For this reason the Messenger (ﷺ), when a man asked him about someone who comes to take his property, said: "Do not give it to him." The man said: "What if he fights me?" He said: "Fight him."[[Narrated by Muslim (140/225) from Abu Hurayrah.]] The point is that we say: ﴿and they repel evil with good﴾. (Some say it refers to) them. The correct view is to make it more general. So ﴿and they repel evil with good﴾ [Al-Qasas 54] applies to them in their dealings with Allah, and to others in their dealings with whom? With creation.

He says: (﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ [Al-Qasas 54], meaning they give in charity.) They also give gifts. They are not necessarily obliged to give charity, because a gift may be praiseworthy when its purpose is to create affection: "Exchange gifts, and you will love one another." Is it "tahādū" or "tahādaw"?
* Student: "Tahādū."
* Student: "Tahādaw."
* The Shaykh: Good. Does one say "tahādā al-rajulān, yatahādayān" (the two men exchanged gifts)?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Then it is "Tahādaw tahābbū."[[Narrated by Ahmad (9250) from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

Now, the point is that His saying ﴿and from what We have provided them﴾ [Al-Qasas 54]: ﴿provided them﴾ means "given them." So provision (rizq) means giving. From this is His saying: ﴿And when the division is attended by relatives, orphans and the needy, give them from it﴾ [An-Nisa 8], meaning, give them. So rizq means giving.

As for His saying ﴿from what We have provided them﴾, is "min" here for specifying the kind (bayān al-jins) or for partiality (tab'īd)?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It is better to take it as specifying the kind, because at times spending all of one's wealth is praiseworthy. The Prophet (ﷺ) once urged people to give charity, and 'Umar said: "Today I will outdo Abu Bakr." So he brought half of his wealth. But did Abu Bakr come?
* Student: With all of his wealth.
* The Shaykh: With all of his wealth.[[Narrated by Ahmad in Fada'il al-Sahabah (527) from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.]] So if we take "min" as specifying the kind, then the spending is better. What does (...) include?
* Student: Giving away all of one's wealth.
* The Shaykh: It includes giving away all of one's wealth or part of it. That is, it may be good to give all of it, and it may be good to give part of it, depending on the situation in which one spends. So "min" is better taken as specifying the kind.

As for His saying ﴿they spend﴾ [Al-Qasas 54], spending here means giving, not specifically charity. What led the author (al-Mu'allif) to restrict it to charity is that the context is one of praise. But it is better to keep it general, so that ﴿they spend﴾ means they give and bestow, because giving may be charity, and it may also be giving out of affection, which is also good, and in some situations may be better than charity. Accordingly, we say that it is better to understand spending as giving and bestowing, whether it is charity, a gift, or a present. You know the difference among these three. What is the difference between a bestowal (hibah), a gift (hadiyyah), and charity (sadaqah)?
* Student: A gift (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, and charity is given to someone.
* Student: Charity is given to...
* The Shaykh: To a person.
* Student: To (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: A gift.
* The Shaykh: And a bestowal?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: And a bestowal? Who knows the difference among the three?
* Student: A gift is giving to someone who is equal or a brother, with the intention of showing affection and drawing closer. Charity is giving to someone lower in status, with the intention of spending for Allah.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: As for...
* The Shaykh: Bestowal.
* Student: Bestowal is giving to an equal, meaning not to someone inferior, with the intention of giving.
* The Shaykh: No. The difference between them is this: charity is what is intended for the face of Allah, by which one draws closer to Allah, and the giver does not care whether the recipient is closer to him or not. A gift is what is intended to create affection for the recipient, meaning one wants to draw close to the one receiving it, and for the recipient to draw close to him. A bestowal (hibah) is what is intended only for the benefit of the one who receives it. One does not intend by it to draw close to this recipient, nor to draw close to Allah through it. One intends its benefit to him. This is called a hibah. All of them are praiseworthy in reality, but is some of them better than others? This depends on the situation.

﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ [Al-Qasas 54], and so on to the end.
* Student: The preference in the school of the Basrans regarding the figurative use of a verb?
* The Shaykh: Because it implies two meanings: the meaning of (...) the verb is present, and the meaning of (...). The other (the simple verb with a preposition) implies only one meaning, which is changing the meaning of the particle to the new meaning.
* Student: Shaykh, is this not sufficient (...)?
* The Shaykh: No. Adding a meaning is without doubt better, adding a meaning is a benefit.
* Student: We have one verb.
* The Shaykh: That does not contradict it. One verb absorbs the meaning of a second verb which takes this particle. (...) When the sentence indicates two meanings, it is more complete than when it indicates one.
* Student: In a case like ﴿a spring from which the servants drink﴾ [Al-Insan 6], we do not have "ri" (quenching thirst). We say only "drink."
* The Shaykh: Yes, but its origin is drinking, which may be drinking that does not quench the servant's thirst.
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And it may be drinking that quenches his thirst.
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: The people of Hell drink boiling water like thirsty camels and are not satisfied. What is the benefit of drinking then? But these ones drink from this spring and are satisfied by it. So now it implies the meaning of drinking and the meaning of quenching thirst. How do we understand the meaning of quenching thirst? From the verb being followed by the particle that fits quenching thirst.
* Student: Is it not better that the verb is followed by (...)?
* The Shaykh: What? This is most suitable, because drinking fits with quenching thirst. It does not fit with being full, for example. You cannot say ﴿drink with it﴾ meaning "be filled with it." That is not appropriate.
* Student: It is objected that it is not determined. We had mentioned...
* The Shaykh: No. The objection is answered by saying that it is determined by the context, and a verb must be assumed that fits the second verb, such as being its cause or branching from it, or something similar (...). The point is that the implication indicates two meanings, while the particle indicates one meaning only.
* Student: ﴿So you will drink like thirsty camels﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah 55]. What does it mean?
* The Shaykh: ﴿Al-Hīm﴾ are thirsty camels.
* Student: Not (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, it is water.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No. Thirst (al-hiyām) is of two kinds: thirst for food and thirst for drink.
* Student: Does the thirsty one get quenched?
* The Shaykh: No, whether he is quenched or not. (...) The one who drinks and is not quenched, what is he? Healthy or sick? The one who drinks and is not quenched, is he healthy or sick?
* Student: No, he is sick.
* The Shaykh: This one, yes.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes. (...) The Noble Qur'an. Some of the common people object to some questioners who ask: "Grant me a riyal," and say: "This is polytheism, may Allah protect us!" Yes, (...). Provision (rizq) means giving. (...)

* * *

* From this is derived that Allah, glorified and exalted, did not leave the earth without revelation, because "tawṣīl" means connecting one thing to another.
* And from it is derived that revelation contains the utmost clarity, because we said that "waṣṣala" implies the meaning of "bayyana" (to make clear).
* And from it is derived the manifestation of Allah's blessing upon this Ummah by conveying the word to them: ﴿And We have certainly conveyed to them﴾ [Al-Qasas 51].
* And from it, also, is derived that the wisdom behind revelation is remembrance and admonition, due to His saying: ﴿so that they may remember﴾ [Al-Qasas 51].
* And from it is derived the affirmation of causation (ʿillah) in Allah's cosmic and legislative rulings, and that He does nothing and legislates nothing except for a wisdom.
* We said: from it is derived the rationale of Allah's actions and His cosmic and legislative rulings. Who disagreed with this?
* Student: The Ash'arites.
* The Shaykh: And others? The Jahmiyyah are the origin. They said: Allah's actions are not to be given a reason, and His rulings are not to be given a reason.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture before it, they believe in it﴾ [Al-Qasas 52].

* From this is derived, first, that among the Jews and Christians there are those who believed in the Qur'an, due to His saying: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture before it, they believe in it﴾.
* And from it is also derived that the ruling on an individual may apply to his entire category. What is the meaning of this? The meaning is: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture before it﴾. If we look at it, we find that it is general, including all who were given the Scripture. But are they all general? Did all of those who were given the Scripture before believe in the Qur'an? Not at all. There were Christians who remained Christians, and Jews who remained Jews, but among them were those who believed. This means that we have given the category the ruling of an individual. Or did you not understand this? It is as if it is said: the faith of 'Abdullah ibn Salam and the faith of al-Najashi, for example, is (...). It is not that this one is named 'Abdullah ibn Salam and that one is named al-Najashi. Rather, because they were given the Scripture, they believed, not because of their names, but because of what they knew from their books, that the Messenger (ﷺ) would be sent. This requires that the whole category should be believers, even if they did not all believe.
* The point is that from this verse is derived the principle of giving the category the ruling of the individual, as long as the cause of this ruling encompasses the whole category. For example, what was the cause of 'Abdullah ibn Salam's faith? His knowledge of the attributes of the Messenger (ﷺ) in the Torah. Is this knowledge specific to him, or does it include all the Jews? It includes all the Jews. So here we have given the category the ruling of the individual, because of the cause that encompasses him and others. Otherwise, someone might say: we do not see that those to whom We gave the Scripture before it believe in it, since not all of them believed. But we say: only some of them believed, yet this faith among some of them was driven by a cause that encompasses the whole category.
* So we derive from this: we give the category the ruling of the individual when the cause of this ruling encompasses all. When the cause of this ruling encompasses all, the category is given the ruling of the individual.
* From this verse is also derived the great praise of those who believed in the Qur'an and the earlier books, due to His saying: ﴿they believe in it﴾.
* And from it is derived that the attributes of the Prophet (ﷺ) are present in the earlier books: the Torah and the Gospel. This is clear in the verse of al-A'raf, in His saying: ﴿whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, who enjoins them what is right...﴾ and so on to the end [Al-A'raf 157].

Then He said: ﴿And when it is recited to them, they say, "We believe in it. Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed, we were Muslims before it."﴾ [Al-Qasas 53].

* From this verse is also derived: increased praise for these people, that they believe in everything that is recited to them. They did not believe in the Qur'an merely as a whole, but in its entirety and in its details. We derive this from His saying: ﴿And when it is recited﴾. The verb ﴿is recited﴾ is in the present tense, which indicates occurrence and continuity. Yes, it indicates renewal and occurrence, and that this is their characteristic whenever it is recited to them.
* And also from the noble verses is derived that they believed not merely out of desire, but believed with a faith based on conviction. From where is this taken? From their saying: ﴿We believe in it. Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord﴾. They did not believe simply by following others, but believed out of conviction: ﴿Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord﴾.
* And from it is also derived that the Qur'an is from Allah, due to His saying: ﴿from our Lord﴾.
* And from it is derived the perfection of the intellect of those who believed, in that they expressed it with reference to lordship (rubūbiyyah): ﴿from our Lord﴾, rather than divinity (ulūhiyyah), because the context requires that. For the Lord has authority to judge as He wills, both in cosmic and legislative matters.
* And from this is also derived that these people were believers, Muslims, submitting to the earlier books, due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, we were Muslims before it﴾.
* And from it is derived the permissibility of a person praising himself with praiseworthy attributes, on condition that there is a benefit in it, and that it does not involve boasting or superiority over others. This is due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, we were Muslims before it﴾. This is something that actually occurred from the Prophet (ﷺ), from the Companions, and from the scholars. The Prophet (ﷺ) said:
«I am the Prophet, no lie, I am the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib.»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4315) and Muslim (1776/78) from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib.]]
And Ibn Mas'ud said: "If I knew that anyone whom the camels could reach had more knowledge of the Book of Allah than I, I would go to him."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5002) and Muslim (2463/115).]] This is praise of himself, but for a benefit. Scholars, whenever they write a book, praise it with the attributes of praise that the book warrants. It is well known that praising the book is praising its author. If you praised this building and said, "Masha Allah, this is a good, sturdy and beautiful building," whom have you actually praised? You have praised the builder. Yes, the builder. So this matter is permissible for a person: he may praise himself with attributes of praise, on condition that he does not intend by it to boast over others, and the second condition is that there be a benefit in it. As for the first condition, its reason is clear: if he intends by it boasting and superiority over people, then this intention is forbidden. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: «I am the master of the children of Adam on the Day of Resurrection, and I say this without boasting.»[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (3148) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

Likewise, the condition that there be a benefit: if there is no benefit in it, it is idle talk, at the very least. It is idle talk because why would a person praise himself without a benefit? Only if he wants to display his qualities so that he can boast about them over others would he do it. Even if he says, "I do not want boasting," we say: then why?

* * *

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice, for what they patiently endured, and they repel evil with good, and from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ [Al-Qasas 54].
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Their benefit is that it urges them to take from it.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: But, all right, if we have shown that he memorizes such-and-such, then I, for example, may not have these things, so I strive for them. Or I know, for example, that he has memorized more than I have, so I refer to him for questions. The point is that scholars, especially those known for virtue, are not believed to want merely to display their praiseworthy qualities. That meaning is not sound at all. Rather, they intend a benefit, and this benefit differs according to circumstances.
* Student: So, Shaykh, do we not say that the default is (...)?
* The Shaykh: No. We say the default is that this is idle talk, since there is no benefit in it. The Messenger (ﷺ) said: «Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say what is good or remain silent.»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6018) and Muslim (47/74) from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] So as long as there is no good in it... Furthermore, it leads to harm, because even if we suppose that this man, one hundred percent, did not intend boasting, he opens a door for others, a door through which others will boast about it.

And His saying, exalted: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice, for what they patiently endured, and they repel evil with good, and from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ [Al-Qasas 54].
* From this noble verse is derived: that the People of the Book who believe have two rewards. The first reward is for believing in their own Scripture, and the second is for believing in the Qur'an.

Among its benefits: the affirmation of Allah's justice, exalted is He, in that He does not waste their first reward by means of the second, nor their second reward by means of the first.

It is also derived from this that reward is in proportion to deeds: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it. And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [Az-Zalzalah 7–8]. These people had their reward doubled, because they did what?
Student: Twice.
Shaykh: Twice.

Among the benefits of the verse also: the affirmation of causes and reasons, due to His saying: ﴿because they were patient﴾.

Among its benefits: the virtue of patience (ṣabr). Since patience is a cause of reward, it is undoubtedly a praiseworthy and excellent attribute. Yes, and I think we mentioned in the tafsir (exegesis) that patience is divided into three categories:
Student: Patience in obedience to Allah, patience in refraining from disobedience to Allah, and patience in the painful decrees of Allah.
Shaykh: The painful decrees, and the best of them is the first, then the second, then the third.

It is also derived from it: that good deeds wipe out bad deeds, due to His saying: ﴿and they repel evil with good﴾.

Among its benefits also: that one should repay the wrongdoer with kindness. The verse, as we said, is general: it covers their repelling their own evil deeds with their good deeds, and their repelling the evil deeds of others by doing good to them, and we brought evidence for that from the Qur'an. But this repelling is heavy upon a person, and repelling the evil of others by doing good to them is very heavy upon a person. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿None is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 35]. Most people say: "By Allah, I will give him a sa' for a sa', and a slap for a slap, two for one!" But the matter is not like that. ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾. What is the result? ﴿Then the one between you and him is enmity will become as though he was a devoted friend﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 34]. Note that He used ("idhā") of sudden occurrence, to indicate that this matter changes quickly: this enemy quickly becomes as though he were a close, devoted friend to you.

So we say: what is derived from it? That good deeds wipe out bad deeds, and that one should repay offense with kindness. However, we have mentioned that this should not be a display of weakness in a person. If it is a display of weakness in a person, then it is not appropriate, because Allah says: ﴿And whoever retaliates after being wronged, those, there is no blame upon them﴾ [Ash-Shūrā 41].
Student: Even if he is a sinner (fāsiq)?
Shaykh: Yes, even if he is a sinner. This is with regard to your own personal right.
Student: Yes.
Shaykh: As for the right of Allah, no. He is dealt with according to what the Sharia (sacred law) requires.
Student: (...)?
Shaykh: With regard to (...): ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds﴾ [Hūd 114].
Student: (...)?
Shaykh: Yes, perhaps evil deeds may wipe out good deeds by way of counterbalancing, because good and evil deeds are weighed on the Day of Resurrection. Whichever of them outweighs, the ruling belongs to it.

Also derived from this verse: the virtue of spending from the provision of Allah: ﴿and from what We have provided them﴾.

Also derived from it: the one who spends has not spent from what he made or earned by himself, but he spends from what? From the provision of Allah. Allah is the One who provided for you, and He is the One who commanded you. You are, in reality, a servant, a slave who acts according to the command of his master. He told you to earn, so you earned; He told you to spend, so you spent.

Now, as for His saying: ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 54], how do we reconcile what is here with His description of the servants of the Most Merciful: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever, between that, justly moderate﴾ [al-Furqān 67], and with His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched﴾ [al-Isrā' 29]?

We say: we reconcile them by saying that the general state of people is not to spend all their wealth, because spending all of one's wealth may harm him. But at times, spending all of one's wealth is praiseworthy. Therefore He said: ﴿do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾, meaning do not spend at all; ﴿nor extend it fully outstretched﴾, meaning do not spend everything you have. But other texts indicate that the matter is based on what? On the ruling changing with changing circumstances. It may be, for example, that spending all of one's wealth is best, and it may be that keeping some of it is better.

Also derived from the noble verse, His saying ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾: spending from the provision of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, is praiseworthy. Provision (rizq), as we learned in the chapter on creed ('aqīdah), is what benefits from the lawful and its opposite. And what is its opposite? The unlawful. So is a person praised if he spends from the unlawful? No, because he is not rewarded for it, and what is obligatory upon him is to return the thing and rid himself of it. That is what is obligatory upon him. But what is meant here is the provision from which spending is praised when it is lawful provision. As for the one who earned something unlawful, the Prophet (ﷺ) informed that if he spends it, it will not be blessed for him; if he gives it in charity, it will not be accepted from him; and if he leaves it behind, it will be his provision to the Fire. This shows that spending from what is forbidden does not benefit a person. But it benefits him when? If he spends it wanting to be rid of it, then it benefits him in the sense that none of its consequences will befall him, and it benefits him because spending it to be rid of it is repentance, and repentance benefits the servant. For example: if a person has a hundred thousand dirhams earned unlawfully and he spends it to be rid of it, does he receive the reward of one who gives charity from it? No. But he receives a reward for repenting from this sin he committed. As for what (...). But if he earned it lawfully and spent it, he is given reward according to its amount, and in proportion to the multiplication mentioned in the text.

* * *

Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And when they hear vain talk﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 55].
Student: (...)?
Shaykh: If... it does not benefit the person, because the one who is incapable leaves something due to his inability to do it. So what is the station of (...)? That is why Allah said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning and Competent﴾ [an-Nisā' 149]. He praised Himself for pardoning while having the power to retaliate. As for one who pardons out of incapacity, what is the benefit? For example, someone is struck by a soldier and he cannot confront the soldier, so he says: "(...) may Allah reward you with good, may Allah be good to you." Yes, we say this is one who is incapable. But if someone strikes him who is (...), what does he do to him? Perhaps he gives back a sa' for a sa' twice over.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 51–54 (part 1 of 4):

﴿And We have certainly conveyed to them the word, that they may remember.﴾ [Al-Qasas: 51].
﴿Wassalna﴾ comes from tawsil (conveying), and its root letters are (w-s-l). Reaching a thing (wusul) means arriving at its goal. The meaning is that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, emphasizes in this sentence with three particles: the oath, the lam, and (qad), that He has indeed conveyed the word to them.
As for His saying ﴿wassalna lahum﴾: it is well known that (wasala) takes (ila) (to), as one says (wasala ilayhi), and one says (awsala ilayhi), which is the common usage. Here it is followed by the lam, and its transitivity with the lam is because it includes the meaning of arrival and clarification. For this reason the author said in explaining it: (We made it clear to them).
It has already passed with us that the Arabic language sometimes makes a verb transitive, or, more generally, makes a governing word transitive by means other than what it normally takes. Why? We have mentioned that the grammarians have two approaches to this: the first approach: figurative use through the particle, and the second approach: figurative use through the verb.
For example, here is the clearest example for you, the saying of the Exalted: ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾ [Al-Insan: 6]. Is the spring drunk "with it" or "from it"?
* Student: From it.
* Shaykh: It is drunk from it. The thing that is drunk with is a vessel, yes. But the spring is drunk from; and in the noble verse Allah said: ﴿yashrabu biha﴾. It is known that the verb here is made transitive by other than what it normally takes. Some grammarians said: the figurative use is in the particle, and the ba' has the meaning of (min) (from), so it is partitive.
Some other grammarians said: rather, the figurative use is in the verb (yashrabu), and it has been made to include the meaning of (rawiya, yarwa) (to be quenched/satisfied), so the meaning of ﴿yashrabu biha﴾ is: they are quenched by it when they drink from it. In reality, this is (...) the school of the Basrans, who hold that this is figurative use, and that it is expressed as figurative use in agreement with them.
So here we say: ﴿wassalna lahum﴾. It is well known that (wasala) or (wassala) takes what? (Wasala) takes what, which preposition?
* Student: It takes (ila).
* Shaykh: (Ila). Here it is followed by the lam. So we say: either the lam has the meaning of (ila), or we make (wassala) include a meaning?
* Student: Clarification.
* Shaykh: Clarification: including the meaning of clarification. The meaning: ﴿wassalna﴾ to them by clarification.
﴿wassalna lahumu al-qawl﴾: (al-qawl) the author says is (the Qur'an). Perhaps it is more general than what the author said, and that the intended "word" is our word, yes. Allah, exalted is He, continually sends down to His servants, from His word and revelation, that which sets their affairs right.
I say: Allah, exalted is He, has continually conveyed the word, which is revelation, to His servants, until it reached Muhammad ﷺ, the Qur'an.
﴿And We have certainly conveyed to them the word, that they may remember﴾ [Al-Qasas: 51], meaning: We did not neglect them, rather Our words have continually reached creation and made things clear to them, ﴿that they may remember﴾.
(Li'allahum) here is for causation, or for the purpose that they may remember. Remembrance means recalling a thing, but not mere recalling; rather, being admonished by it. For this reason the author, may Allah have mercy on him, always explains (yatadhakkarun) by its necessary consequence, which is being admonished. Otherwise, the basic sense of tadhakkur (I remembered the thing) is that I was mindful of it. But there is a necessary consequence, which is admonition. As for mere recall without admonition, this does not benefit. The author says: (they are admonished), meaning the admonition and the word affect them, (so they believe).
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book﴾ [Al-Qasas: 52]. ﴿Atainahum﴾ means gave. Is the giving here legislative or decreed? Legislative: a legislative giving. It may also be a decreed giving, meaning We decreed that the Book, which is revelation, would come to them, and it came to them.
As for His saying ﴿al-kitab﴾, it means the written thing, and what is intended is the Torah, and likewise the Gospel; the Torah and the Gospel are both called a book.
As for His saying ﴿min qablihi﴾: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, ﴿We gave them the Book before it﴾, meaning: before the Qur'an.
﴿Hum﴾: meaning those whom We gave.
﴿bihi﴾: (meaning: with the Qur'an).
﴿yu'minun﴾: meaning they affirm and submit to it.
The parsing now: the pronoun is the subject of ﴿Alladhina atainahumu al-kitab﴾, the clause ﴿atainahum﴾ is the relative clause, ﴿hum﴾ is a second subject, and ﴿bihi yu'minun﴾ is the predicate of the second subject. The clause consisting of the second subject and its predicate is the predicate of the first subject. Begin with it?
* Student: ﴿Hum﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, correct.
﴿Hum bihi yu'minun﴾ [Al-Qasas: 52]. The clause consisting of the second subject and its predicate is the predicate of the first subject. The benefit of repeating the subject is so that the attribution is doubled: as if the attribution of belief to them is stated twice, once by the pronoun ﴿hum﴾ and once by the first subject ﴿alladhina﴾. What is (...)?
* Student: Yes indeed.
* Shaykh: Good. ﴿Hum bihi﴾ and he brought ﴿yu'minun﴾ in the present tense, which indicates continuity, signaling that they received it with acceptance and submission, and that they still remain on this matter. This sentence, in relation to what precedes it, is in meaning like an evidence against those who denied the Qur'an. It is as if he says: "Those given the Book before you believed in the Qur'an", which indicates what? That it is true or false? That it is true; for they, although they are People of the Book, abandoned their book and believed in the Qur'an, while you are people of ignorance without a book, so it was right for you to be before them in belief, because it is difficult for a person to move from his book or his religion to another religion, but it is not difficult for a person to move from ignorance to truth and knowledge.
Furthermore, in this there is also a rebuke to those people, and also evidence that it is true, because those given the Book believed in it only with knowledge, and so it is. There is no doubt that the Prophet ﷺ was written about among the Children of Israel in the Torah and the Gospel: ﴿They recognize him as they recognize their own sons﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 146]. Even his physical attributes are present among them, setting aside his method and conduct: ﴿He enjoins on them what is right and forbids them what is wrong, makes lawful for them the good things and prohibits for them the evil, and relieves them of their burdens and the shackles that were upon them﴾ [Al-A'raf: 157]. All of this is present and known in the Torah and the Gospel. For this reason the Jews gathered in Medina so that they would receive this Prophet whose description they found among them and believe. ﴿And they had been, before, seeking victory over those who disbelieved﴾, as Allah the Exalted said, meaning seeking victory against them through this Prophet. ﴿But when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 89].
So the summary is that in this verse, I say, its connection with what precedes it is in two respects:
The first respect: a rebuke to these ignorant people for disbelieving in Muhammad ﷺ, even though the People of the Book, who were upon a religion, moved from their religion to his, so you were more deserving of following him.
The second respect: it is an evidence for the truth of what the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, brought, because those who have knowledge from the Book only moved from it on knowledge that it is true. So the connection with the texts before it is very clear.
There is also no doubt that in this verse there is praise of those among the People of the Book who believed in the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him; for this reason ﴿hum bihi yu'minun﴾, so they did not act arrogantly toward it despite having their own book.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, I mean the verse ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾ [Al-Qasas: 52] (...).
* Student: Then, O Shaykh, why did he not say (...)?
* Shaykh: (...) for the genus, it negates the saying, (...) this Book (...) He says: ﴿No warner came to them before you﴾ [Al-Qasas: 46], yes?
* Student: Nor a prohibition?
* Shaykh: Nor a prohibition, nor a negation. But this is in the category of the genus, meaning that We did not leave them, rather the word reached them as it reached others, just as we said in its explanation: that Allah, exalted is He, continually sends down books to those before.
He says: (also). What is the meaning of (also)? (﴿They believe in it also﴾)? What is the meaning of (also)?
* Student: That is, likewise.
* Student: That is, those after them.
* Shaykh: That is, just as they believed in their books. And (also) they say is one of the nouns that are necessarily in the accusative as a verbal noun, because its verb is (ada, ya'iidu, aydan), like (baa'a, yabee'u, bay'an), and its meaning is "returned". Yes. So the meaning is: they too believe in the Qur'an. The author said: (It was revealed concerning a group of Jews who embraced Islam, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and others, and of Christians who came from Abyssinia and from Syria), and likewise from other than Syria.
(Among the Jews who embraced Islam was Abdullah ibn Salam.) Abdullah ibn Salam is famous for Islam, and he was from the Jews, because he was a rabbi among the rabbis of the Jews, and as the Jews themselves said about him in the presence of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: he is the best of them and the son of the best of them, their master and the son of their master [Reported by al-Bukhari (4480) from the hadith of Anas], acknowledging his virtue, knowledge and leadership. For this reason they used to cite him as an example. For such a man, O people, who is a master among his people, leadership may carry him to (...), and love of leadership may also lead him to not follow others, because if he follows another he becomes subordinate rather than leader, right? But he, may Allah be pleased with him, (...) humbled himself to the truth, so he believed in the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him.
The story of his faith is well known. The Messenger hid him, summoned the Jews, and asked them about him, and they praised him. He asked them about the message of the Messenger, and they denied the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. So he said to them: "What is your opinion if Abdullah ibn Salam embraced Islam?" They said: God forbid, he will not embrace it, for he is among their best. So he came out and said: I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. Then they came out only speaking ill of him, because he had embraced Islam [Reported by al-Bukhari (4480) from the hadith of Anas].
Likewise it was revealed concerning (a group of Christians who came from Abyssinia). I do not know an example of this; do you know an example? Christians came from Najran and embraced Islam, and concerning them was revealed: ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflow with tears﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 83]. But it is known that some Christians embraced Islam in Abyssinia, such as the Negus, who embraced Islam and entered the religion of Islam while he was upon Christianity. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, described him as a brother to the Companions and a righteous man, and he was so, meaning: a brother to them and a righteous man.
So in any case, what concerns us is not the identities of those who embraced Islam; the important point is that among those given the Book, Jews and Christians, there are people who believed in the Qur'an as well.
﴿And when it is recited to them﴾, the Qur'an, ﴿they say: We believe in it﴾ [Al-Qasas: 53].
Masha'Allah. "And when it is recited to them, they say": (idha), as we know, is conditional, and the response of the condition is directly connected to its verb, or not?
* Student: To the verb of the condition.
* Shaykh: Yes, to the verb of the condition. The response of the condition is directly connected to its verb, or not?
* Student: ﴿Yutla alayhim qalu﴾.
* Shaykh: Let me ask you: is this a general rule, that the response of the condition is directly connected to its verb?
* Student: It is not necessary.
* Shaykh: Meaning that whenever the verb of the condition exists, its response exists; this does not mean verbal adjacency, but occurrential connection: when the condition exists, the conditioned exists. Do you follow? And of course it depends on the situation; it does not mean it must be immediate, it may even be in the future. Here he says: ﴿And when it is recited to them, they say: We believe in it﴾ [Al-Qasas: 53]. He did not say (idhautliya), so that means any verse recited to them, they say: We believe in it. They did not believe in the Qur'an as a whole only; they believed in the Qur'an in detail, because the present tense verb indicates what? It indicates continuity. So whenever a verse was recited to them, they believed in it, and it increased them in faith.
﴿And when it is recited to them﴾, meaning it is read to them, ﴿they say: We believe in it﴾, with hesitation, doubt and reflection, or do they immediately believe?
* Student: They believe immediately.
* Shaykh: Immediately; because we said that the response of the condition directly follows the verb of the condition: "And when it is recited, they say: We believe in it", meaning in what was recited to them of the Qur'an, whether little or much.
Then they explained that their belief is from conviction and on a basis: ﴿Indeed it is the truth from our Lord﴾ [Al-Qasas: 53]. ﴿Innahu﴾ means what was recited to them of the Qur'an, ﴿al-haqq﴾ means the established thing, the real, the true in report, the just in judgment.
Their saying ﴿min rabbina﴾, and not "from Allah," because the Lord is the one who has absolute disposal, for He disposes of His servants legislatively; and what else?
* Student: And by decree.
* Shaykh: And by decree; He disposes of them legislatively and by decree. So it is as if they say: our Lord will not leave us without sending down the Qur'an, and He has absolute authority and disposal, cosmic and legislative.
Their saying ﴿min rabbina﴾ indicates that they, may Allah be pleased with them, take pride in their attribution to Allah: ﴿from our Lord﴾.
As for His saying ﴿Indeed it is the truth from our Lord﴾, the clause in terms of meaning, what is its position relative to what precedes it?
* Student: Causal.
* Shaykh: Causal: meaning, "We believe in it" not because its beauty, eloquence and rhetoric impressed us, but we believed in it because it is the truth from our Lord.
If someone says: if (innahu) is causal, why is the hamza not opened: that it is ﴿the truth from our Lord﴾?
Because a causal clause is on the presumption of the lam, and when the lam is joined to (inna), the hamza of it must be opened, so you say: li-anna dhalika kadha (because that is so), and you do not say: li-inna dhalika kadha. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful that they will return to their Lord﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 60], and He did not say: innahum ila rabbihim. So here, why was it not causal?
We said: a causal clause may be causal only in meaning, meaning it is considered only for its meaning, and it may be causal where both the wording and the meaning are considered. If both wording and meaning are considered, the hamza is opened, because it is on the presumption of the lam; and if only the meaning is considered, the hamza is kept. Here what was considered?
* Student: The meaning.
* Shaykh: The meaning only; only the meaning was considered. And which is preferable, considering the meaning or considering the wording? We say: each situation has its own speech. The benefit of considering the meaning is that the clause is, in terms of wording, detached from what precedes it, as if it were an independent declarative sentence, and as if detached from the wording; but the causal sense is derived from the context.
As for the verbal causal, it is connected to what precedes it. And if you want something that clarifies this, read the words of Ibn Malik: (so kasr in the beginning), this is the difference between a causal clause intended for both wording and meaning, and one intended for meaning only.
﴿InnA kunna min qablihi muslimin﴾ [Al-Qasas: 53], before what?
Before the Qur'an, ﴿Inna kunna min qablihi﴾, meaning: before the Qur'an.
﴿Muslimin﴾: the author said: (monotheists). Although if he had explained Islam by its apparent meaning, it would have been better, because Islam means submission and compliance, and its origin is from the absence of opposition and warfare; for this reason one says: al-silm and al-Islam, meaning non-opposition and non-warfare.
So the phrase ﴿min qablihi muslimin﴾ means: compliant, submitting to the truth.

**Ibn 'Uthaymin's commentary (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 28, verses 51–54 (part 2 of 4):**

Their saying, ﴿Indeed we were Muslims before it﴾, does not definitely mean boasting or self-admiration over their deeds, because the context is one of praise. Rather, it means praising Allah for what they were upon in both states: the earlier state and the later state. In the later state, ﴿when it is recited to them, they say, "We believe in it"﴾ [al-Qasas 53]. In the earlier state, they were ﴿Muslims﴾, submissive and following the Messenger who came to them.

Alright, what is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ﴿مُسْلِمِينَ﴾?

* Student: It is the predicate of *kāna* (the predicate of "was"), O Shaykh.
* Shaykh: The predicate of *kāna*? 
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes, the predicate of *kāna*. Or is ﴿مِنْ قَبْلِهِ﴾ the predicate?
* Student: No, ﴿مُسْلِمِينَ﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿مُسْلِمِينَ﴾ is the predicate. Even if ﴿مِنْ قَبْلِهِ﴾ precedes it, because the predicate is that by which the benefit is achieved, whether it comes before or after.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They will be given their reward twice, for what they patiently endured﴾ [al-Qasas 54].

Who are the ones referred to by ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾? Those who were given the Book and then believed in the Prophet ﷺ. They were given the Book before and believed in it, then they believed in the Messenger.

﴿يُؤْتَوْنَ أَجْرَهُمْ﴾ means they are given ﴿their reward﴾. And this contains evidence for yesterday's lesson, or not? ﴿They are given their reward﴾. Our lesson in grammar?

* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: (...)?
* Student: No, this ﴿يُؤْتَوْنَ﴾ is from the category of the *kasr* (the broken-plural/ending-type pattern, i.e., the verb form with the *wāw* as a pronoun).
* Shaykh: From the category of *kasr*. Yes, correct.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The position of the doer (*nā'ib al-fā'il*, the deputy subject), because (...) the object, and it is the *wāw*, the deputy subject of ﴿يُؤْتَوْنَ﴾. And the second object of ﴿يُؤْتَوْنَ﴾? Where is the second object in ﴿يُؤْتَوْنَ﴾? ﴿أَجْرَهُمْ﴾, yes.

As for His saying ﴿مَرَّتَيْنِ﴾, it is an absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*), meaning that it indicates the verbal noun but not with its own wording. Everything that indicates the verbal noun without its wording is an absolute object.

(﴿مَرَّتَيْنِ﴾ for their belief in both Books.) So they are given their reward twice: the first time for believing in the earlier Book, and the second time for believing in the Qur'an. As for the people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) who believed in the Qur'an, they are given their reward once, because they did not believe twice.

This is established by a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ, in addition to this verse. The Prophet ﷺ mentioned those who are given their reward twice: a man who believed in the Book that was revealed to him and then believed in what was revealed to Muhammad; a man who frees a slave-woman and marries her; and a third, a slave who does well in worshipping Allah and in dealing with his masters.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3011) and Muslim (154).]]

He said: ﴿They will be given their reward twice, for what they patiently endured﴾ [al-Qasas 54]. The *bāʾ* is causative (*bāʾ al-sababiyyah*, the *bāʾ* of cause), and *mā* is verbal (*mā maṣdariyyah*, the *mā* that forms a verbal noun).

What is meant by "verbal" or what is its sign? Its sign is that it can be converted so that what follows it becomes a verbal noun. Here we say, in the conversion, as the author said: "for their patience" (*li-ṣabrihim*). And I ask you now: can *mā* be a relative pronoun (*ism mawṣūl*)?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The phrase ﴿بِمَا صَبَرُوا﴾ is valid? The phrase ﴿بِمَا صَبَرُوا﴾, ﴿They are given their reward twice﴾ by that which ﴿they endured﴾? No, it is not valid, because what is the meaning of "by that which they endured"? Moreover, if it were a relative pronoun, it would require a pronoun in the construction: "by that which they endured it," and this is not correct. So here it is definite that it is verbal, meaning "by their patience." It is one of the ten meanings of *mā*. We repeat it so that it stays in your minds.
* Student: Memorize it.
* Shaykh: Memorize it. Recite it to us.
* Student:
  The meanings of "mā" are ten, if you want to count them, so keep to a verse free of poetic flaw.
  You will understand the condition of connection; marvel at its denial (ref. *nukr*)
  with *kaf* and negation, and *zīd* (added), the magnification of the verbal noun (*maṣdar*).
* Shaykh: Yes, may Allah bless you. Repeat it. Yes, good:
  You will understand the condition of connection; marvel at its denial
  with *kaf* and negation, and *zīd*, the magnification of the verbal noun.
  What concerns us from this verse is his saying: "verbal noun" (*maṣdar*).

As for His saying ﴿بِمَا صَبَرُوا﴾, it means "by their patience in acting upon both." Is this patience in acting upon both from the category of patience in obeying Allah, or from the category of patience in refraining from disobeying Allah, or from the category of patience in Allah's decrees?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes. We say: all three come together. ﴿They endured﴾ in obeying Allah, because the Sharia contains commands that are hard on the souls and need effort. So this is patience in obeying Allah.

In the laws there are prohibitions from which people are forbidden. It may be hard on the soul to abandon them, so there is patience in what? Refraining from disobeying Allah.

Likewise, in the laws there is harm, since the criminals harm the believers, and sometimes they strike them, and sometimes they kill them, is that not so? And this is patience in what?

* Student: In Allah's decrees.
* Shaykh: In Allah's painful decrees.

So, based on this, patience in the Sharia includes patience in its three types: patience in obeying Allah, refraining from His disobedience, and patience in His painful decrees. Or not?

* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Alright. ﴿They endured and they repel﴾ [al-Qasas 54]. The origin of *ṣabr* (patience) linguistically is restraint. From it comes their saying, "So-and-so was killed *ṣabran*," meaning held back for execution: he was restrained and killed. So the meaning of patience is restraining the self. The self needs restraint in obeying Allah the Exalted, because how many people has their conscience told: do such-and-such an act of obedience, and some do it and then become unable and do not restrain themselves. Likewise regarding sins: the soul at peace restrains a person from sin, but the commanding soul to evil comes to him and orders him to sin, and then the two souls struggle, and success is in the hand of Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

Likewise regarding decrees: among people are those who do not endure the decrees. Rather, when a decree strikes them, they may, may Allah protect us, disbelieve, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge; if good befalls him, he is reassured by it; but if an ordeal strikes him, he turns back on his face. He has lost this world and the Hereafter. That is the clear loss﴾ [al-Hajj 11]. Some people do not endure painful decrees, and you find them despairing. There are people who, it is said, when afflicted with calamities, kill themselves! Are these people the epitome of patience?!

* Student: No.
* Shaykh: No? On the contrary: there is no patience in them. These people did not endure the decrees, so they killed themselves, so that they will be punished by that with which they killed themselves in the fire of Hell, may Allah protect us, and they will abide in it forever. But patience in painful decrees is something a person can endure, and by which he holds himself accountable until he becomes upright in his actions.

So the point is that patience is of three categories: patience in obeying Allah, refraining from His disobedience, and patience in His painful decrees. Which of them is higher and more perfect?

* Student: Patience in obeying Allah.
* Shaykh: Yes, in terms of (...) patience in obeying Allah, patience in obedience is better, because in it there are two struggles: a struggle in the action, and a struggle in bearing the action.

Then patience in refraining from sin, because (...) it is one struggle: in the action or in bearing its abandonment? Bearing its abandonment. There is no action in it. It is said: "Do not commit adultery," yes. You were not commanded or charged to do anything.

Patience in harmful or painful decrees is the lowest, because it is patience in what a person has no choice in, as some of the early scholars said: "Either you endure with the patience of the noble, or you forget like the beasts." Every person, when struck by a calamity and time passes over it, does it remain in his soul or not? He forgets; he forgets like the beasts. For example, you find the animal (...), but if you give it good fodder and good water, it forgets. So either you endure with the patience of the noble, or you forget like the beasts.

For this reason, Yusuf's patience in abandoning adultery with the wife of the ruler was more perfect than his patience over what happened with his brothers, without doubt. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Thus, that We might avert from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was of Our chosen servants﴾ [Yusuf 24], and He did not say something like this when they threw him into the bottom of the well.

* Student: We said that patience in obedience is greater than patience in refraining from sin.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: But the sins, their number (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, it pains you, but it is something beyond your choice.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Beyond your choice. That is, you abandoned the sins by your choice.
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: You are able to do them, but you did not do them. But this (the calamity) you cannot lift.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The calamity that descended upon you, you cannot lift. So suppose a calamity descended upon a person. Can he lift it if he stands striking his face or tearing his garment?
* Student: No, he cannot.
* Shaykh: He cannot.
* Student: But if he endures and submits (...).
* Shaykh: No, because submission to the Sharia is better than submission to the decree. Submission to the Sharia is what a person is praised for, commended, and extolled for. But submission to the decree, all people submit to the decree. Even, you know, do you not hear the saying of the pre-Islamic poet:

  "And my showing of fortitude to the scorners, showing them
  that I do not yield to the vicissitudes of time."

Even the disbelievers now, their deeds bring calamities upon them, but they say: "It does not matter," and they endure and suffer, while they are disbelievers. They do not hope for reward or recompense by it.

* Student: But there is an aspect, O Shaykh (...), patience in hardships. Patience in acts of obedience trains a person in it through practice; he becomes accustomed to it.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: Like training in prayer, in fasting (...).
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: But if a great calamity befalls him, like (...) for example.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: Is this something he has not trained in?
* Shaykh: Yes, but perhaps he trains in it if it strikes him (...). He does not train. Even acts of worship like Hajj come only once in a lifetime.
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Therefore it is considered patience in obedience, along with its physical, financial, and security hardships. The matter of occurrence and non-occurrence is another issue. Moreover, we say: which is better, a man who struggles with obedience and finds in himself difficulty in managing it while performing the act of obedience, or another person who has trained in obedience so that it has become, as it were, an easy matter for him?
* Student: The one for whom it is easy.
* Shaykh: As for the first, his action is more arduous, while the second is more perfect in state. The second, for whom obedience has become like an innate disposition in his soul, is without doubt more perfect in state than the first, because it is as if obedience has become instinctive due to his love for it and its ease for him. But the first's action is more arduous, so this one receives the reward of the perfect, and that one receives the reward of the patient, because there is a kind of struggle and hardship in it. The scholars differ on this question: which is better? But the correct view is this distinction: it is said that the one who performs an act of obedience which is easy for him and submits to it without struggle is without doubt more perfect in state than the first, without doubt. The second, for whom it is harder, is rewarded according to the degree of his inner hardship.

Now look, for example, at a person who attends the lesson easily and willingly and sees it as a treasure, and another who does not, struggling with himself (...), leaving the house, for example, in order to attend the lesson. Which of them is more perfect in state?

* Student: The first.
* Shaykh: The first. Although the second is rewarded for his act, the first is more perfect in state and closer in rank.

Alright. ﴿They will be given their reward for what they patiently endured﴾ [al-Qasas 54]. The *bāʾ* in His saying ﴿بِمَا صَبَرُوا﴾ — why is it there? It is causative, meaning: because of their patience.

﴿And they repel evil with good﴾ [al-Qasas 54]: they repel (*yadfaʿūn*) ﴿evil with good﴾.

﴿Evil﴾ is the object. The *bāʾ* in His saying ﴿بِالْحَسَنَةِ﴾ is the *bāʾ* of instrument (*bāʾ al-ālah*), just as you say: "I slaughtered with the knife, and struck with the stick." So we have the one who repels, the one repelled, and the thing used to repel. Who is the one who repels in the verse?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, in the verse, who is the one who repels? The doers, and the one repelled?
* Student: Evil.
* Shaykh: Evil. And the thing used to repel is the good deed. Just as you say, "I slaughtered with the knife," so we have: slaughterer, slaughtered, and the instrument by which the slaughter is done. So the good deed is for them like the instrument by which they reach their goal.

﴿And they repel evil with good﴾: ﴿evil﴾. The author says: "from among them." So if they commit an evil, they follow it with a good deed, and the evil is repelled. This good deed, by which evil is repelled, is divided into two types: a type that removes the evil by way of counterbalance, and another type that removes the evil by way of erasure and removal. Have you taken note, O brothers? The good deeds by which evil deeds are repelled are of two kinds: one by way of counterbalance, and one by way of erasure and removal. If the good deed by which evil is repelled is repentance, and repentance is among the good deeds, or not? ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant﴾ [al-Baqarah 222]. If it is by way of repentance, then it is by way of erasure and removal. If it is another good deed, as when someone repels evil deeds by prayer: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the first hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds﴾ [Hud 114]. Then this repelling is by way of what?

* Student: Counterbalance.
* Shaykh: By way of counterbalance, meaning the reward of the good deed is set against the punishment of the evil deed, by way of weighing. If the reward of the good deed outweighs, the evil deed is erased; otherwise not.

Which of them is more perfect? Which of the two kinds of repelling is more perfect? The first or the second?

The first is more perfect, because when the first occurs, the second good deed becomes an additional increase in rank, and not a counterbalance to an evil deed. Moreover, if the repelling is by way of counterbalance, the second good deed may be weak, since the good deed may be too weak to counterbalance the evil deed. So repelling by repentance is more perfect than repelling by performing another good deed that counterbalances the evil deed. Both achieve repelling.

The author's words: "from among them."

In reality, this statement is appropriate. But if we say that it is more general, and that they repel with good and evil, from among themselves and from others, how is it "from among themselves and from others"? Meaning: if they are wronged, they repel the wrong with kindness. So here it is praise of them in terms of how they treat creation. Is this appropriate or not? It is appropriate. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The good and the evil are not equal. Repel [evil] with that which is better, and then the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as though he were a close friend. But none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune﴾ [Fussilat 34–35].

Based on this, we interpret the verse as having both meanings: they repel evil with good regarding what occurs from them in the worship of Allah, and they repel evil with good regarding what occurs from others in dealings. If they are treated, and someone wrongs them, they respond...

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 28, verses 51–54 (part 3 of 4):**

* The Shaykh: For weakness. Repelling an evil deed with a good one is praiseworthy when it stems from strength. But if it stems from weakness, it is not praiseworthy. Suppose a highway robber comes to someone and says, "Come on, give me your clothes." He replies, "I'll give you my clothes and the stick I have on the camel!" What would happen then? Or suppose he says, "Come on, give me the camel's saddle," and he replies, "Wait, wait, let me take care of it for you so you don't get tired. I'll unload it and put it on your camel." Is this good or not?
* Student: No, it is not good.
* The Shaykh: It is not good. This is weakness. For this reason the Messenger (ﷺ), when a man asked him about someone who comes to take his property, said: "Do not give it to him." The man said: "What if he fights me?" He said: "Fight him."[[Narrated by Muslim (140/225) from Abu Hurayrah.]] The point is that we say: ﴿and they repel evil with good﴾. (Some say it refers to) them. The correct view is to make it more general. So ﴿and they repel evil with good﴾ [Al-Qasas 54] applies to them in their dealings with Allah, and to others in their dealings with whom? With creation.

He says: (﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ [Al-Qasas 54], meaning they give in charity.) They also give gifts. They are not necessarily obliged to give charity, because a gift may be praiseworthy when its purpose is to create affection: "Exchange gifts, and you will love one another." Is it "tahādū" or "tahādaw"?
* Student: "Tahādū."
* Student: "Tahādaw."
* The Shaykh: Good. Does one say "tahādā al-rajulān, yatahādayān" (the two men exchanged gifts)?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Then it is "Tahādaw tahābbū."[[Narrated by Ahmad (9250) from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

Now, the point is that His saying ﴿and from what We have provided them﴾ [Al-Qasas 54]: ﴿provided them﴾ means "given them." So provision (rizq) means giving. From this is His saying: ﴿And when the division is attended by relatives, orphans and the needy, give them from it﴾ [An-Nisa 8], meaning, give them. So rizq means giving.

As for His saying ﴿from what We have provided them﴾, is "min" here for specifying the kind (bayān al-jins) or for partiality (tab'īd)?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It is better to take it as specifying the kind, because at times spending all of one's wealth is praiseworthy. The Prophet (ﷺ) once urged people to give charity, and 'Umar said: "Today I will outdo Abu Bakr." So he brought half of his wealth. But did Abu Bakr come?
* Student: With all of his wealth.
* The Shaykh: With all of his wealth.[[Narrated by Ahmad in Fada'il al-Sahabah (527) from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.]] So if we take "min" as specifying the kind, then the spending is better. What does (...) include?
* Student: Giving away all of one's wealth.
* The Shaykh: It includes giving away all of one's wealth or part of it. That is, it may be good to give all of it, and it may be good to give part of it, depending on the situation in which one spends. So "min" is better taken as specifying the kind.

As for His saying ﴿they spend﴾ [Al-Qasas 54], spending here means giving, not specifically charity. What led the author (al-Mu'allif) to restrict it to charity is that the context is one of praise. But it is better to keep it general, so that ﴿they spend﴾ means they give and bestow, because giving may be charity, and it may also be giving out of affection, which is also good, and in some situations may be better than charity. Accordingly, we say that it is better to understand spending as giving and bestowing, whether it is charity, a gift, or a present. You know the difference among these three. What is the difference between a bestowal (hibah), a gift (hadiyyah), and charity (sadaqah)?
* Student: A gift (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, and charity is given to someone.
* Student: Charity is given to...
* The Shaykh: To a person.
* Student: To (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: A gift.
* The Shaykh: And a bestowal?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: And a bestowal? Who knows the difference among the three?
* Student: A gift is giving to someone who is equal or a brother, with the intention of showing affection and drawing closer. Charity is giving to someone lower in status, with the intention of spending for Allah.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: As for...
* The Shaykh: Bestowal.
* Student: Bestowal is giving to an equal, meaning not to someone inferior, with the intention of giving.
* The Shaykh: No. The difference between them is this: charity is what is intended for the face of Allah, by which one draws closer to Allah, and the giver does not care whether the recipient is closer to him or not. A gift is what is intended to create affection for the recipient, meaning one wants to draw close to the one receiving it, and for the recipient to draw close to him. A bestowal (hibah) is what is intended only for the benefit of the one who receives it. One does not intend by it to draw close to this recipient, nor to draw close to Allah through it. One intends its benefit to him. This is called a hibah. All of them are praiseworthy in reality, but is some of them better than others? This depends on the situation.

﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ [Al-Qasas 54], and so on to the end.
* Student: The preference in the school of the Basrans regarding the figurative use of a verb?
* The Shaykh: Because it implies two meanings: the meaning of (...) the verb is present, and the meaning of (...). The other (the simple verb with a preposition) implies only one meaning, which is changing the meaning of the particle to the new meaning.
* Student: Shaykh, is this not sufficient (...)?
* The Shaykh: No. Adding a meaning is without doubt better, adding a meaning is a benefit.
* Student: We have one verb.
* The Shaykh: That does not contradict it. One verb absorbs the meaning of a second verb which takes this particle. (...) When the sentence indicates two meanings, it is more complete than when it indicates one.
* Student: In a case like ﴿a spring from which the servants drink﴾ [Al-Insan 6], we do not have "ri" (quenching thirst). We say only "drink."
* The Shaykh: Yes, but its origin is drinking, which may be drinking that does not quench the servant's thirst.
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And it may be drinking that quenches his thirst.
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: The people of Hell drink boiling water like thirsty camels and are not satisfied. What is the benefit of drinking then? But these ones drink from this spring and are satisfied by it. So now it implies the meaning of drinking and the meaning of quenching thirst. How do we understand the meaning of quenching thirst? From the verb being followed by the particle that fits quenching thirst.
* Student: Is it not better that the verb is followed by (...)?
* The Shaykh: What? This is most suitable, because drinking fits with quenching thirst. It does not fit with being full, for example. You cannot say ﴿drink with it﴾ meaning "be filled with it." That is not appropriate.
* Student: It is objected that it is not determined. We had mentioned...
* The Shaykh: No. The objection is answered by saying that it is determined by the context, and a verb must be assumed that fits the second verb, such as being its cause or branching from it, or something similar (...). The point is that the implication indicates two meanings, while the particle indicates one meaning only.
* Student: ﴿So you will drink like thirsty camels﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah 55]. What does it mean?
* The Shaykh: ﴿Al-Hīm﴾ are thirsty camels.
* Student: Not (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, it is water.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No. Thirst (al-hiyām) is of two kinds: thirst for food and thirst for drink.
* Student: Does the thirsty one get quenched?
* The Shaykh: No, whether he is quenched or not. (...) The one who drinks and is not quenched, what is he? Healthy or sick? The one who drinks and is not quenched, is he healthy or sick?
* Student: No, he is sick.
* The Shaykh: This one, yes.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes. (...) The Noble Qur'an. Some of the common people object to some questioners who ask: "Grant me a riyal," and say: "This is polytheism, may Allah protect us!" Yes, (...). Provision (rizq) means giving. (...)

* * *

* From this is derived that Allah, glorified and exalted, did not leave the earth without revelation, because "tawṣīl" means connecting one thing to another.
* And from it is derived that revelation contains the utmost clarity, because we said that "waṣṣala" implies the meaning of "bayyana" (to make clear).
* And from it is derived the manifestation of Allah's blessing upon this Ummah by conveying the word to them: ﴿And We have certainly conveyed to them﴾ [Al-Qasas 51].
* And from it, also, is derived that the wisdom behind revelation is remembrance and admonition, due to His saying: ﴿so that they may remember﴾ [Al-Qasas 51].
* And from it is derived the affirmation of causation (ʿillah) in Allah's cosmic and legislative rulings, and that He does nothing and legislates nothing except for a wisdom.
* We said: from it is derived the rationale of Allah's actions and His cosmic and legislative rulings. Who disagreed with this?
* Student: The Ash'arites.
* The Shaykh: And others? The Jahmiyyah are the origin. They said: Allah's actions are not to be given a reason, and His rulings are not to be given a reason.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture before it, they believe in it﴾ [Al-Qasas 52].

* From this is derived, first, that among the Jews and Christians there are those who believed in the Qur'an, due to His saying: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture before it, they believe in it﴾.
* And from it is also derived that the ruling on an individual may apply to his entire category. What is the meaning of this? The meaning is: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture before it﴾. If we look at it, we find that it is general, including all who were given the Scripture. But are they all general? Did all of those who were given the Scripture before believe in the Qur'an? Not at all. There were Christians who remained Christians, and Jews who remained Jews, but among them were those who believed. This means that we have given the category the ruling of an individual. Or did you not understand this? It is as if it is said: the faith of 'Abdullah ibn Salam and the faith of al-Najashi, for example, is (...). It is not that this one is named 'Abdullah ibn Salam and that one is named al-Najashi. Rather, because they were given the Scripture, they believed, not because of their names, but because of what they knew from their books, that the Messenger (ﷺ) would be sent. This requires that the whole category should be believers, even if they did not all believe.
* The point is that from this verse is derived the principle of giving the category the ruling of the individual, as long as the cause of this ruling encompasses the whole category. For example, what was the cause of 'Abdullah ibn Salam's faith? His knowledge of the attributes of the Messenger (ﷺ) in the Torah. Is this knowledge specific to him, or does it include all the Jews? It includes all the Jews. So here we have given the category the ruling of the individual, because of the cause that encompasses him and others. Otherwise, someone might say: we do not see that those to whom We gave the Scripture before it believe in it, since not all of them believed. But we say: only some of them believed, yet this faith among some of them was driven by a cause that encompasses the whole category.
* So we derive from this: we give the category the ruling of the individual when the cause of this ruling encompasses all. When the cause of this ruling encompasses all, the category is given the ruling of the individual.
* From this verse is also derived the great praise of those who believed in the Qur'an and the earlier books, due to His saying: ﴿they believe in it﴾.
* And from it is derived that the attributes of the Prophet (ﷺ) are present in the earlier books: the Torah and the Gospel. This is clear in the verse of al-A'raf, in His saying: ﴿whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, who enjoins them what is right...﴾ and so on to the end [Al-A'raf 157].

Then He said: ﴿And when it is recited to them, they say, "We believe in it. Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed, we were Muslims before it."﴾ [Al-Qasas 53].

* From this verse is also derived: increased praise for these people, that they believe in everything that is recited to them. They did not believe in the Qur'an merely as a whole, but in its entirety and in its details. We derive this from His saying: ﴿And when it is recited﴾. The verb ﴿is recited﴾ is in the present tense, which indicates occurrence and continuity. Yes, it indicates renewal and occurrence, and that this is their characteristic whenever it is recited to them.
* And also from the noble verses is derived that they believed not merely out of desire, but believed with a faith based on conviction. From where is this taken? From their saying: ﴿We believe in it. Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord﴾. They did not believe simply by following others, but believed out of conviction: ﴿Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord﴾.
* And from it is also derived that the Qur'an is from Allah, due to His saying: ﴿from our Lord﴾.
* And from it is derived the perfection of the intellect of those who believed, in that they expressed it with reference to lordship (rubūbiyyah): ﴿from our Lord﴾, rather than divinity (ulūhiyyah), because the context requires that. For the Lord has authority to judge as He wills, both in cosmic and legislative matters.
* And from this is also derived that these people were believers, Muslims, submitting to the earlier books, due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, we were Muslims before it﴾.
* And from it is derived the permissibility of a person praising himself with praiseworthy attributes, on condition that there is a benefit in it, and that it does not involve boasting or superiority over others. This is due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, we were Muslims before it﴾. This is something that actually occurred from the Prophet (ﷺ), from the Companions, and from the scholars. The Prophet (ﷺ) said:
«I am the Prophet, no lie, I am the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib.»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4315) and Muslim (1776/78) from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib.]]
And Ibn Mas'ud said: "If I knew that anyone whom the camels could reach had more knowledge of the Book of Allah than I, I would go to him."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5002) and Muslim (2463/115).]] This is praise of himself, but for a benefit. Scholars, whenever they write a book, praise it with the attributes of praise that the book warrants. It is well known that praising the book is praising its author. If you praised this building and said, "Masha Allah, this is a good, sturdy and beautiful building," whom have you actually praised? You have praised the builder. Yes, the builder. So this matter is permissible for a person: he may praise himself with attributes of praise, on condition that he does not intend by it to boast over others, and the second condition is that there be a benefit in it. As for the first condition, its reason is clear: if he intends by it boasting and superiority over people, then this intention is forbidden. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: «I am the master of the children of Adam on the Day of Resurrection, and I say this without boasting.»[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (3148) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

Likewise, the condition that there be a benefit: if there is no benefit in it, it is idle talk, at the very least. It is idle talk because why would a person praise himself without a benefit? Only if he wants to display his qualities so that he can boast about them over others would he do it. Even if he says, "I do not want boasting," we say: then why?

* * *

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice, for what they patiently endured, and they repel evil with good, and from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ [Al-Qasas 54].
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Their benefit is that it urges them to take from it.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: But, all right, if we have shown that he memorizes such-and-such, then I, for example, may not have these things, so I strive for them. Or I know, for example, that he has memorized more than I have, so I refer to him for questions. The point is that scholars, especially those known for virtue, are not believed to want merely to display their praiseworthy qualities. That meaning is not sound at all. Rather, they intend a benefit, and this benefit differs according to circumstances.
* Student: So, Shaykh, do we not say that the default is (...)?
* The Shaykh: No. We say the default is that this is idle talk, since there is no benefit in it. The Messenger (ﷺ) said: «Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say what is good or remain silent.»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6018) and Muslim (47/74) from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] So as long as there is no good in it... Furthermore, it leads to harm, because even if we suppose that this man, one hundred percent, did not intend boasting, he opens a door for others, a door through which others will boast about it.

And His saying, exalted: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice, for what they patiently endured, and they repel evil with good, and from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ [Al-Qasas 54].
* From this noble verse is derived: that the People of the Book who believe have two rewards. The first reward is for believing in their own Scripture, and the second is for believing in the Qur'an.

Among its benefits: the affirmation of Allah's justice, exalted is He, in that He does not waste their first reward by means of the second, nor their second reward by means of the first.

It is also derived from this that reward is in proportion to deeds: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it. And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [Az-Zalzalah 7–8]. These people had their reward doubled, because they did what?
Student: Twice.
Shaykh: Twice.

Among the benefits of the verse also: the affirmation of causes and reasons, due to His saying: ﴿because they were patient﴾.

Among its benefits: the virtue of patience (ṣabr). Since patience is a cause of reward, it is undoubtedly a praiseworthy and excellent attribute. Yes, and I think we mentioned in the tafsir (exegesis) that patience is divided into three categories:
Student: Patience in obedience to Allah, patience in refraining from disobedience to Allah, and patience in the painful decrees of Allah.
Shaykh: The painful decrees, and the best of them is the first, then the second, then the third.

It is also derived from it: that good deeds wipe out bad deeds, due to His saying: ﴿and they repel evil with good﴾.

Among its benefits also: that one should repay the wrongdoer with kindness. The verse, as we said, is general: it covers their repelling their own evil deeds with their good deeds, and their repelling the evil deeds of others by doing good to them, and we brought evidence for that from the Qur'an. But this repelling is heavy upon a person, and repelling the evil of others by doing good to them is very heavy upon a person. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿None is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 35]. Most people say: "By Allah, I will give him a sa' for a sa', and a slap for a slap, two for one!" But the matter is not like that. ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾. What is the result? ﴿Then the one between you and him is enmity will become as though he was a devoted friend﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 34]. Note that He used ("idhā") of sudden occurrence, to indicate that this matter changes quickly: this enemy quickly becomes as though he were a close, devoted friend to you.

So we say: what is derived from it? That good deeds wipe out bad deeds, and that one should repay offense with kindness. However, we have mentioned that this should not be a display of weakness in a person.
