So we have the one who repels, the one repelled, and the thing used to repel. Who is the one who repels in the verse?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, in the verse, who is the one who repels? The doers, and the one repelled?
* Student: Evil.
* Shaykh: Evil. And the thing used to repel is the good deed. Just as you say, "I slaughtered with the knife," so we have: slaughterer, slaughtered, and the instrument by which the slaughter is done. So the good deed is for them like the instrument by which they reach their goal.

﴿And they repel evil with good﴾: ﴿evil﴾. The author says: "from among them." So if they commit an evil, they follow it with a good deed, and the evil is repelled. This good deed, by which evil is repelled, is divided into two types: a type that removes the evil by way of counterbalance, and another type that removes the evil by way of erasure and removal. Have you taken note, O brothers? The good deeds by which evil deeds are repelled are of two kinds: one by way of counterbalance, and one by way of erasure and removal. If the good deed by which evil is repelled is repentance, and repentance is among the good deeds, or not? ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant﴾ [al-Baqarah 222]. If it is by way of repentance, then it is by way of erasure and removal. If it is another good deed, as when someone repels evil deeds by prayer: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the first hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds﴾ [Hud 114]. Then this repelling is by way of what?

* Student: Counterbalance.
* Shaykh: By way of counterbalance, meaning the reward of the good deed is set against the punishment of the evil deed, by way of weighing. If the reward of the good deed outweighs, the evil deed is erased; otherwise not.

Which of them is more perfect? Which of the two kinds of repelling is more perfect? The first or the second?

The first is more perfect, because when the first occurs, the second good deed becomes an additional increase in rank, and not a counterbalance to an evil deed. Moreover, if the repelling is by way of counterbalance, the second good deed may be weak, since the good deed may be too weak to counterbalance the evil deed. So repelling by repentance is more perfect than repelling by performing another good deed that counterbalances the evil deed. Both achieve repelling.

The author's words: "from among them."

In reality, this statement is appropriate. But if we say that it is more general, and that they repel with good and evil, from among themselves and from others, how is it "from among themselves and from others"? Meaning: if they are wronged, they repel the wrong with kindness. So here it is praise of them in terms of how they treat creation. Is this appropriate or not? It is appropriate. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The good and the evil are not equal. Repel [evil] with that which is better, and then the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as though he were a close friend. But none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune﴾ [Fussilat 34–35].

Based on this, we interpret the verse as having both meanings: they repel evil with good regarding what occurs from them in the worship of Allah, and they repel evil with good regarding what occurs from others in dealings. If they are treated, and someone wrongs them, they respond...

Shaykh: In this prohibition, he said: this negation is a negation of truth, meaning of the true deity, for there is no god but Allah in His measure.

............................ ∗∗∗ they are not in any evil, even if...
They repay the injustice of the unjust with forgiveness, and the evil of the evil people with kindness.
Would that I had among them a people who, when they ride, raid as horsemen and riders.

Now (...)?

* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: (...) (They repay the injustice of the unjust with forgiveness).
* Student: (...).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 28, verses 51–54 (part 3 of 4):**

* The Shaykh: For weakness. Repelling an evil deed with a good one is praiseworthy when it stems from strength. But if it stems from weakness, it is not praiseworthy. Suppose a highway robber comes to someone and says, "Come on, give me your clothes." He replies, "I'll give you my clothes and the stick I have on the camel!" What would happen then? Or suppose he says, "Come on, give me the camel's saddle," and he replies, "Wait, wait, let me take care of it for you so you don't get tired. I'll unload it and put it on your camel." Is this good or not?
* Student: No, it is not good.
* The Shaykh: It is not good. This is weakness. For this reason the Messenger (ﷺ), when a man asked him about someone who comes to take his property, said: "Do not give it to him." The man said: "What if he fights me?" He said: "Fight him."[[Narrated by Muslim (140/225) from Abu Hurayrah.]] The point is that we say: ﴿and they repel evil with good﴾. (Some say it refers to) them. The correct view is to make it more general. So ﴿and they repel evil with good﴾ [Al-Qasas 54] applies to them in their dealings with Allah, and to others in their dealings with whom? With creation.

He says: (﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ [Al-Qasas 54], meaning they give in charity.) They also give gifts. They are not necessarily obliged to give charity, because a gift may be praiseworthy when its purpose is to create affection: "Exchange gifts, and you will love one another." Is it "tahādū" or "tahādaw"?
* Student: "Tahādū."
* Student: "Tahādaw."
* The Shaykh: Good. Does one say "tahādā al-rajulān, yatahādayān" (the two men exchanged gifts)?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Then it is "Tahādaw tahābbū."[[Narrated by Ahmad (9250) from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

Now, the point is that His saying ﴿and from what We have provided them﴾ [Al-Qasas 54]: ﴿provided them﴾ means "given them." So provision (rizq) means giving. From this is His saying: ﴿And when the division is attended by relatives, orphans and the needy, give them from it﴾ [An-Nisa 8], meaning, give them. So rizq means giving.

As for His saying ﴿from what We have provided them﴾, is "min" here for specifying the kind (bayān al-jins) or for partiality (tab'īd)?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It is better to take it as specifying the kind, because at times spending all of one's wealth is praiseworthy. The Prophet (ﷺ) once urged people to give charity, and 'Umar said: "Today I will outdo Abu Bakr." So he brought half of his wealth. But did Abu Bakr come?
* Student: With all of his wealth.
* The Shaykh: With all of his wealth.[[Narrated by Ahmad in Fada'il al-Sahabah (527) from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.]] So if we take "min" as specifying the kind, then the spending is better. What does (...) include?
* Student: Giving away all of one's wealth.
* The Shaykh: It includes giving away all of one's wealth or part of it. That is, it may be good to give all of it, and it may be good to give part of it, depending on the situation in which one spends. So "min" is better taken as specifying the kind.

As for His saying ﴿they spend﴾ [Al-Qasas 54], spending here means giving, not specifically charity. What led the author (al-Mu'allif) to restrict it to charity is that the context is one of praise. But it is better to keep it general, so that ﴿they spend﴾ means they give and bestow, because giving may be charity, and it may also be giving out of affection, which is also good, and in some situations may be better than charity. Accordingly, we say that it is better to understand spending as giving and bestowing, whether it is charity, a gift, or a present. You know the difference among these three. What is the difference between a bestowal (hibah), a gift (hadiyyah), and charity (sadaqah)?
* Student: A gift (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, and charity is given to someone.
* Student: Charity is given to...
* The Shaykh: To a person.
* Student: To (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: A gift.
* The Shaykh: And a bestowal?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: And a bestowal? Who knows the difference among the three?
* Student: A gift is giving to someone who is equal or a brother, with the intention of showing affection and drawing closer. Charity is giving to someone lower in status, with the intention of spending for Allah.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: As for...
* The Shaykh: Bestowal.
* Student: Bestowal is giving to an equal, meaning not to someone inferior, with the intention of giving.
* The Shaykh: No. The difference between them is this: charity is what is intended for the face of Allah, by which one draws closer to Allah, and the giver does not care whether the recipient is closer to him or not. A gift is what is intended to create affection for the recipient, meaning one wants to draw close to the one receiving it, and for the recipient to draw close to him. A bestowal (hibah) is what is intended only for the benefit of the one who receives it. One does not intend by it to draw close to this recipient, nor to draw close to Allah through it. One intends its benefit to him. This is called a hibah. All of them are praiseworthy in reality, but is some of them better than others? This depends on the situation.

﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ [Al-Qasas 54], and so on to the end.
* Student: The preference in the school of the Basrans regarding the figurative use of a verb?
* The Shaykh: Because it implies two meanings: the meaning of (...) the verb is present, and the meaning of (...). The other (the simple verb with a preposition) implies only one meaning, which is changing the meaning of the particle to the new meaning.
* Student: Shaykh, is this not sufficient (...)?
* The Shaykh: No. Adding a meaning is without doubt better, adding a meaning is a benefit.
* Student: We have one verb.
* The Shaykh: That does not contradict it. One verb absorbs the meaning of a second verb which takes this particle. (...) When the sentence indicates two meanings, it is more complete than when it indicates one.
* Student: In a case like ﴿a spring from which the servants drink﴾ [Al-Insan 6], we do not have "ri" (quenching thirst). We say only "drink."
* The Shaykh: Yes, but its origin is drinking, which may be drinking that does not quench the servant's thirst.
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And it may be drinking that quenches his thirst.
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: The people of Hell drink boiling water like thirsty camels and are not satisfied. What is the benefit of drinking then? But these ones drink from this spring and are satisfied by it. So now it implies the meaning of drinking and the meaning of quenching thirst. How do we understand the meaning of quenching thirst? From the verb being followed by the particle that fits quenching thirst.
* Student: Is it not better that the verb is followed by (...)?
* The Shaykh: What? This is most suitable, because drinking fits with quenching thirst. It does not fit with being full, for example. You cannot say ﴿drink with it﴾ meaning "be filled with it." That is not appropriate.
* Student: It is objected that it is not determined. We had mentioned...
* The Shaykh: No. The objection is answered by saying that it is determined by the context, and a verb must be assumed that fits the second verb, such as being its cause or branching from it, or something similar (...). The point is that the implication indicates two meanings, while the particle indicates one meaning only.
* Student: ﴿So you will drink like thirsty camels﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah 55]. What does it mean?
* The Shaykh: ﴿Al-Hīm﴾ are thirsty camels.
* Student: Not (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, it is water.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No. Thirst (al-hiyām) is of two kinds: thirst for food and thirst for drink.
* Student: Does the thirsty one get quenched?
* The Shaykh: No, whether he is quenched or not. (...) The one who drinks and is not quenched, what is he? Healthy or sick? The one who drinks and is not quenched, is he healthy or sick?
* Student: No, he is sick.
* The Shaykh: This one, yes.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes. (...) The Noble Qur'an. Some of the common people object to some questioners who ask: "Grant me a riyal," and say: "This is polytheism, may Allah protect us!" Yes, (...). Provision (rizq) means giving. (...)

* * *

* From this is derived that Allah, glorified and exalted, did not leave the earth without revelation, because "tawṣīl" means connecting one thing to another.
* And from it is derived that revelation contains the utmost clarity, because we said that "waṣṣala" implies the meaning of "bayyana" (to make clear).
* And from it is derived the manifestation of Allah's blessing upon this Ummah by conveying the word to them: ﴿And We have certainly conveyed to them﴾ [Al-Qasas 51].
* And from it, also, is derived that the wisdom behind revelation is remembrance and admonition, due to His saying: ﴿so that they may remember﴾ [Al-Qasas 51].
* And from it is derived the affirmation of causation (ʿillah) in Allah's cosmic and legislative rulings, and that He does nothing and legislates nothing except for a wisdom.
* We said: from it is derived the rationale of Allah's actions and His cosmic and legislative rulings. Who disagreed with this?
* Student: The Ash'arites.
* The Shaykh: And others? The Jahmiyyah are the origin. They said: Allah's actions are not to be given a reason, and His rulings are not to be given a reason.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture before it, they believe in it﴾ [Al-Qasas 52].

* From this is derived, first, that among the Jews and Christians there are those who believed in the Qur'an, due to His saying: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture before it, they believe in it﴾.
* And from it is also derived that the ruling on an individual may apply to his entire category. What is the meaning of this? The meaning is: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture before it﴾. If we look at it, we find that it is general, including all who were given the Scripture. But are they all general? Did all of those who were given the Scripture before believe in the Qur'an? Not at all. There were Christians who remained Christians, and Jews who remained Jews, but among them were those who believed. This means that we have given the category the ruling of an individual. Or did you not understand this? It is as if it is said: the faith of 'Abdullah ibn Salam and the faith of al-Najashi, for example, is (...). It is not that this one is named 'Abdullah ibn Salam and that one is named al-Najashi. Rather, because they were given the Scripture, they believed, not because of their names, but because of what they knew from their books, that the Messenger (ﷺ) would be sent. This requires that the whole category should be believers, even if they did not all believe.
* The point is that from this verse is derived the principle of giving the category the ruling of the individual, as long as the cause of this ruling encompasses the whole category. For example, what was the cause of 'Abdullah ibn Salam's faith? His knowledge of the attributes of the Messenger (ﷺ) in the Torah. Is this knowledge specific to him, or does it include all the Jews? It includes all the Jews. So here we have given the category the ruling of the individual, because of the cause that encompasses him and others. Otherwise, someone might say: we do not see that those to whom We gave the Scripture before it believe in it, since not all of them believed. But we say: only some of them believed, yet this faith among some of them was driven by a cause that encompasses the whole category.
* So we derive from this: we give the category the ruling of the individual when the cause of this ruling encompasses all. When the cause of this ruling encompasses all, the category is given the ruling of the individual.
* From this verse is also derived the great praise of those who believed in the Qur'an and the earlier books, due to His saying: ﴿they believe in it﴾.
* And from it is derived that the attributes of the Prophet (ﷺ) are present in the earlier books: the Torah and the Gospel. This is clear in the verse of al-A'raf, in His saying: ﴿whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, who enjoins them what is right...﴾ and so on to the end [Al-A'raf 157].

Then He said: ﴿And when it is recited to them, they say, "We believe in it. Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed, we were Muslims before it."﴾ [Al-Qasas 53].

* From this verse is also derived: increased praise for these people, that they believe in everything that is recited to them. They did not believe in the Qur'an merely as a whole, but in its entirety and in its details. We derive this from His saying: ﴿And when it is recited﴾. The verb ﴿is recited﴾ is in the present tense, which indicates occurrence and continuity. Yes, it indicates renewal and occurrence, and that this is their characteristic whenever it is recited to them.
* And also from the noble verses is derived that they believed not merely out of desire, but believed with a faith based on conviction. From where is this taken? From their saying: ﴿We believe in it. Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord﴾. They did not believe simply by following others, but believed out of conviction: ﴿Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord﴾.
* And from it is also derived that the Qur'an is from Allah, due to His saying: ﴿from our Lord﴾.
* And from it is derived the perfection of the intellect of those who believed, in that they expressed it with reference to lordship (rubūbiyyah): ﴿from our Lord﴾, rather than divinity (ulūhiyyah), because the context requires that. For the Lord has authority to judge as He wills, both in cosmic and legislative matters.
* And from this is also derived that these people were believers, Muslims, submitting to the earlier books, due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, we were Muslims before it﴾.
* And from it is derived the permissibility of a person praising himself with praiseworthy attributes, on condition that there is a benefit in it, and that it does not involve boasting or superiority over others. This is due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, we were Muslims before it﴾. This is something that actually occurred from the Prophet (ﷺ), from the Companions, and from the scholars. The Prophet (ﷺ) said:
«I am the Prophet, no lie, I am the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib.»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4315) and Muslim (1776/78) from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib.]]
And Ibn Mas'ud said: "If I knew that anyone whom the camels could reach had more knowledge of the Book of Allah than I, I would go to him."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5002) and Muslim (2463/115).]] This is praise of himself, but for a benefit. Scholars, whenever they write a book, praise it with the attributes of praise that the book warrants. It is well known that praising the book is praising its author. If you praised this building and said, "Masha Allah, this is a good, sturdy and beautiful building," whom have you actually praised? You have praised the builder. Yes, the builder. So this matter is permissible for a person: he may praise himself with attributes of praise, on condition that he does not intend by it to boast over others, and the second condition is that there be a benefit in it. As for the first condition, its reason is clear: if he intends by it boasting and superiority over people, then this intention is forbidden. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: «I am the master of the children of Adam on the Day of Resurrection, and I say this without boasting.»[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (3148) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

Likewise, the condition that there be a benefit: if there is no benefit in it, it is idle talk, at the very least. It is idle talk because why would a person praise himself without a benefit? Only if he wants to display his qualities so that he can boast about them over others would he do it. Even if he says, "I do not want boasting," we say: then why?

* * *

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice, for what they patiently endured, and they repel evil with good, and from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ [Al-Qasas 54].
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Their benefit is that it urges them to take from it.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: But, all right, if we have shown that he memorizes such-and-such, then I, for example, may not have these things, so I strive for them. Or I know, for example, that he has memorized more than I have, so I refer to him for questions. The point is that scholars, especially those known for virtue, are not believed to want merely to display their praiseworthy qualities. That meaning is not sound at all. Rather, they intend a benefit, and this benefit differs according to circumstances.
* Student: So, Shaykh, do we not say that the default is (...)?
* The Shaykh: No. We say the default is that this is idle talk, since there is no benefit in it. The Messenger (ﷺ) said: «Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say what is good or remain silent.»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6018) and Muslim (47/74) from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] So as long as there is no good in it... Furthermore, it leads to harm, because even if we suppose that this man, one hundred percent, did not intend boasting, he opens a door for others, a door through which others will boast about it.

And His saying, exalted: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice, for what they patiently endured, and they repel evil with good, and from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ [Al-Qasas 54].
* From this noble verse is derived: that the People of the Book who believe have two rewards. The first reward is for believing in their own Scripture, and the second is for believing in the Qur'an.

Among its benefits: the affirmation of Allah's justice, exalted is He, in that He does not waste their first reward by means of the second, nor their second reward by means of the first.

It is also derived from this that reward is in proportion to deeds: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it. And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [Az-Zalzalah 7–8]. These people had their reward doubled, because they did what?
Student: Twice.
Shaykh: Twice.

Among the benefits of the verse also: the affirmation of causes and reasons, due to His saying: ﴿because they were patient﴾.

Among its benefits: the virtue of patience (ṣabr). Since patience is a cause of reward, it is undoubtedly a praiseworthy and excellent attribute. Yes, and I think we mentioned in the tafsir (exegesis) that patience is divided into three categories:
Student: Patience in obedience to Allah, patience in refraining from disobedience to Allah, and patience in the painful decrees of Allah.
Shaykh: The painful decrees, and the best of them is the first, then the second, then the third.

It is also derived from it: that good deeds wipe out bad deeds, due to His saying: ﴿and they repel evil with good﴾.

Among its benefits also: that one should repay the wrongdoer with kindness. The verse, as we said, is general: it covers their repelling their own evil deeds with their good deeds, and their repelling the evil deeds of others by doing good to them, and we brought evidence for that from the Qur'an. But this repelling is heavy upon a person, and repelling the evil of others by doing good to them is very heavy upon a person. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿None is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 35]. Most people say: "By Allah, I will give him a sa' for a sa', and a slap for a slap, two for one!" But the matter is not like that. ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾. What is the result? ﴿Then the one between you and him is enmity will become as though he was a devoted friend﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 34]. Note that He used ("idhā") of sudden occurrence, to indicate that this matter changes quickly: this enemy quickly becomes as though he were a close, devoted friend to you.

So we say: what is derived from it? That good deeds wipe out bad deeds, and that one should repay offense with kindness. However, we have mentioned that this should not be a display of weakness in a person. If it is a display of weakness in a person, then it is not appropriate, because Allah says: ﴿And whoever retaliates after being wronged, those, there is no blame upon them﴾ [Ash-Shūrā 41].
Student: Even if he is a sinner (fāsiq)?
Shaykh: Yes, even if he is a sinner. This is with regard to your own personal right.
Student: Yes.
Shaykh: As for the right of Allah, no. He is dealt with according to what the Sharia (sacred law) requires.
Student: (...)?
Shaykh: With regard to (...): ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds﴾ [Hūd 114].
Student: (...)?
Shaykh: Yes, perhaps evil deeds may wipe out good deeds by way of counterbalancing, because good and evil deeds are weighed on the Day of Resurrection. Whichever of them outweighs, the ruling belongs to it.

Also derived from this verse: the virtue of spending from the provision of Allah: ﴿and from what We have provided them﴾.

Also derived from it: the one who spends has not spent from what he made or earned by himself, but he spends from what? From the provision of Allah. Allah is the One who provided for you, and He is the One who commanded you. You are, in reality, a servant, a slave who acts according to the command of his master. He told you to earn, so you earned; He told you to spend, so you spent.

Now, as for His saying: ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 54], how do we reconcile what is here with His description of the servants of the Most Merciful: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever, between that, justly moderate﴾ [al-Furqān 67], and with His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched﴾ [al-Isrā' 29]?

We say: we reconcile them by saying that the general state of people is not to spend all their wealth, because spending all of one's wealth may harm him. But at times, spending all of one's wealth is praiseworthy. Therefore He said: ﴿do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾, meaning do not spend at all; ﴿nor extend it fully outstretched﴾, meaning do not spend everything you have. But other texts indicate that the matter is based on what? On the ruling changing with changing circumstances. It may be, for example, that spending all of one's wealth is best, and it may be that keeping some of it is better.

Also derived from the noble verse, His saying ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾: spending from the provision of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, is praiseworthy. Provision (rizq), as we learned in the chapter on creed ('aqīdah), is what benefits from the lawful and its opposite. And what is its opposite? The unlawful. So is a person praised if he spends from the unlawful? No, because he is not rewarded for it, and what is obligatory upon him is to return the thing and rid himself of it. That is what is obligatory upon him. But what is meant here is the provision from which spending is praised when it is lawful provision. As for the one who earned something unlawful, the Prophet (ﷺ) informed that if he spends it, it will not be blessed for him; if he gives it in charity, it will not be accepted from him; and if he leaves it behind, it will be his provision to the Fire. This shows that spending from what is forbidden does not benefit a person. But it benefits him when? If he spends it wanting to be rid of it, then it benefits him in the sense that none of its consequences will befall him, and it benefits him because spending it to be rid of it is repentance, and repentance benefits the servant. For example: if a person has a hundred thousand dirhams earned unlawfully and he spends it to be rid of it, does he receive the reward of one who gives charity from it? No. But he receives a reward for repenting from this sin he committed. As for what (...). But if he earned it lawfully and spent it, he is given reward according to its amount, and in proportion to the multiplication mentioned in the text.

* * *

Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And when they hear vain talk﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 55].
Student: (...)?
Shaykh: If... it does not benefit the person, because the one who is incapable leaves something due to his inability to do it. So what is the station of (...)? That is why Allah said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning and Competent﴾ [an-Nisā' 149]. He praised Himself for pardoning while having the power to retaliate. As for one who pardons out of incapacity, what is the benefit? For example, someone is struck by a soldier and he cannot confront the soldier, so he says: "(...) may Allah reward you with good, may Allah be good to you." Yes, we say this is one who is incapable. But if someone strikes him who is (...), what does he do to him? Perhaps he gives back a sa' for a sa' twice over.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 55:

He said: ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it﴾ [al-Qasas 55].

﴿And when they hear﴾: We must know the difference between "sami'a" (to hear) and "istama'a" (to listen). The one who hears (sami') is the one who perceives a sound without intending to, while the one who listens (mustami') is the one who perceives it with intention, who perceives the sound deliberately. For this reason we say: prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa) is recommended for whom? For the listener (al-mustami'), not the mere hearer.

Here He said: ﴿when they hear idle talk﴾, which indicates that these people do not listen to it, but rather they hear it. The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan 72]: "they pass by" it, they do not stop at it, but when they "pass by" it.

Likewise, here: ﴿when they hear idle talk﴾. The author says: (insult and harm from the disbelievers). This is also a restriction of what is more general, for idle talk includes what the author mentioned, "insult and harm," and it also includes every speech that contains no good, whether or not it contains evil; it is all idle talk. These people are at the utmost of seriousness and of guarding their time; they do not listen to idle talk. Allah, blessed and exalted, praised those who do not listen to idle talk. And the Prophet ﷺ said: «Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day» — what comes after it?

* Students: «let him say what is good or remain silent».

* The Shaykh: «let him say what is good or remain silent»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6018) and Muslim (47/74) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. «Let him say what is good»; and the opposite of good is what? Evil. And what is neither good nor evil? It is idle talk.

So the more correct view is that ﴿when they hear idle talk﴾ includes every speech in which there is no good, whether or not it contains harm and evil.

﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it﴾ [al-Qasas 55]: ﴿they turn away from it﴾ with their bodies? Or with their bodies and hearts? Or with their hearts only? The basic meaning is the hearts, but it may also include the bodies, such that when they hear speech with no good in it, they stand up and leave the place, even if it is not forbidden. As for turning away of the body while the heart remains present, does this benefit? It does not benefit.

So the situations regarding idle talk are of four kinds:

Sometimes a person turns toward it with his body and heart, and in that case he is a participant in its people.

Sometimes he turns away from it with his body and heart, so that he does not listen to it and gets up.

Sometimes he turns away with his heart but not his body.

Sometimes he turns away with his body but not his heart.

And the focus here is on what? Turning away with the heart.

﴿They turn away from it and say: "To us our deeds, and to you your deeds"﴾ [al-Qasas 55]. It is as if He is saying: if they are told, "Why do you get up? Why do you not respond? Why do you not submit to their harm?" they say: ﴿To us our deeds, and to you your deeds﴾: we are not questioned about what you do, and you are not questioned about what we do, and we do not agree with you on this conduct. This does not mean that they do not enjoin good and forbid evil, because the discussion here is about idle talk, which is speech contrary to good; as for what is reprehensible (munkar), there is no doubt that they forbid it and enjoin what is right.

﴿Peace be upon you﴾ [al-Qasas 55]: is it a greeting of peace, or peace other than a greeting?

The author says: (peace of parting, meaning: you are safe from us from insult and the like). They do not offer it as a greeting of peace; rather, when they hear idle talk they turn away, get up, and say to these people: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾, meaning: peace upon you from us, not from Allah. ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ from us, so you are safe; we will not repay you with what you do to us. This is from the author on the basis that the intended meaning of ﴿idle talk﴾ is insult and harm from the disbelievers.

But if we take the general meaning, it is possible that the peace here means peace from Allah, that is, a greeting of peace, since it is legislated for one who rises from a gathering to give greeting; and it is possible that it is a peace of parting. If we wish, we may divide it: if we say that idle talk is insult and harm, then the peace here is a peace of parting, meaning you are safe from us and we are safe from you; and if we say that the intended meaning of idle talk is speech with no good in it, even if it is not abuse or insult, then it is a greeting of peace, because these people have not wronged those who turn away, so that they should say to them, "Peace be upon you from us." It is also permissible that we take the peace, that is, the meaning of peace, whether it is a parting or a greeting, in accordance with the sense of idle talk.

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed, like that, yes.

He said: (﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾ [al-Qasas 55], we do not accompany them). This explanation by the author is deficient; I think it is deficient. Let us see whether you agree or not. ﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾; he says: (we do not accompany them)?

* Student: Deficient.

* The Shaykh: If the matter were so, He would have said: "We do not accompany the ignorant." But: ﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾. Ibtigha' means seeking, as in ﴿they seek bounty from their Lord and approval﴾ [al-Ma'idah 2], that is, they seek. So the meaning of ﴿we do not seek﴾ is we do not seek. And if the seeking of the ignorant is negated, is the negation of their companionship...?

* Student: A fortiori.

* The Shaykh: A fortiori? Do you say this because it is a record we always repeat, or do you say it out of conviction?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: If the seeking of the ignorant is negated, companionship is negated all the more, because they themselves do not seek the ignorant nor look for them, let alone accompany them if they find them. Which is more eloquent: the author's explanation or the apparent meaning of the verse?

* Student: The apparent meaning of the verse.

* The Shaykh: The apparent meaning of the verse is better and more eloquent. That is: we do not seek the ignorant, let alone accompany them; because they are people of knowledge and insight, and a person of knowledge and insight does not seek the ignorant so as to be with them. Rather, they accompany only the good, people of knowledge, manliness, honor and religion. As for the ignorant, they do not seek them, do not look for them, and do not want them either.

Here "the ignorant" means the foolish (safih). Is it the one who lacks knowledge, or the foolish? The foolish, yes. It means the foolish, even if he is a scholar, because if he mishandles matters even though he is a scholar, he is in the position of the ignorant, indeed worse than the ignorant, because one who opposes knowingly is worse than one who opposes out of ignorance. The one who opposes knowingly is called foolish and is called a compound ignorant, yes, when he claims he knows. Unlike the ignorant person to whom knowledge has not come at all, for this one may be set right once he knows.

Good. So "the ignorant" here are not those who do not know, but the foolish.

If someone asks: what shows that ignorance (jahl) may mean foolishness (safah)?

We say: the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Repentance from Allah is only for those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon. Those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [an-Nisa' 17]. The phrase ﴿in ignorance﴾ undoubtedly means: in foolishness. For one who does evil while ignorant, without knowledge, has no sin for which he would need to repent. So ignorance here means foolishness. ﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾ [al-Qasas 55], that is, the foolish who act in ignorance.

Now, the one who is ignorant in the sense of not knowing: does a person seek him?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, perhaps he seeks him, to teach him. Perhaps he seeks him to teach him, as long as he is ignorant. For this reason the Messenger ﷺ used to present himself to the tribes during the season of Hajj[[Abu Dawud (4734) narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to present himself to the people at the place of standing, saying: "Is there not a man who will carry me to his people, for Quraysh have prevented me from conveying the speech of my Lord?"]], coming to a tribe (...) and calling them to Allah. He was seeking these ignorant ones in order to teach them. But the meaning of ignorance here is foolishness, because the fool's conduct is in reality exactly like the conduct of the ignorant, since he opposes the truth and does not act by it; yet he is worse than the ignorant, because he is not excused, and (...) and so on.

Now, we and you (...) these qualities. Is the intent that we recite them for knowledge or for action?

For both knowledge and action; for some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, used to learn ten verses and would learn what they contained of knowledge and action. Most people, when they read such verses, say: "How excellent their qualities are! How beautiful their deeds are!" and this is the furthest they benefit from the verse. But this is not sufficient. The purpose of mentioning these praiseworthy qualities, whether by way of reporting a state or by way of narrative, is admonition, that the person may take lesson from what has occurred: ﴿Indeed, in their stories there is a lesson for people of understanding﴾ [Yusuf 111]. We ask Allah to help us all to understand His Book and to act upon the revelation.

(...)

On the one who turns away from idle talk, by His saying: ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it﴾ [al-Qasas 55].

Second: it is recommended to turn away from idle talk, which is speech with no benefit and no good in it, and action is analogous to it, is it not? It is analogous to it. A person should not spend his time in deeds with no good in them.

Know that goodness is intrinsic and accidental: a thing may be good in itself, and it may be good for something else because of an incidental cause. For example, prayer's goodness is intrinsic, while walking toward it is good accidentally, since mere walking is not an act of worship in itself, but a means to another act of worship. Accordingly, if a person speaks about something that is neither remembrance, nor knowledge, nor enjoining good and forbidding evil, but it is speech intended to bring joy to his companions, is this good or not? Yes, it is good; but it is not intrinsically good by this speech, rather it is accidentally good, meaning good arising from the good intention in it. And this in reality, on this assessment, (...).

Clear? Note also that there is no equality between accidental good and intrinsic good, because accidental good loses its goodness when the cause ceases, while intrinsic good is established and permanent.

So we say: it is derived from this that abandoning idle talk is among what is praised. I think we mentioned this?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The praise for abandoning idle talk.

* Student: But (...)?

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, no. Since we said it is accidental good (...), since we said it is accidental good, then when it ends and the cause for which it was spoken ceases, what remains is idle talk with no benefit, and it is better to abandon it: «Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say what is good or remain silent»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6018) and Muslim (47/74) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]].

* Student: Yes, does this apply to other gatherings, or to the same gathering?

* The Shaykh: To this same gathering. As for other gatherings, each gathering has its own ruling, each gathering has its own ruling. But even regarding this gathering, if the cause for which I speak to them ceases, the goodness departs, so one may move them to another beneficial topic or the like. The discerning person in reality can manage this.

Among the best things is that some people, when they accompany someone, may direct to him beneficial questions about religion, for example, in order to occupy people from idle talk with no benefit, and also to draw them into inquiry, because a person may have a question he has forgotten, and when the door opens he remembers it. This is among the best things, especially for students of knowledge, who should be beneficial to people in their gatherings. A student of knowledge should not have a gathering like the gathering of the common folk; rather he should be keen on benefit as far as possible.

* From the noble verses it is derived: one should disassociate from the people of idle talk and not sit with them, by their saying: ﴿To us our deeds, and to you your deeds﴾ [al-Qasas 55].

* It is also derived from it: the legitimacy of greeting upon departure, by His saying: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ [al-Qasas 55]. Does this apply according to the author's explanation of it, or not?

* Student: No, (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, I want the general one.

Well; because the meaning of the author's statement, this benefit does not hold according to the author's explanation, since he holds that peace here is a peace of parting, not a greeting of peace. On this basis this benefit is not derived; he understood it as a peace of parting only on the basis of his explanation of idle talk as insult and slander. In truth, this explanation is deficient, because insult and abuse may not be called merely idle talk, but idle talk and transgression, yes, so it is more specific than being mere idle talk.

* Student: What is the benefit (...)?

* The Shaykh: This benefit (...), the legitimacy of greeting.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...); because we have preferred that it is general, yes.

* Student: O Shaykh, does it not contradict the verse (...)?

* The Shaykh: It does not contradict the verse, because His saying: ﴿when they hear idle talk﴾ refers to speech with no good in it and speech with evil in it. Speech with no good in it, one can (...) turn away from them, and say: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ as a greeting of peace, because it is not forbidden.

* From the benefits of the verse: it is not fitting for a sensible person to seek fools, let alone sit with them, by His saying: ﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾ [al-Qasas 55]; for seeking them in reality leads to sitting with them, and sitting with the ignorant is sinful, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a conversation other than that. And if Satan should cause you to forget, then do not sit after the reminder with the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-An'am 68]. So a person should not seek out the people of foolishness and sit with them, or at least take pleasure in what they do, for this is among the qualities that the people of goodness and faith do not have.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 56:

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾ [Al-Qasas 56].

The author said: (It was revealed concerning his (ﷺ) eagerness for the faith of his uncle Abu Talib).

Abu Talib is Abu 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. This uncle sheltered the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), defended him and supported him. But, may Allah protect us, he was prevented from faith because of the wretchedness that Allah had decreed for him.

In this there is a great wisdom: his not believing. For had he believed, he would not have been able to provide the defence that he gave the Messenger (ﷺ), since, had he believed, he would himself have become a target of harm from the polytheists. But because he remained upon their religion, they respected him to some degree, so his remaining in disbelief contained a wisdom of Allah that is evident. Otherwise he would not have been able to protect the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, with that protection.

This man had a virtue upon Islam because of his defence of it, and for this reason Allah permitted His Prophet (ﷺ) to intercede for him, although no other disbeliever could be interceded for. No one among the disbelievers has been interceded for, and none will be, except this man, because of his virtue upon Islam in protecting and defending the Messenger (ﷺ). However, this intercession did not benefit him fully; that is, it could not benefit him completely (...). It benefited him only in that he was in a shallow fire, with two sandals of fire upon him whose heat boils his brain, while he thinks that he is the most severely punished of the people of the Fire, when he is in fact the least of them, may Allah protect us. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Had it not been for me, he would have been in the lowest depth of the Fire." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3883), and Muslim (209/375), from the hadith of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, may Allah be pleased with him.] "Had it not been for me" means: because I interceded for him, or because he also did what he did in protecting the Messenger (ﷺ).

This uncle, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was extremely eager that he should believe, to the extent that at the time of death he said to him: "O uncle, say: There is no god but Allah, a word by which I may argue on your behalf before Allah." But he said, as his last words, that he was upon the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib, may Allah protect us, and that he would not abandon the way of the elders, the great elders of the Jahiliyyah. [Al-Bukhari (1360) and Muslim, with his wording (24/39), with their two chains from the hadith of al-Musayyab ibn Hazn, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: When death came to Abu Talib, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to him and found Abu Jahl and 'Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah ibn al-Mughirah with him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O uncle, say: There is no god but Allah, a word by which I may testify for you before Allah." Abu Jahl and 'Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah said: O Abu Talib, will you turn away from the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kept presenting it to him and repeating that statement until Abu Talib's last words to them were: He is upon the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib, and he refused to say: There is no god but Allah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Allah, I will surely seek forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden from it." Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to seek forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire﴾ [At-Tawbah 113], and Allah the Exalted revealed concerning Abu Talib, and said to His Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills, and He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾ [Al-Qasas 56].]

* Student: Does he not have (...)?

* Shaykh: Yes, he had two men from the polytheists instructing him: Will you turn away from the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib? So he, may Allah protect us, was sealed with the seal of wretchedness, and this attempt from the Messenger (ﷺ) did not benefit him.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, regretted this matter and said: "I will surely seek forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden from it." [See the previous hadith.] So he was forbidden from it, and it was said to him: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to seek forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire﴾ [At-Tawbah 113].

As for his regret over his uncle's not believing, Allah the Exalted consoled him with this matter: (﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾ [Al-Qasas 56] — his guidance).

﴿Indeed, you﴾: O Muhammad, the address is to him, and others are included a fortiori?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: Yes, others than the Messenger are included all the more so. If the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, who is the most noble of creation in the sight of Allah and the greatest of them in rank, cannot guide anyone, then how could anyone else?

As for His saying ﴿you do not guide﴾, the guidance meant here is the guidance of tawfiq (divine enabling), meaning: you do not place guidance in people's hearts. It is not the guidance of indication and direction (hidayat al-dalalah wa al-irshad), for that guidance is established for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, by His saying: ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ [Ash-Shura 52]. But the guidance of tawfiq, which is the placing of guidance into hearts, belongs to whom? It belongs to Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, alone.

As for His saying ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾, the author supplied (his guidance), (﴿whom you like﴾ his guidance), whereas the correct reading is: whom you like, ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom﴾ you like.

Why did the author shift to: (﴿you like﴾ his guidance)?

He said: because the Messenger could not love Abu Talib while he was a disbeliever, since the believer does not love disbelievers. But we say: this natural love does not contradict faith. A person may love, for example, his relative even if he is a disbeliever, but it is a natural love, just as a mother loves her child. Yes, religious love of this kind is not permitted between a believer and a disbeliever: ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers, their sons, their brothers﴾ [Al-Mujadilah 22].

Also, the author says (﴿whom you like﴾ his guidance). In reality, if we took it according to what the author said, it would be general to all people, since the Messenger loves to guide all people, not only his uncle Abu Talib. But (whom you like) is specific to Abu Talib, for example, or to his other relatives.

Also, if we said as the author said, there would be an ellipsis (idmar) in the verse. What is the ellipsis according to the author's assumption?

* Student: The ellipsis of guidance.

* Shaykh: The ellipsis of guidance. For the principle regarding the relative clause's pronoun (damir al-silah) is that it refers back to the relative clause itself, and ﴿you do not guide whom﴾: "whom" here is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), referring to whom? To Abu Talib. And the returning pronoun of the relative clause returns to the relative clause itself.

Thus it is clear that the preferred reading is (whom you like) for three reasons: one semantic and two verbal. The semantic reason: the verse was revealed concerning Abu Talib, and if we said (﴿whom you like﴾ his guidance) it would be general?

The two verbal reasons: if we assume (his guidance), there must be something omitted in the verse, and the principle is not to omit.

The second of the two verbal reasons: the returning pronoun of the relative clause returns to what?

* Student: To the relative clause.

* Shaykh: No, it does not return to the relative clause. The returning pronoun of the relative clause returns to the relative pronoun. So when it returns to ﴿man﴾ in His saying ﴿whom you like﴾, the meaning becomes: whom you like, he himself.

As for what the author noticed, it appears to me that the author noticed that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, could not love Abu Talib. The answer to that is that love is of two kinds: natural love and legislated love. Natural love does not contradict legislated love; they may coincide and may exist separately. If a believer is your relative, both are present in him. Which two?

* Student: The two loves.

* Shaykh: The two loves. If he is distant from you, only one love exists in him, the legislated one. If he is a relative but not a believer, only one love exists, the natural one.

﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾ [Al-Qasas 56]: then to whom does guidance belong?

﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [Al-Qasas 56]. ﴿Guides﴾ — guidance of what kind?

* Student: The guidance of tawfiq.

* Shaykh: The guidance of tawfiq.

﴿Whom He wills﴾: that is, whom He wills to guide (...), whom He wills to guide, by His saying: ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾.

And His saying ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ attaches the action to the will, and every action that Allah attaches to His will among His actions is accompanied by wisdom, since all of Allah's actions are based on wisdom. So ﴿whom He wills﴾ to guide is not arbitrary; the matter is governed by wisdom: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is upon a straight path﴾ [Hud 56]. No one is guided except one who is fit for guidance. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [Al-An'am 124]. Likewise, He knows best where this message should be. Whoever is fit for the message is sent, and whoever is fit to carry out the duty of the message is guided to that.

So the absoluteness in His saying ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ is, in what way? In accordance with wisdom. Yes.

He said: ﴿And He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾ [Al-Qasas 56]. The author said: (That is: knowing ﴿of those who are guided﴾).

Strange of the author. We have mentioned that we refute the author, and we refute him on two grounds. The first ground: is this a distortion of the Qur'an or not?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: Since he changed ﴿a'lam﴾, which indicates perfection in knowledge and superiority in it, into (knowing ('alim)), which does not prevent others from sharing this attribute. Do I not say: Muhammad is knowing, Zayd is knowing, Bakr is knowing, and so on to the end, or not? But if I say, for example: Zayd is more knowing (a'lam), it means no one equals him in his knowledge.

So the author has now distorted the Qur'an in that he explained ﴿a'lam﴾ as ('alim), explaining what indicates perfection by what indicates sharing.

The second ground: we say that describing Allah as ﴿a'lam﴾ is more complete than describing Him as ('alim), more complete without doubt. So what prevents us from saying the more complete form? He seems to intend that we should not say "Allah is more knowing," lest we make a sharer with Allah in knowledge.

We say: you have not made for Allah an equal sharer; you have made for Allah a sharer who falls short of Allah's knowledge. Allah is more knowing. But if you say that Allah is knowing ('alim), it is said to you: you have ascribed to Allah a knowledge that another may equal in it. So the correct view is that a'lam is an elative form (ism tafdil) and that it is on its proper pattern.

As for His saying ﴿most knowing of those who are guided﴾: is it of those who are actually guided, or of those who deserve to be among the guided?

If we say: ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills, and He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾, or of who is receptive to guidance, because the discussion now concerns the creation of guidance in a person's heart, then ﴿most knowing of those who are guided﴾ means not those who have been guided, but rather most knowing of who deserves to accept guidance. For this reason some of them explained it as those who are guided in Allah's knowledge, that is, those whom Allah knows will be guided.

In any case, the guided (al-muhtadi) means: one who is receptive to guidance, and it also means one who has actually been guided. Which is intended in the verse, the first or the second? The first: that is, He knows best who accepts guidance, so He guides him.

﴿And He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾.

Now, "those who are guided" here means those who were guided, in the sense that they accepted the guidance and held fast to it.

As for the connection between this verse and the verse we mentioned a little earlier: ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ [Ash-Shura 52], that the affirmed is not the negated, is it not?

* Student: Yes, indeed.

* Shaykh: ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾, and ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾?

So we say: ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ means the guidance of indication (hidayat al-dalalah), like His saying: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat 17]. ﴿We guided them﴾ means: We indicated the guidance to them, but they, may Allah protect us, preferred blindness over it and were not guided. As for the guidance here, it is the guidance of tawfiq, and this belongs to no one but Allah, the Glorified and Exalted.

From this verse we will indeed benefit that when a person strives and exerts himself in calling people to guidance and they are not guided, he should console himself with this verse: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾. Many people now have relatives, either in their homes or outside them, whom they call to guidance and who are not guided. So we say: praise be to Allah, who has made clear that this matter is not for us but for Him. If they are guided, then they and we both have the reward of guiding; if they are not guided, then we have the reward of indication and calling, and upon them is the burden of error.

* Student: ﴿A'lam﴾ (...)?

* Shaykh: No, its origin: we said that it is permissible to omit the subject and predicate. Also, the elative form is not necessarily followed by a verb governing an object, because the elative form can never govern a direct object. Do you understand?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: It can raise the agent under conditions that will come to us, Allah willing, in the conditions of the elative form, in the chapter on the action of the elative form. Yes.

* Student: (...) ﴿Allah is most knowing﴾?

* Shaykh: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [Al-An'am 124].

* Student: Yes. ﴿Allah is most knowing﴾ (...)?

* Shaykh: No, in it is ﴿Knowing ('alim)﴾: ﴿And Allah is knowing of what they do﴾ [An-Nur 41].

* Student: ﴿Indeed Allah is Knower of the unseen of the heavens﴾.

* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿Indeed Allah is Knower of the unseen of the heavens﴾ [Fatir 38], and this does not work: (a'lam ghayb al-samawat), (Indeed Allah is a'lam ghayb al-samawat) does not work.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verses 57–58:

He says: ("And they said" [al-Qasas 57], i.e., his people), meaning whose people? The people of the Messenger (ﷺ). "And they said," meaning the Quraysh: "If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched away from our land" [al-Qasas 57]. I seek refuge in Allah.

Whether they said this out of conviction or out of something other than conviction, this statement is false: "And they said, 'If we follow the guidance with you...'" The "with" (ma'a) here denotes accompaniment and following, meaning: "If we follow the guidance" and be "with you" in what you call to. By "the guidance" is meant what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought.

In their saying, "If we follow the guidance with you," there is an acknowledgment that what is with the Messenger is guidance. It is strange of them that they say, "If we follow the guidance with you," thereby admitting that it is guidance, and then after that they disbelieve. And what results from that?

"If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched away from our land." The author says: (i.e., we will be quickly removed from it). Al-khatf (snatching) is the swift taking away of a thing. That is, people will snatch us away, they will seize us and overpower us, because we have opposed what they were upon of shirk and idols, so they will quickly bring us to an end.

This is like His saying, Exalted is He: "It is only the Shaytan who instills fear of his allies" [Al 'Imran 175]. The Shaytan frightens the believers with the disbelievers, saying: "Look, if you believe, such and such will happen; if you hold fast to your religion, such and such will happen; if you oblige people to follow Islam outwardly and inwardly, the people will rise up against you; three-quarters of people desire wickedness, so if you oblige them with the religion, they will rise against you." There is no doubt that the Shaytan casts this into the hearts of people: "It is only the Shaytan who instills fear of his allies." But what is our obligation in this situation? "So do not fear them, but fear Me, if you are believers" [Al 'Imran 175]. The obligation is not to fear. As long as we see that we are walking upon the truth, we will not fear anyone. Rather, we know with certainty that if we were upon the truth, the people would fear us and we would not fear them, or not? "Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing, for them is security" [al-An'am 82]. Security from whom?

* Student: From Allah.

* Shaykh: Security from Allah, but security from what? Security from fear: "He who fed them against hunger and secured them from fear" [Quraysh 4]. "For them is security" from fear, neither from Allah nor from others; that is, they do not fear the punishment of Allah, because they believed with clear faith (...).

Likewise, Allah grants them security from what they fear, and this is one of the two interpretations of His saying: "The Believer, the Guardian" [al-Hashr 23]: that al-Mu'min is the One who grants security to His obedient servants from what they fear. Do you understand? But this requires faith in reality, requires true faith. When true faith exists and the Shari'ah is implemented, then I guarantee that complete security will be attained, more than what is attained by tanks, machine guns and the like. These conditions that we hear of now, especially this year, of assassinations, explosions and other things: do the countries in which this has happened not have weapons to deter people? They have powerful weapons, stronger than the weapons of these saboteurs, but they do not have faith through which security is attained. However powerful (...) it will not bring security. Security is truly achieved by faith; faith and security go together.

Here these disbelievers say: "If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched away from our land." Is this statement correct or not? It is not correct. Whether they said it to repel what the Messenger (ﷺ) calls them to, out of something other than conviction, or they said it out of conviction, the matter does not occur. The evidence: "Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary, to which the fruits of every thing are brought?" [al-Qasas 57]. "We established for them a secure sanctuary," meaning: We made for them a place, yes, like: "If We have established them in the land" [al-Hajj 41], i.e., We made for them a place in which they are established. Here: "We established for them a secure sanctuary," meaning We made for them a place, that secure sanctuary.

As for His saying "ḥaraman" [a sanctuary]: "ḥaraman" is on the pattern of "baṭal," so it is an adjective of resemblance (ṣifah mushabbahah), from ḥurmah (sanctity), meaning a sacred place, i.e., one possessing sanctity. There is no doubt that Makkah al-Mukarramah has great sanctity in people's souls, even in the Jahiliyyah.

As for His saying "āminan" [secure], here the word "āmin" is an active participle. Is the sanctuary the one that is secure, or is the one within it secure?

* Student: Both.

* Shaykh: How both?

* Student: Meaning the sanctuary itself (...).

* Shaykh: The author says: (they are secure therein from raids and killing carried out by some Arabs against others), so he made "āmin" mean that its people are secure, meaning he explained "āminan" with his words "they are secure," so the meaning is: its people are secure.

In my view, the description here applies to the sanctuary, because the author (...) now is a descriptive attribute by association (wasf sababī), and I see that it is a real attribute (wasf ḥaqīqī). They have a term for an epithet: they call it a real epithet (na't ḥaqīqī) and a causal epithet (na't sababī). The real epithet is that which is an attribute of the described noun, and the causal is that which is an attribute of something else connected to it. Yes. So if you say: "I have a fasting man," this epithet is real, since "fasting" refers to "man." "I have a fasting man whose father..." this epithet is causal, because the attribute "fasting" refers to the one described or to what is connected to him? To what is connected to him. Yes.

The author (...) is of the category of the causal epithet, meaning those whose people are secure. In my view it is a real epithet, and that the sanctuary itself is the secure one. When a place is secure, without doubt whoever is in it will be secure. So this place is secure, and as Muhammad said: it is secure, no one transgresses against it, and whoever intends it with evil, Allah destroys him: "And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing, We will make him taste a painful punishment" [al-Hajj 25].

Now, this secure sanctuary: even the Arabs with their disbelief, however much the Quraysh did, could never raid this House. Moreover, the people of this House are the masters of the Arabs even in the Jahiliyyah, so how can they say: "we will be snatched away from our land" [al-Qasas 57]?! This is impossible, because the sanctuary is secure, so they are secure within it; they cannot be snatched away within it. Furthermore, this town, along with being secure, is also a comfortable living, and no hardship afflicts its people; hence He said: "to which the fruits of every thing are brought" [al-Qasas 57].

"Yujbā" (is brought): the author says: (with the upper and lower letters, i.e., with ta' and ya').

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: (...) (with the upper and lower letters)?

* Student: "Yujbā" and "Tujbā" [in the readings].

* Shaykh: "Yujbā" and "Tujbā" are two readings of the seven canonical readings. The meaning of "yujbā" is "is gathered," from al-jibāyah, which is collecting.

His saying "ilayhi" (to it): its meaning (...). "Yujbā" also means "is brought to," so the fruits of every land are gathered and come to it, they come to this town, and this is the reality. Ibrahim said: "Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without cultivation, by Your Sacred House, our Lord, that they may establish prayer. So make hearts among the people incline toward them and provide for them from the fruits, that they may be grateful" [Ibrahim 37]. So the fruits used to come to this town at every season, from nearby places like al-Ta'if and others, and from distant places.

* Student: The deed of the Barmakids (...)?

* Shaykh: (...) with the House? It does not contradict it; we will mention it, God willing, later.

His saying: "from every direction" [min kulli awb]: meaning from every direction, "awb" means "ṣawb," and "ṣawb" and "awb" mean the side, i.e., from every side. ("A provision" for them "from Us" [from ladunna].)

"Rizqan" [a provision]: what is its meaning? What is the meaning of provision?

* Student: Gift.

* Shaykh: Gift. Provision is gift, and it is accusative as an object of purpose, or as an infinitive, or as an absolute object of His saying "yujbā"; "yujbā" is a gift.

His saying "min ladunnā" [from Us] means: from Our presence, and they have no power or ability over it; rather, the command from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is what made these fruits be brought to them.

("But most of them do not know" [al-Qasas 57] that what you say is true.)

His saying "but most of them do not know": the object of knowing is omitted in the verse. He did not say "they do not know" such-and-such; the author restricted it with his words: ("they do not know" that what you say is true). In my view the matter is more general and comprehensive, because omitting the object indicates generality. So we say: ("they do not know" that what you say is true), and they also do not know the outcome. For the outcome is that if this sanctuary was secure in a state of disbelief, and fruits were brought to it in a state of disbelief, then what about a state of faith? How, when Ibrahim said: "And provide its people with fruits, those of them who believe in Allah and the Last Day" [al-Baqarah 126]? So if the people of this town are believers, their security will be greater, on the one hand because the place itself is secure, and on the other because the believer in this place is also secure. If this security exists even though these are polytheists, then when they are believers it will be greater. For this reason, when what happened among the Muslims of the violation of this great town occurred, those tyrants who were empowered over them were empowered, such as the case of the Barmakids, and as will happen at the end of time, when a man from Abyssinia will be empowered over the House, who will come to it and demolish it stone by stone. Therefore, in truth, we fear greatly what we see in Makkah of wickedness and sins; we fear that this may be the beginning of a grave violation of the sanctuary, until this wretch is empowered over it. But we do not know what will happen in the future; sins in the sanctuary have a great effect, either on the sanctuary itself or on those around it.

Now, he says: "But most of them do not know" [al-Qasas 57]. So we say: "do not know" is not restricted to the truth of what he brought (...), but is general, even regarding the end and the final outcome they would have if they believed.

"And how many a town have We destroyed which exulted in its livelihood" [al-Qasas 58].

The benefit of mentioning the destruction of the previous towns is so that it may be said to the Quraysh: disbelief does not prevent fear and does not prevent punishment; rather, it is the cause of punishment. You say that if we believe, people will snatch us away; this is not the reality, but rather the opposite is the reality. For this reason He said: "And how many a town have We destroyed which exulted in its livelihood" [al-Qasas 58]. It is as if Allah is giving evidence to refute these people, that disbelief does not save, by what He destroyed the previous nations with, those who exulted in their livelihood.

Now, the statement of these disbelievers to the Messenger (ﷺ): "If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched away from our land" [al-Qasas 57]. Allah, Exalted, refuted it by negation and affirmation. As for the affirmation, He said: We have established for them a secure sanctuary; this town cannot be fearful. So if it was secure in a state of disbelief, then in a state of faith it is even more so.

As for the negation, His saying: "And how many a town have We destroyed which exulted in its livelihood" [al-Qasas 58]: disbelief does not secure its companion; rather it is the cause of what? Of his destruction. So your remaining in disbelief is not what saves you from people snatching you away; rather it is the cause of your ruin. This is the reality: the chiefs and leaders of Quraysh went out to Badr to destroy themselves, did they not? The sanctuary was secure and nothing came to it, but they were the ones who went out to their own destruction, and they were killed at Badr.

So the conclusion is that Allah says: We deny what you said for two reasons. One is a positive matter: that this sanctuary is secure, and people are the ones who are snatched away around it: "Do they not see that We made a secure sanctuary while people are being snatched away all around them?" [al-'Ankabut 67]. Second: that disbelief is not a cause of survival, or is it?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: What is the evidence? "And how many a town have We destroyed which exulted in its livelihood" [al-Qasas 58]. So believe, so that you may be in security and in a secure place.

As for His saying "awa lam numakkin" [Have We not established], the hamzah here, what does it mean? It means affirmation: meaning, indeed We have established, as in His saying: "Did We not expand for you your breast?" [al-Sharh 1], i.e., indeed We expanded for you.

As for His saying "awa lam" [or did not]: I think we have passed over many such expressions, and we said that the grammarians have two positions on this. The first position: that the hamzah enters upon something implied, and the waw or fa' is a conjunction on that implied element. The second position: that the position of the hamzah is after the waw, but it was moved forward because it is an interrogative particle, and its original form is "wa-alam yaraw" [and have they not seen].

* Student: What is the implied element in the verse?

* Shaykh: The implied element according to what suits the context: "And they said, 'If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched away from our land'" [al-Qasas 57]. Yes: were they snatched away while We had not established for them a secure sanctuary?

So if you want a cause that will save you from the punishment of Allah, then hold fast to guidance by the guidance of Allah, for it is the cause that saves from the punishment of Allah.

The Exalted said: ﴿And the day He calls them, and says, "What did you answer the messengers?"﴾ [Al-Qasas 28:65].

* In this verse: ﴿﴿And the day He calls them﴾﴾. At the beginning of the sentence: what preceded in His words ﴿And the day He calls them, and says, "Where are My partners?"﴾ [Al-Qasas 28:62], namely the affirmation that Allah's speech is with a voice, that it is heard, and that it is with letters, or not? All of this has preceded.

* And it is derived from His words ﴿﴿What did you answer the messengers?﴾﴾: that people are questioned about their faith in the messengers just as they are questioned about tawhid. ﴿What did you answer the messengers?﴾

* And it is derived from it: that the questioning in the Hereafter is general to all creation, or not?

* Student: Yes.

* Sheikh: ﴿The messengers﴾ means Muhammad and others. As for questioning in the grave, many scholars have held that it is specific to this Ummah, based on his saying (ﷺ): "Indeed this Ummah will be tested in its graves" [narrated by Muslim (2867/67) from the hadith of Zayd ibn Thabit, may Allah be pleased with him]. And his saying: "It has been revealed to me that you will be tested in your graves" [narrated by al-Bukhari (86) from the hadith of Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with her and her father, with the wording: "It was revealed to me that you will be tried in your graves"]. The matter is one of difference of opinion, and it was discussed under tawhid. Rather, on the Day of Resurrection the questioning is general by the explicit text of the Qur'an.

* And among the benefits of the verse: the manifestation of the virtue of the messengers, peace be upon them, in that Allah the Exalted established the truth of His messengership in this great station.

* And among the benefits of the verse: that the news becomes blind to the disbelievers on that day, even if they were knowledgeable?

* Student: Yes.

* Sheikh: Even if they were knowledgeable. This is like the deceased when he is asked in his grave: "Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is your Prophet?" [Abu Dawud (4753) with his chain from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Seek refuge in Allah from the punishment of the grave," twice or thrice, and said: "Indeed he hears the sound of their sandals when they turn away, when it is said to him: 'O you, who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is your Prophet?'"]. Even if he was knowledgeable, for if he is not a believer, he does not answer correctly.

* And among them: that no one will avail anyone on the Day of Resurrection, by His words: ﴿so they will not question one another﴾ [Al-Qasas 28:66], for no one will avail anyone anything on that day, nor will he rescue him from what befalls him.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿As for one who repents and believes and does righteousness, it is expected that he will be among the successful﴾ [Al-Qasas 28:67].

* Student: (...)?

* Sheikh: Yes. Even His words ﴿And the day He calls them, and says, "Where are My partners?"﴾ [Al-Qasas 28:62] are general, to all the polytheists.

* Student: (...)?

* Sheikh: From among the polytheists. Therefore He said: ﴿So the news became blind to them﴾ [Al-Qasas 28:66]. As for the believers, they are believers and are not questioned; their questioning in their graves suffices (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 67–72 (part 1 of 3):

He said: ﴿As for him who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds﴾.
(As for, ʾammā) is a conditional particle, and its response is His saying: ﴿then perhaps he will be among the successful﴾.
As for His saying: ﴿As for him who repents﴾: repentance (tawbah) has already been explained to us as returning to Allah, the Exalted, from disobedience to Him to obedience to Him. It has five conditions: remorse, giving up the sin, resolving never to return to it, that it be before death, and that it be before the sun rises from the West.[[Abu Dawud (2479) related with his chain from Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Migration will not cease until repentance ceases, and repentance will not cease until the sun rises from the West."]]
* Student: And sincerity.
* The Shaykh: Yes, and sincerity, and that it be at a time when it is accepted, which is before death and before the sun rises from the West.
As for his saying (from shirk): perhaps the author felt it necessary to restrict repentance here to repentance from shirk, by His saying ﴿and believes﴾, because faith comes after shirk. The sinner is a believer even if he is sinful, and this is what led the author to restrict repentance to repentance from shirk.
As for his saying (﴿and believes﴾ means he affirms the Oneness of Allah): this is a deficiency in the explanation of faith, because faith in the Sharia is not merely tasdiq (affirmation). It is true that in the lexicon faith means affirmation, but in the Sharia it is what?
* Student: Affirmation.
* The Shaykh: Affirmation, on condition that it includes acceptance and submission. There must be acceptance and submission, otherwise one is not a believer, merely one who affirms. Abu Talib, for example, affirmed the message of the Messenger ﷺ, yet he was a disbeliever, because he did not accept it and did not submit.[[Al-Bukhari (3884) and Muslim (24/39) related from al-Musayyab ibn Hazn, who said: When Abu Talib's death approached, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to him and found with him Abu Jahl and 'Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah ibn al-Mughirah. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O uncle, say: There is no god but Allah, a word by which I will testify for you before Allah." Abu Jahl and 'Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah said: O Abu Talib, will you turn away from the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib?
