It is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he asks Allah, mighty and majestic, for permission to intercede, and he prostrates beneath the Throne, and Allah then opens for him praises of Him that He had not opened for him before.[[This is in the long hadith of intercession narrated by the two Shaykhs: al-Bukhari (4712) and Muslim (194/327), from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "I will fall prostrate before my Lord, mighty and majestic. Then Allah will open for me from His praises and good praise of Him something He has not opened for anyone before me..." The hadith.]] This is before entering Paradise, indeed before the creation is judged. So to Allah, the Exalted, belongs all praise in the Hereafter.

﴿وَلَهُ الْحُكْمُ﴾ ("To Him belongs the judgment"): "lahu" is a predicate placed before its subject, and placing the predicate first conveys exclusivity (ḥaṣr). ﴿وَلَهُ الْحُكْمُ﴾ The author said: (the binding decree over everything). And ﴿al-ḥukm﴾ includes the decree (qaḍāʾ), which is the cosmic judgment, as the author said, and it includes the legislative judgment (ḥukm sharʿī). So judgment belongs to Allah, both in decree and in legislation. There is no judge except Allah, the Exalted. Whoever seeks judgment from other than Allah has gone astray; whoever follows the guidance of Allah will not go astray nor be wretched.

Here we noted that placing the predicate first conveys exclusivity, because judgment belongs to Allah alone. This is so when the intended meaning is absolute judgment. Absolute judgment belongs to Allah; no one shares it with Him. He is the One who makes a thing obligatory, forbids it, recommends it, or permits it. Likewise in cosmic matters, He is the One who sends down rain, removes drought, gives life, causes death, and provides sustenance. All of this is among the cosmic judgments.

Has anyone disputed with Allah over these two kinds of judgment? Yes. Humans have disputed with their Lord over both the cosmic judgment and the legislative judgment. Among them are those who affirmed a creator alongside Allah, and among them are those who claimed to be a lord who acts as he wills. Violations in legislative judgment are more numerous and more evident. How many there are who legislate and consider their legislation binding, like the law of Allah or even higher! These, it has already been established, are disbelievers, even if they pray, pay zakah, fast, and perform Hajj; they are disbelievers.

Likewise, what else relates to judgment, such as whom?
* Student: Like Pharaoh.
* Shaykh: Like Pharaoh, because he disputed with Allah over the decree, and he said: ﴿O chiefs, I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas 38], and he said: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Nazi'at 24].

We have understood that absolute judgment belongs to Allah. But is there a restricted judgment? We say: Yes, there is a restricted judgment, but it is by the command of Allah. This is why in the books of the scholars we read: (they go to the judge), (the legitimate judge said), (by the permission of the judge), and similar expressions. Is the judgment that this person holds restricted or unrestricted? It is restricted and confined: restricted to being under the judgment of Allah, confined to a specific place and a specific time. So absolute judgment belongs to whom? To Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in this world and in the Hereafter.

As for restricted judgment, it belongs to other than Allah, such as what? Such as what the scholars say: the legitimate judge, and the judge decides between them, and similar things. This judgment is restricted in its time, its place, and its kind. As for time, it is known that it is restricted: does this legitimate judge remain forever? No. As for place, he judges only in a certain patch of earth, not over the earth and the heavens. As for kind, it is restricted to being under the judgment of Allah; his judgment is not absolute, but is under the judgment of Allah, so he has no power to change anything of the judgments of Allah, the Exalted.

﴿وَلَهُ الْحُكْمُ وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ ("To Him belongs the judgment, and to Him you will be returned" [al-Qasas 70]). ﴿إِلَيْهِ﴾ also has its complement placed first, because ﴿إِلَيْهِ﴾ is connected to what? ﴿تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ ("you will be returned"). Placing the complement first indicates exclusivity. So the return to Allah, however long the world lasts, however far a person goes, and whatever a person is, his return is to Allah. The author said: (﴿وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ by resurrection), and when is the resurrection?
* Student: On the Day of Resurrection.
* Shaykh: On the Day of Resurrection. So people, indeed all creatures, have their return to Allah, the Exalted, and that is on the Day of Resurrection. Nothing remains that will not be gathered, even the ant?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Everything will be gathered, until it becomes clear that the whole matter returns to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* * *

(﴿Say﴾ to the people of Makkah, ﴿Have you considered﴾ tell me). The address is to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Say﴾. But who is addressed? The author says: (the people of Makkah). The correct view is that it is general to everyone: (﴿أَرَأَيْتُمْ﴾ meaning: inform me). The author's explanation of it as (inform me) is an explanation of meaning rather than of wording, because ra'aytum (رأى) here is from visual sight, and the meaning is: Did you see that, then inform me about it. But the author and others among the scholars explain it by its necessary implication, because what necessarily accompanies seeing is a person reporting what he sees.

﴿أَرَأَيْتُمْ﴾: the scholars say that ra'aytum here takes two objects, even though it is visual, it takes two objects. The first object may be present or may be omitted; most often it is omitted, but it may be present. For example: ﴿Say: Have you considered what Allah has sent down to you of provision, and you made of it lawful and unlawful? Say: Did Allah permit you?﴾ [Yunus 59]. Here the first object is present: ﴿مَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾ ("what Allah has sent down").

﴿Say: Have you considered what you invoke besides Allah? Show me what they have created of the earth﴾, and so on to the end [al-Ahqaf 4]. Here the first object is omitted. Here: ﴿Have you considered if Allah makes﴾ [al-Qasas 71]. The first object is omitted, and the estimate is: ﴿أَرَأَيْتُمْ﴾ your condition? That is: inform me about your condition, what would it be if such and such happened? So the first object is omitted, and the clause ﴿مَنْ إِلَهٌ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ﴾ [al-Qasas 71] is in the accusative position as the second object.

(﴿Have you considered if Allah makes for you the night perpetual﴾, continuing forever): ﴿جَعَلَ﴾ means "made," so its first object is ﴿اللَّيْلَ﴾ and its second object is ﴿سَرْمَدًا﴾: that Allah should make ﴿عَلَيْكُمُ اللَّيْلَ سَرْمَدًا﴾ ("the night perpetual over you").

﴿اللَّيْلَ﴾ ("the night"): from the sunset to its rising. This is the night; its meaning is that the disappearance of the sun below the horizon is the night, and its appearance is the day. The light that follows it after sunset or precedes it after dawn is from the beginnings of the day or its ends. Otherwise, the reality is that the night is from sunset to sunrise.

As for ﴿سَرْمَدًا﴾: it is said that its origin is sardan, and sard means succession, that is, consecutive. On this explanation the nun is extra, and its morphological pattern is?
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿سَرْمَدًا﴾?
* Student: (fa'malan).
* Shaykh: (fa'malan), because the nun is extra. It is also said that the nun is original and that it comes from (sarmada) when it continues. On this view its morphological pattern is (fa'lalan), because the nun is original.

What concerns us is the meaning of sarmad: it means lasting and continuous.

﴿إِلَى يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ﴾ ("until the Day of Resurrection"). If the night were perpetual until the Day of Resurrection, could anyone bring the day? No one can, indeed no one can bring the day forward before its time or delay it after its time. Now, if the whole world gathered to make the sun rise at twelve, for example, could they, if the whole world gathered to make it rise at twelve minus one minute, could they? They could not. How (...) once? Or to make it delayed until twelve and one minute, they could not; or to shift it slightly from its place? They cannot (...).

So whoever cannot change it, neither in time nor in place, cannot bring it or bring the day ever. This is why the Exalted said: (﴿Who is a god other than Allah﴾, by your claim, ﴿who would bring you light﴾, daytime in which you seek livelihood).

﴿مَنْ﴾ is the subject, ﴿إِلَهٌ﴾ is its predicate, ﴿غَيْرُ اللَّهِ﴾ is its qualifier, and ﴿يَأْتِيكُمْ﴾ is a circumstantial clause describing ﴿إِلَهٌ﴾. That is: which god ﴿would bring you light﴾.

The author's statement (by your claim) is something only a person who understands the Arabic language would notice, because ﴿مَنْ﴾ is used to ask for specification, and it accepts plurality, since specification is sought only when? When there are multiple things. When things are multiple, specification is requested. So if you say: Who stood up? you have now established by this question that a number of people stood up, but you are asking for the specification of this one who stood. When He says ﴿مَنْ إِلَهٌ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ﴾, its meaning now is that he has affirmed in the verse that there are gods, and what is sought by ﴿مَنْ﴾ is what? Specification: identify for me the god who brings you?

Is the reality that there are many gods? This is why the author said (by your claim), meaning: if you claim that there are gods, then which god brings you light? This is more forceful as a challenge. If he had said: (Is there a god other than Allah?), the question would be about the existence of a god, not the specification of the god. But asking for its specification is more forceful as a challenge; that is: even on your claim that these are gods, we challenge you: where is the god who brings this thing? If you say: By Allah, none of our gods does this, it becomes clear that their divinity is false, because a god must be capable, hearing, seeing... to the end (...).

I seem to be speaking in English now! ﴿مَنْ﴾ is used to seek what?
* Student: Specification.
* Shaykh: It seeks specification among a plurality. Here ﴿مَنْ إِلَهٌ﴾ requires that there be multiple gods, and this is not literal, but according to the claim of these polytheists, who claim that there is a god deserving worship. If that is so, by your claim that it deserves worship, then let it be capable; if it is not capable, it does not deserve worship.

﴿يَأْتِيكُمْ بِضِيَاءٍ﴾ [al-Qasas 71]: the ba' here is for transitivity; that is, it brings light to you. He said (ḍiyāʾ, light) because it is the sign of the day, indeed it is in reality the day itself, either its sign or it is the day itself.

(﴿أَفَلَا تَسْمَعُونَ﴾ ("Will you not hear?"), that is, hearing with understanding by which you turn back from association).

﴿أَفَلَا تَسْمَعُونَ﴾: meaning, have your ears been struck deaf so that you do not hear? The intended meaning of the question here is the hearing of understanding by which a person is restrained from his error, not mere hearing of perception (...).

Here someone may say: Why did He not say (Will you not see)? Because the day is the place of seeing, and seeing is clearer there (...). Rather He said ﴿أَفَلَا تَسْمَعُونَ﴾?

We say: Because it is an explanation of His saying ﴿عَلَيْكُمُ اللَّيْلَ سَرْمَدًا﴾, and is the night a place of sight or a place of hearing? A place of hearing. This is why He said ﴿أَفَلَا تَسْمَعُونَ﴾, and it is not an explanation at the end of the verse ﴿مَنْ إِلَهٌ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ يَأْتِيكُمْ بِضِيَاءٍ﴾, but rather an explanation at the beginning of the verse.

The meaning: you do not hear with the hearing from which you benefit, because the night is the place of hearing and not the place of sight (...).

Absolute monotheism belongs to Allah alone?
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ﴾.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What is the benefit?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The saying of the Exalted: ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ﴾ ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾ [al-Qasas 70].
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ﴾.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿لَهُ الْحَمْدُ﴾?
* Student: Yes (...).
* Shaykh: Upon them (...) with this?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: And what does he say?
* Student: Yes (...)?
* Shaykh: ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾?
* Student: Virtue (...).
* Shaykh: No, this (...).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿مَا تُكِنُّ صُدُورُهُمْ وَمَا يُعْلِنُونَ﴾ [al-Qasas 69].
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: So the generality: it became ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ﴾.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾. From it is derived: the affirmation of Allah's divinity.
* Second: His being singular in divinity, by His saying ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾.
* Third benefit: Allah, the Exalted, is specially deserving of absolute praise, by His saying ﴿لَهُ الْحَمْدُ﴾, absolute praise encompassing this world and the Hereafter.
* From the benefits of the verse: the manifestation of the perfection of Allah's attributes, in this world and the Hereafter, because praise describes the praised one with perfection.
* From the benefits of the verse: Allah, the Exalted, is specially the One who judges, that He alone is the Judge, by His saying ﴿وَلَهُ الْحُكْمُ﴾. What was mentioned of affirming judgment to others is a restricted matter, like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And when you judge between people, judge with justice﴾ [al-Nisa' 58]. This is restricted.
* From the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of resurrection, by His saying ﴿وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾.

﴿Say: Have you considered if Allah makes for you the night perpetual until the Day of Resurrection﴾, and so on to the end.
* From the benefits of the verse: the challenge to these polytheists that their idols should bring good or repel harm.
* Second: the demonstration of Allah's power, the Exalted, since nothing can prevent Him from making the night perpetual until the Day of Resurrection.
* Third: reminding of Allah's blessing, the Exalted, reminding the servants of Allah's blessing, since things are made evident by their opposites.
* From the benefits of the verse: no one can change Allah's sunnah in the universe; if He made it perpetual, no one could remove it.
* From the benefits of the verse: encouragement to hear what is recited of the Book of Allah with understanding and acceptance, by His saying ﴿أَفَلَا تَسْمَعُونَ﴾.
* From the benefits of the verse: the explanation of Allah's blessing upon the servants in the light of day. How much energy does this light save?
* Student: Countless.
* Shaykh: Countless. That is, if all the lighting of the night were to fall during the day, and how much energy does a nation consume to light the night? Although it is not like the light of day, in this we know the measure of Allah's blessing, the Exalted, in this light that reaches people in great quantities (...).

The last benefit? An explanation?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) the day.

﴿Say: Have you considered if Allah makes for you the day perpetual until the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Qasas 72].
* Student: The saying of the Exalted (...)?
* Shaykh: No, the intended point is the limit.

And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: Have you considered if Allah makes for you the day perpetual until the Day of Resurrection? Who is a god other than Allah who would bring you a night in which you rest? Will you not see?﴾ [al-Qasas 72].
* What is derived from this verse is what is derived from the verse before it, except that it has an addition, which is: the explanation of Allah's blessing, the Exalted. What is derived from the verse is what is derived from what precedes it in what they share.
* From it: the explanation of Allah's blessing, the Exalted, in the night, which He made a place of rest, by His saying ﴿in which you rest﴾.
* From it: that sleep at night is more beneficial to the body than sleep by day, since Allah made the night the place and time of rest, and this is an observed matter.
* From it: encouragement to reflect upon the signs of Allah, the Exalted, by His saying ﴿Will you not see?﴾, because this indicates encouragement for a person to reflect upon these signs that Allah, the Exalted, has made, so that he may take evidence from them of the perfection of the Creator's power.

As for the explanation of Allah's power and the like, it has already passed.

He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And out of His mercy﴾ [al-Qasas 73].
* Student: Doesn't this verse benefit (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, (...) we mentioned that sleep at night is more beneficial to the body than by day, because in it there is stillness. But (...) of the night; a person feels rest, but it is not like the night.
* Student: Meaning (...)?
* Shaykh: It is not equal to it in any case, taking health into consideration (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 67–72 (part 1 of 3):

He said: ﴿As for him who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds﴾.
(As for, ʾammā) is a conditional particle, and its response is His saying: ﴿then perhaps he will be among the successful﴾.
As for His saying: ﴿As for him who repents﴾: repentance (tawbah) has already been explained to us as returning to Allah, the Exalted, from disobedience to Him to obedience to Him. It has five conditions: remorse, giving up the sin, resolving never to return to it, that it be before death, and that it be before the sun rises from the West.[[Abu Dawud (2479) related with his chain from Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Migration will not cease until repentance ceases, and repentance will not cease until the sun rises from the West."]]
* Student: And sincerity.
* The Shaykh: Yes, and sincerity, and that it be at a time when it is accepted, which is before death and before the sun rises from the West.
As for his saying (from shirk): perhaps the author felt it necessary to restrict repentance here to repentance from shirk, by His saying ﴿and believes﴾, because faith comes after shirk. The sinner is a believer even if he is sinful, and this is what led the author to restrict repentance to repentance from shirk.
As for his saying (﴿and believes﴾ means he affirms the Oneness of Allah): this is a deficiency in the explanation of faith, because faith in the Sharia is not merely tasdiq (affirmation). It is true that in the lexicon faith means affirmation, but in the Sharia it is what?
* Student: Affirmation.
* The Shaykh: Affirmation, on condition that it includes acceptance and submission. There must be acceptance and submission, otherwise one is not a believer, merely one who affirms. Abu Talib, for example, affirmed the message of the Messenger ﷺ, yet he was a disbeliever, because he did not accept it and did not submit.[[Al-Bukhari (3884) and Muslim (24/39) related from al-Musayyab ibn Hazn, who said: When Abu Talib's death approached, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to him and found with him Abu Jahl and 'Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah ibn al-Mughirah. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O uncle, say: There is no god but Allah, a word by which I will testify for you before Allah." Abu Jahl and 'Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah said: O Abu Talib, will you turn away from the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ kept presenting it to him and repeating that statement, until Abu Talib's last word to them was: He is upon the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib, and he refused to say: There is no god but Allah. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "By Allah, I will surely seek forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden from it." Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to seek forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they are close relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire﴾, and Allah revealed concerning Abu Talib, saying to His Messenger ﷺ: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills, and He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾.]]
And the author's saying (affirms the Oneness of Allah) is also deficient, because faith is not merely that you affirm the unity of Allah, but that you affirm everything that must be believed in. The Messenger ﷺ explained that faith is that you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and you believe in predestination, its good and its evil.[[As in the hadith of Gabriel related by Muslim (8/1) from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, in which: "He said: Then inform me about faith." He said: "That you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and that you believe in divine decree, its good and its evil..."]]. So these six pillars are necessary in faith.
As for His saying ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾: the author said (he performs the obligatory duties). This too is deficient. Rather, what is meant is ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾, i.e., he does a righteous deed that includes the obligatory duties, and what else? And the voluntary acts.
Righteous deeds are those that combine two matters: sincerity and following the Sunnah, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion, inclining to truth﴾ [al-Bayyinah 5]. ﴿Being sincere to Him in religion﴾ is sincerity, and ﴿inclining to truth﴾ is following. The ḥanīf is one who is not deviating, and whoever departs from following is deviating.
So a righteous deed is then: every deed that includes sincerity and following. Its opposite is the corrupt, which contains shirk or innovation, shirk or innovation. This is not a righteous deed.
Whoever combines these three attributes: ﴿then perhaps he will be among the successful﴾.
﴿Perhaps (ʿasā)﴾: (ʿasā) is from which verbs?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, it is of the verbs of hope (tarajjī). But with regard to Allah, Exalted is He, it is not for hope; it is for causation (taʿlīl). For this reason Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "ʿasā" from Allah is obligatory.[[Ibn Abi Hatim related in his Tafsir (5044) from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "ʿasā" from Allah is binding.]] Because the cause is necessarily joined to the effect: when the cause exists, the effect is established. The cause of success is repentance, faith, and righteous deeds; when these exist, success exists.
﴿Then perhaps he will be (ʿasā an yakūna)﴾: ﴿an yakūna﴾ means the one who ﴿repents, believes, and does righteous deeds﴾ ﴿will be among the successful﴾. The author said: (the saved by the promise of Allah), meaning the saved by the promise of Allah, i.e., by what Allah promised them. But success, as the author said, is not merely salvation; rather it is deliverance from what is feared and attainment of what is desired. This is success: that a person be saved from what he flees from and obtain what he loves.
As for His saying ﴿then perhaps he will be among the successful﴾: if we say it is for hope, for instance, it includes a benefit: that a person, even if he does this deed, should be hopeful and not certain. He should hope for success and not be certain of it, because he does not know; there may be obstacles or a defect that prevents success from being attained. So the verse guides, if we say that (ʿasā) is for hope, (...), for hope considered from the standpoint of the agent and not from the standpoint of the one who decides. The benefit of it is what? That a person, even if he acts, does not become certain, but remains hopeful. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts tremble, because they will return to their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun 60]. Here the situation is not one of certainty, but of hope, so let him be hopeful.
Then Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And your Lord creates whatever He wills﴾ [al-Qasas 68].
This verse is a justification for the invalidity of the gods of the polytheists and the affirmation of divinity for Allah, by way of affirming creation, for the Creator is the one who must be worshipped, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you﴾ [al-Baqarah 21]. This attribute is a reason for the command, for the Creator must be the God who is worshipped, as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And those they invoke besides Allah create nothing, while they are created. [They are] dead, not alive, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾ [al-Nahl 20–21]. If they do not create, how can they deserve to be worshipped? And Ibrahim said to his father: ﴿O father, why do you worship that which does not hear and does not see and cannot avail you at all?﴾ [Maryam 42].
Here He said: ﴿And your Lord creates whatever He wills﴾, to compel these polytheists to worship Him alone.
As for His saying ﴿creates (yakhluq)﴾: creation is origination based on measure. Allah, Exalted is He, decrees and then creates, so His creation is founded on wisdom.
﴿Creates whatever He wills (mā yashāʾ)﴾, and He did not say "whoever He wills (man yashāʾ)", although among the created beings there are rational ones. Why did He say ﴿mā yashāʾ﴾ rather than (man yashāʾ)? For prevalence?
* Student: For the prevalence of the non-rational.
* The Shaykh: For the prevalence of the non-rational, because it is more numerous; then so that it includes essences and attributes. Attributes are known not to be rational, and when attributes are referred to, one uses (mā). Consider His saying: ﴿So marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisa' 3], and He did not say "man (whoever)" in ﴿ṭāba﴾, although the one married is rational. But since the woman is married for her attributes, He said: ﴿marry what seems good (mā ṭāba)﴾, meaning: observe the attribute. So here ﴿creates what He wills (mā yashāʾ)﴾ is expressed with ﴿mā﴾, prevailing for the non-rational because of its abundance, and what else? And so that it includes essences and attributes. Allah, Exalted is He, is the Creator of everything, essences and attributes. For this reason, it is the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah that Allah, Exalted is He, is the Creator of the servant and of the servant's actions, which are his attributes. So Allah, Exalted is He, creates what He wills.
As for His saying ﴿mā yashāʾ﴾, meaning what He wills to create, the object is thus omitted. This willing, every act of Allah's that He mentions as following His will is joined with wisdom, because among Allah's names is (al-Hakim, the All-Wise). He creates nothing in vain and decrees nothing in vain. Whatever He wills is joined with wisdom.
As for His saying ﴿and chooses (wa-yakhtār)﴾: the author said: (﴿and chooses﴾ what He wills). Choice (al-ikhtiyar) is taking the better of two matters. He, Glorified and Exalted, likewise takes what He sees as better among His acts and rulings. The fashioning of creation returns to the origin of existence, and choice returns to specification based on complete will. He has no one to question His wisdom and none to repel His decree. He chooses what He wills, Glorified and Exalted. He creates man in this form, He chose that he be in this form; He created the beast of burden, and He chose that it be in this form. Yes, likewise He chose that His Sharia be such, even if it is not created, in this form.
So choice is more general than creation in one respect, since it includes the created and the uncreated. He chooses, Glorified and Exalted, what He wills of Sharia, which is more general in this respect. As for creation, it is more general in that it includes essences and attributes.
As for his saying (﴿mā kāna lahumu﴾ — for the polytheists — ﴿al-khiyarah﴾ — the choice):
His saying ﴿mā kāna﴾: is it negating or a relative pronoun? Some said it is a relative pronoun, meaning: ﴿and chooses what there is for them of choice﴾, i.e., what contains good for them, He chooses that which has good for them. On this view, His saying ﴿mā kāna lahumu al-khiyarah﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿and chooses﴾, since it is its object. This view was taken by the Mu'tazilah, who say that it is obligatory upon Allah to do what is best or most beneficial. So they said: He, Exalted is He, chooses only what contains good, and what contains no good He does not choose. This means that He, Glorified and Exalted, does what is most beneficial or what is beneficial.
But most exegetes, headed by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, say that ﴿mā﴾ is negating, and as the author said, the meaning is: there is no choice for these polytheists, nor for their idols either. Their idols do not create and do not choose, and likewise they have no right of choice regarding what Allah wills. This view is the correct one. On this basis, the pause is at His saying ﴿and chooses﴾, then you begin: ﴿mā kāna lahumu al-khiyarah﴾. This is the correct view regarding this verse: that Allah alone has absolute choice, and no one has choice. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And it is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decreed a matter, that they should have any choice in their affair﴾ [al-Ahzab 36]. So they choose nothing of their affair except what Allah has chosen.
We have previously discussed in the book of ʿAqidah in detail the question: is it obligatory upon Allah to do what is best and most beneficial, or not? We mentioned that it is binding upon Him by the requirement of wisdom, not by the requirement of our intellects. Allah, Exalted is He, being Wise, does only what is beneficial or most beneficial; it is impossible for Him to do what is neither beneficial nor most beneficial, because He is Wise. But does this mean that we impose obligations upon Allah and say: this is better than that, and He must do such-and-such? No. Rather He, Glorified and Exalted, does it, and we may not know the aspect of its being most beneficial or beneficial. It does not follow that we know. How many things we think that wisdom lies in opposing what Allah commanded, or what occurred by decree, when wisdom is in what the Sharia brought and what Allah decreed in His destiny.
﴿Mā kāna lahumu al-khiyarah subḥāna Allāh﴾ [al-Qasas 68]: ﴿mā kāna lahumu al-khiyarah﴾ means: (the choice in anything). The author explained ﴿al-khiyarah﴾ as ﴿al-ikhtiyar﴾. So it is a verbal noun (ism maṣdar)? Why? Because every word that contains the meaning of the infinitive without its letters is a verbal noun. The parallel to ﴿al-khiyarah﴾ is al-ṭiyarah, for al-ṭiyarah is a verbal noun meaning the act of taking omens; likewise ﴿al-khiyarah﴾ is a verbal noun meaning: choosing.
(﴿Subḥāna Allāhi wa-taʿālā ʿammā yushrikūn﴾ [al-Qasas 68]: exalted above their associating.)
His saying ﴿Subḥāna Allāh﴾: we have explained more than once that it is a verbal noun meaning glorification (tasbīh), and glorification is declaring Allah, Glorified and Exalted, free from what does not befit Him. What is it that does not befit Allah and must be declared far from Him?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: And other than that?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...), deficiency and resemblance to created beings. Resemblance to created beings is impossible for Allah, and deficiency is impossible for Him, Exalted is He. So ﴿Subḥāna Allāh﴾ is a declaration of Allah's freedom from everything unbefitting Him, whether deficiency or resemblance to created beings.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No; because it may be an attribute of perfection, and if one likens Allah to it, it becomes a deficiency. And the matter may involve no resemblance to created beings at all, and no (...) similarity, meaning attributes specific to Allah. These attributes specific to Him are free of deficiency. For this reason Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned: ﴿There is nothing like Him﴾ [al-Shura 11], thereby affirming the negation of anything deficient, and He said: ﴿And no fatigue touched Us﴾ [Qaf 38], affirming the negation of deficiency.
As for His saying ﴿ʿammā yushrikūn﴾ [al-Qasas 68], he says: (exalted above their associating).
From the author's explanation we benefit that (mā) is a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle, so the declaration of freedom is from their act. It is possible that (mā) is a relative pronoun and the returning pronoun is omitted, and the meaning would be: exalted above what they associate with Him, so that He is free of the partners, which are the idols.
As for His saying ﴿wa-taʿālā﴾ [al-Qasas 68], it derives from elevation, but it conveys the meaning of declaring freedom together with elevation. That is, (taʿālā) means elevation and declaring freedom with loftiness. It is more eloquent than your saying (ʿalā), because (ʿalā) conveys elevation, but (taʿālā) conveys with elevation the declaration of freedom and avoidance of what they associate with Him, or of their association with Him. When Allah, Blessed and Exalted, explained the generality of His creation, and that He alone has absolute choice, and that none of His creation has choice, so choice belongs to Him alone — and note His saying ﴿mā kāna lahumu al-khiyarah﴾ [al-Qasas 68]; there will be discussion of it, Allah willing, when we mention the benefits — He mentioned that He is knowing of everything?
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, (taṭayyara, yataṭayyaru, taṭayyuran).
* Student: So?
* The Shaykh: A verbal noun, meaning the act of taking omens.
﴿And your Lord knows what their breasts conceal﴾ [al-Qasas 69]. ﴿Your Lord﴾: the address in it and in the previous verse is either to the Messenger ﷺ, or to anyone to whom address may be directed.
(﴿He knows what their breasts conceal﴾ — what their hearts hide of disbelief and other than it.)
﴿Yukinnu﴾ means: conceal and hide. ﴿Ṣudūruhum﴾ means: their hearts. The term "breasts" is used because the heart is in it, and the heart is connected to what? To the chest. So the chest is what conceals the heart, the one that covers it. What is in the heart of hidden matters, Allah knows it: ﴿He knows what their breasts conceal﴾.
The author's saying (of disbelief and other than it) is correct: of disbelief and of what is other than disbelief. Nothing that is in the heart is hidden from Him. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him﴾ [Qaf 16]. ﴿Whispers to him (tuwaswisu bihi)﴾ means: speaks to himself about it. He, Glorified and Exalted, has nothing hidden from Him; rather He knows what you do not know either. He knows, for example, that you will whisper such-and-such on a certain day before it happens from you, does He not?
* Student: Yes indeed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 67–72 (part 2 of 3):

* The Shaykh: (﴿مَا تُكِنُّ صُدُورُهُمْ وَمَا يُعْلِنُونَ﴾ [al-Qasas 69] by their tongues from that). ﴿يُعْلِنُونَ﴾ means they manifest. The author's restricting of manifestation to the tongues is deficient, because declaring (i'lan) may be by the tongue and may be by other limbs. It may be by the tongue, so one speaks; and it may be by other limbs, so one acts with his hands, feet, eyes, or otherwise. Thus it is more general than what the author said.
Then he said: ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ لَهُ الْحَمْدُ فِي الْأُولَى وَالْآخِرَةِ﴾ [al-Qasas 70].
﴿وَهُوَ﴾: the pronoun refers to (Rabb), meaning: that Lord who creates and who knows is ﴿اللَّهُ﴾ (Allah). ﴿اللَّهُ﴾ originally is al-Ilah (the God), the hamzah was dropped for lightness due to frequent use, as in (unas) which becomes (nas). So the hamzah is dropped for lightness, and ﴿اللَّهُ﴾ Ta'ala's meaning originally is (al-Ilah), then the hamzah was dropped for lightness and it became ﴿اللَّهُ﴾.
So what is the meaning of ilah? (Ilah) means (ma'luh), not (alih). It is in the sense of (ma'luh), like (ghirass) meaning (maghrus), (bina') meaning (mabni), and (firash) meaning (mafrush); its examples are many.
So (ilah) means (ma'luh), that is, worshipped; the worshipped one is called ma'luh because the heart yearns for him (ya'lahuhu), that is, inclines toward him. You find that (a-l-h) agrees in the minor derivation with (a-h-l), does it not? It agrees in the minor derivation with (a-h-l), since it contains the hamzah, the ha' and the lam. In divinity (uluhiyyah), which is worship, there is a kind of attachment and tranquility, because the one who is an ilah to a thing is at rest in it. Therefore (ilah) means the worshipped, because the worshipper takes him as an ilah, that is, inclines toward him and finds tranquility in him. And (ilah) does not mean (alih, the creator). The theologians (mutakallimun) said: ilah means alih, that is, the one capable of innovation (ikhtira'), meaning the one capable of creation, but they have philosophical expressions: capable of creation. If we explained ilah as the one capable of creation, then the polytheists whom the Prophet ﷺ fought would be monotheists, would they not? Because they say: there is no creator and none capable of creating except Allah. Undoubtedly this leads to nullifying the message and tawhid.
From this we know the error of some writers today regarding tawhid, who focus on tawhid al-rububiyyah and forget tawhid al-uluhiyyah, and this is a grave error, because tawhid is not merely affirming and acknowledging the Creator, since this is found among the polytheists whose blood and property the Prophet ﷺ made lawful. Rather (ilah) means the worshipped, which is a matter above the capable one or the creator.
He, Exalted, says: ﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾ [al-Qasas 70]. Having established His divinity with the nominal sentence ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ﴾, this is a nominal sentence both of whose parts are definite, and it is known among the rhetoricians that a nominal sentence whose two parts are definite conveys restriction (hasr).
He confirmed this with ﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾, so this is also a restriction of divinity to Allah alone; there is no other ilah with Him. Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿مَا اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ مِنْ وَلَدٍ وَمَا كَانَ مَعَهُ مِنْ إِلَهٍ إِذًا لَذَهَبَ كُلُّ إِلَهٍ بِمَا خَلَقَ﴾ [al-Mu'minun 91]. This shows that the ilah is the worshipped one who creates; therefore He said: ﴿لَذَهَبَ كُلُّ إِلَهٍ بِمَا خَلَقَ﴾. Do not think this verse supports the theologians' interpretation, since He said: ﴿لَذَهَبَ كُلُّ إِلَهٍ بِمَا خَلَقَ﴾, as if to say that this proves the ilah means the creator. Otherwise He would have said: "each ilah would have gone off with whom he worshipped." No, rather, because the true ilah is the creating ilah, He said: ﴿لَذَهَبَ كُلُّ إِلَهٍ بِمَا خَلَقَ﴾.
Is the restriction here real (haqiqi) or relative (idafi): ﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾ [al-Qasas 70]? The restriction is real. Some people may be confused and say it is relative, because if we make this restriction real, it raises a great difficulty: Allah has affirmed other ilahs, when He said: ﴿فَمَا أَغْنَتْ عَنْهُمْ آلِهَتُهُمُ الَّتِي يَدْعُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ مِنْ شَيْءٍ﴾ [Hud 101], and He said of Ibrahim that he said to his people: ﴿أَئِفْكًا آلِهَةً دُونَ اللَّهِ تُرِيدُونَ﴾ [al-Saffat 86].
Likewise the disbelievers said to the Messenger ﷺ, they said about him: ﴿أَجَعَلَ الْآلِهَةَ إِلَهًا وَاحِدًا إِنَّ هَذَا لَشَيْءٌ عُجَابٌ﴾ [Sad 5]. So one may think that we cannot combine this verse with affirming the divinity of idols unless we make the restriction relative, meaning we affirm divinity but in another sense, and the negation here is in another sense different from what we affirmed. We say in reply: the true ilah in reality is the Creator; the true ilah is the Creator. As for those gods worshipped besides Allah, they are false gods, lies. Therefore Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said: ﴿أَئِفْكًا آلِهَةً﴾, so he made that a falsehood and not a reality. Though they are worshipped and called gods, they are not gods. Therefore you find that all the messengers, peace and blessings of Allah be upon them, each said to his people: ﴿اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ مَا لَكُمْ مِنْ إِلَهٍ غَيْرُه﴾ [al-Mu'minun 32], meaning: no ilah that is worshipped and deserves to be worshipped in truth other than Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
He, Exalted, said: ﴿إِنَّكُمْ وَمَا تَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ حَصَبُ جَهَنَّمَ أَنْتُمْ لَهَا وَارِدُونَ (٩٨) لَوْ كَانَ هَؤُلَاءِ آلِهَةً مَا وَرَدُوهَا﴾ [al-Anbiya' 98, 99]. What is the meaning of ﴿آلِهَةً﴾? It means worshipped in truth; otherwise Allah would not have affirmed worship for them: ﴿إِنَّكُمْ وَمَا تَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ حَصَبُ جَهَنَّمَ﴾.
On this basis we say: the reconciliation of this restriction with what was mentioned about affirming divinity for idols is that the ilah is the one worshipped in truth. This ilah is the one worshipped in truth, and this applies only to Allah, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala. As for what is worshipped without right, although it is called an ilah, it does not deserve to be an ilah, as Allah said: ﴿لَوْ كَانَ هَؤُلَاءِ آلِهَةً مَا وَرَدُوهَا وَكُلٌّ فِيهَا خَالِدُونَ﴾ [al-Anbiya' 99].
As for His saying: ﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾, is it mentioned on its own, meaning that it is prescribed for you to say: ﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾, ﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾, ﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾? Or is it not mentioned on its own unless the pronoun has a referent preceding it?
* A student: With a referent.
* The Shaykh: This is what is required. You cannot say ﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾ unless the pronoun has a referent that is mentioned or spoken, mentioned such as: ﴿اللَّهُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾ [al-Baqarah 255], or spoken, such as when some act of Allah comes and you say: ﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾. As for ﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ﴾ [al-Anbiya' 87], it is valid, because you are addressing Allah; so it is required.
We said that at the outset: ﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾ must have a referent, contrary to the Sufis. The Sufis say ﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾ and they repeat the pronoun, saying: Huwa, huwa, huwa, huwa... to the end, worshipping Allah with a single word, and mentioning Allah only with the pronoun, and dropping ﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾, so they keep saying: huwa, huwa, huwa. When you see them in their gatherings, they sway their heads, beat drums, and raise their voices, saying: huwa, huwa; and perhaps they injure themselves from intense excitement and ecstasy. We ask Allah for well-being.
The summary is that this is only valid with a preceding referent.
He said: ﴿لَهُ الْحَمْدُ فِي الْأُولَى وَالْآخِرَةِ وَلَهُ الْحُكْمُ وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ [al-Qasas 70].
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, only ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ﴾ [al-Qasas 70]. (...)
﴿فَأَمَّا مَنْ تَابَ وَآمَنَ وَعَمِلَ صَالِحًا فَعَسَى أَنْ يَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُفْلِحِينَ﴾ [al-Qasas 67].
* In this: the virtue of these three attributes: repentance, faith, and righteous action.
* Among its benefits: these three attributes are a cause of success (falah), by His saying: ﴿فَعَسَى أَنْ يَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُفْلِحِينَ﴾.
* Among them: success is a lofty rank that is attained only by those possessing praiseworthy attributes: the repentant, the faithful, those who do righteous deeds.
* Among the benefits of the verse: deeds are beneficial only if they are righteous (salih), which is what combines two conditions as mentioned earlier: sincerity (ikhlas) and following the Messenger ﷺ.
And His saying: ﴿وَرَبُّكَ يَخْلُقُ مَا يَشَاءُ وَيَخْتَارُ مَا كَانَ لَهُمُ الْخِيَرَةُ سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ وَتَعَالَى عَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ﴾ [al-Qasas 68].
* Among its benefits: the affirmation that Allah alone is the Creator; by His saying: ﴿مَا كَانَ لَهُمُ الْخِيَرَةُ﴾, because one who has no choice by nature has no creating.
* Among them: that Allah, Exalted, is capable of all things; because (He creates what He wills) means what?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That He is capable. How could He want to create it?
* Among them: the affirmation of will for Allah, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala, by His saying: ﴿وَيَخْتَارُ﴾. Is the will here legislative (shar'i) or universal (kawni)?
* A student: Legislative.
* Another student: Both.
* The Shaykh: If we look at its being joined with creation, we say it is universal (kawni). If we look at its wording apart from its being joined with creation, we say it encompasses both the universal and the legislative, and that He, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala, chooses, both universally and legislatively, what He wills. This is more preferable; generality is preferable, so that it includes both universal and legislative choice.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, (...). But does He choose in what He creates, or is it general? The context requires that He chooses what He creates; the meaning of choosing differs from the meaning of creating.
* Among them: that man has no choice, and the Jabriyyah have held to this, by His saying: ﴿مَا كَانَ لَهُمُ الْخِيَرَةُ﴾. They said: this verse shows that man has no choice and is compelled in his action. The answer to this is to say: ﴿مَا كَانَ لَهُمُ الْخِيَرَةُ﴾ means absolute choice, that is, choice without Allah. Allah chooses and they choose. The proof that ﴿مَا كَانَ لَهُمُ الْخِيَرَةُ﴾ refers to absolute choice is that many verses and hadiths show that man has will: ﴿مِنْكُمْ مَنْ يُرِيدُ الدُّنْيَا وَمِنْكُمْ مَنْ يُرِيدُ الْآخِرَةَ﴾ [Al 'Imran 152], ﴿لِمَنْ شَاءَ مِنْكُمْ أَنْ يَسْتَقِيمَ﴾ [al-Takwir 28]. Yes, He, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala, affirmed for man a will and affirmed for him a volition. Reality bears witness to this, does it not? Reality bears witness to this, and man distinguishes between a voluntary act and an involuntary act, does he not? When a man descends from the roof by the stairs, his descent is voluntary; but if someone pushes him from the top of the stairs so that he tumbles, his descent is involuntary.
So His saying: ﴿مَا كَانَ لَهُمُ الْخِيَرَةُ﴾ [al-Qasas 68], the negation here applies to what: to absolute choice or to choice in general?
* A student: To absolute choice.
* The Shaykh: To the absolute choice that does not conflict; this is not for man. Rather man is managed and has a will.
As for it being a negation of choice in general, this is impossible, because the verses and reality testify that man has choice, does he not? Here the scholars say that in many expiations: one is given the option between such and such, or not?
* A student: Yes.
* Another student: (...)?
* Among them also, and among its benefits: the singularity of Allah, Tabaraka wa Ta'ala, in will: absolute will, or will in general? In absolute will: no one can dispute His wisdom, and none can repel His decree.
* Among them: the glorification of Allah, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala, above what is not fitting for Him; by His saying: ﴿سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ﴾ [al-Qasas 68].
* Among them also, among the benefits of the verse: His exaltation and transcendence above these polytheists, whether we take (ma) as a verbal (masdariyyah) particle or as a relative (mawsulah) particle. He, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala, is exalted above the polytheists, above their idols and above their shirk.
﴿وَرَبُّكَ يَعْلَمُ مَا تُكِنُّ صُدُورُهُمْ وَمَا يُعْلِنُونَ﴾ [al-Qasas 69]. In this is the affirmation of knowledge for Allah, and that it encompasses what is concealed and what is declared.
* Among its benefits: warning and encouragement. What is the warning and encouragement? A warning to a person not to conceal or declare evil, because Allah knows it; and encouragement for him to conceal or declare good, because Allah knows it. Allah knows best what good or evil one conceals; it means that it will not be lost, and it is recorded, as Allah, Tabaraka wa Ta'ala, said in many verses that on the Day of Resurrection He will know and inform of what these people did. In the verse is encouragement and warning: whoever conceals good and declares it, that is an encouragement for him; and whoever conceals evil or declares it, that is a warning for him.
* * *
Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ لَهُ الْحَمْدُ فِي الْأُولَى وَالْآخِرَةِ وَلَهُ الْحُكْمُ وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ [al-Qasas 70].
Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿لَهُ الْحَمْدُ﴾. The prepositional phrase ﴿لَهُ﴾ is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), and fronting what should be postponed conveys restriction. So ﴿لَهُ﴾ alone has ﴿الْحَمْدُ فِي الْأُولَى وَالْآخِرَةِ﴾. As for others, they do not possess the praise that Allah deserves, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter.
As for His saying: ﴿الْحَمْدُ﴾, the (al) here is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), meaning all kinds of praise and whatever relates to it, whether good or evil. So Allah, Exalted, has all praise; He is the One who is not praised for evil other than Himself, and He is praised in every state, as the Prophet ﷺ said: «الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ عَلَى كُلِّ حَالٍ»[[Narrated by Ibn Majah (3803) from the hadith of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her.]].
As for His saying: ﴿لَهُ﴾, is the lam here for exclusivity (ikhtisas) or for entitlement (istihqaq)?
* A student: Both.
* The Shaykh: Is it for exclusivity or for entitlement?
* A student: Both.
* The Shaykh: For entitlement, yes.
Now, has what passed before you (...) been for entitlement or exclusivity?
* A student: Both, Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: We mentioned that the lam is for exclusivity and for entitlement. Absolute praise is exclusive to Allah, and the one truly deserving praise is Allah, because whoever else deserves to be praised, what he has of the causes of praise comes from Allah, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala, and at most he is a means. For example, a person is praised for his perfect attributes and his kindness to creation and the like, but from whom is this? From where did this come about?
* A student: From Allah.
* The Shaykh: From Allah. So praise in truth belongs to Allah; the one who deserves praise is Allah, and the one who is exclusively praised absolutely in all states is who? It is Allah, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala. So it is for both entitlement and exclusivity.
And (﴿لَهُ الْحَمْدُ فِي الْأُولَى﴾ is the worldly life): He is praised in this world for the universal decrees He executes and the legislative rulings He prescribes; He is praised for them with complete praise.
Likewise, He has praise in the Hereafter. The author said: (Paradise), and that is not so. The Hereafter includes from the time people are resurrected until they reach their abodes. Allah, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala, is praised then; indeed Allah opens up for His Prophet on that day praises that He had not opened to him before[[Mentioned in the long hadith of intercession narrated by the two Shaykhs: al-Bukhari (4712) and Muslim (194/327) from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, the Prophet ﷺ said: «Then I fall prostrate to my Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, then Allah opens to me some of His praises and fine commendation of Him that He did not open to anyone before me…» the hadith.]]. He, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala, on the Day of Resurrection manifests His praise to everyone: He manifests His justice, His bounty and kindness, His wisdom and His power, and other great attributes that appear on that day and for which He deserves praise.
So the meaning is not that He is praised only in Paradise; this is a great deficiency on the part of the author, may Allah have mercy on him. Allah, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala, says: ﴿الْحَمْدُ فِي الْأُولَى وَالْآخِرَةِ﴾ [al-Qasas 70], and the Hereafter includes from the time people are raised until each person reaches his abode.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 67–72 (part 3 of 3):

(In the Hereafter, He is praised.) We said: He is praised for what becomes manifest on that Day. From where?
* Student: Justice.
* Shaykh: From justice, power, mercy, wisdom, grace, benevolence, and many other things that become manifest, which do not become manifest now in this world. It is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he asks Allah, mighty and majestic, for permission to intercede, and he prostrates beneath the Throne, and Allah then opens for him praises of Him that He had not opened for him before.[[This is in the long hadith of intercession narrated by the two Shaykhs: al-Bukhari (4712) and Muslim (194/327), from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "I will fall prostrate before my Lord, mighty and majestic. Then Allah will open for me from His praises and good praise of Him something He has not opened for anyone before me..." The hadith.]] This is before entering Paradise, indeed before the creation is judged. So to Allah, the Exalted, belongs all praise in the Hereafter.

﴿وَلَهُ الْحُكْمُ﴾ ("To Him belongs the judgment"): "lahu" is a predicate placed before its subject, and placing the predicate first conveys exclusivity (ḥaṣr). ﴿وَلَهُ الْحُكْمُ﴾ The author said: (the binding decree over everything). And ﴿al-ḥukm﴾ includes the decree (qaḍāʾ), which is the cosmic judgment, as the author said, and it includes the legislative judgment (ḥukm sharʿī). So judgment belongs to Allah, both in decree and in legislation. There is no judge except Allah, the Exalted. Whoever seeks judgment from other than Allah has gone astray; whoever follows the guidance of Allah will not go astray nor be wretched.

Here we noted that placing the predicate first conveys exclusivity, because judgment belongs to Allah alone. This is so when the intended meaning is absolute judgment. Absolute judgment belongs to Allah; no one shares it with Him. He is the One who makes a thing obligatory, forbids it, recommends it, or permits it. Likewise in cosmic matters, He is the One who sends down rain, removes drought, gives life, causes death, and provides sustenance. All of this is among the cosmic judgments.

Has anyone disputed with Allah over these two kinds of judgment? Yes. Humans have disputed with their Lord over both the cosmic judgment and the legislative judgment. Among them are those who affirmed a creator alongside Allah, and among them are those who claimed to be a lord who acts as he wills. Violations in legislative judgment are more numerous and more evident. How many there are who legislate and consider their legislation binding, like the law of Allah or even higher! These, it has already been established, are disbelievers, even if they pray, pay zakah, fast, and perform Hajj; they are disbelievers.

Likewise, what else relates to judgment, such as whom?
* Student: Like Pharaoh.
* Shaykh: Like Pharaoh, because he disputed with Allah over the decree, and he said: ﴿O chiefs, I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas 38], and he said: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Nazi'at 24].

We have understood that absolute judgment belongs to Allah. But is there a restricted judgment? We say: Yes, there is a restricted judgment, but it is by the command of Allah. This is why in the books of the scholars we read: (they go to the judge), (the legitimate judge said), (by the permission of the judge), and similar expressions. Is the judgment that this person holds restricted or unrestricted? It is restricted and confined: restricted to being under the judgment of Allah, confined to a specific place and a specific time. So absolute judgment belongs to whom? To Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in this world and in the Hereafter.

As for restricted judgment, it belongs to other than Allah, such as what? Such as what the scholars say: the legitimate judge, and the judge decides between them, and similar things. This judgment is restricted in its time, its place, and its kind. As for time, it is known that it is restricted: does this legitimate judge remain forever? No. As for place, he judges only in a certain patch of earth, not over the earth and the heavens. As for kind, it is restricted to being under the judgment of Allah; his judgment is not absolute, but is under the judgment of Allah, so he has no power to change anything of the judgments of Allah, the Exalted.

﴿وَلَهُ الْحُكْمُ وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ ("To Him belongs the judgment, and to Him you will be returned" [al-Qasas 70]). ﴿إِلَيْهِ﴾ also has its complement placed first, because ﴿إِلَيْهِ﴾ is connected to what? ﴿تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ ("you will be returned"). Placing the complement first indicates exclusivity. So the return to Allah, however long the world lasts, however far a person goes, and whatever a person is, his return is to Allah. The author said: (﴿وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ by resurrection), and when is the resurrection?
* Student: On the Day of Resurrection.
* Shaykh: On the Day of Resurrection. So people, indeed all creatures, have their return to Allah, the Exalted, and that is on the Day of Resurrection. Nothing remains that will not be gathered, even the ant?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Everything will be gathered, until it becomes clear that the whole matter returns to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* * *

(﴿Say﴾ to the people of Makkah, ﴿Have you considered﴾ tell me). The address is to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Say﴾. But who is addressed? The author says: (the people of Makkah). The correct view is that it is general to everyone: (﴿أَرَأَيْتُمْ﴾ meaning: inform me). The author's explanation of it as (inform me) is an explanation of meaning rather than of wording, because ra'aytum (رأى) here is from visual sight, and the meaning is: Did you see that, then inform me about it. But the author and others among the scholars explain it by its necessary implication, because what necessarily accompanies seeing is a person reporting what he sees.

﴿أَرَأَيْتُمْ﴾: the scholars say that ra'aytum here takes two objects, even though it is visual, it takes two objects. The first object may be present or may be omitted; most often it is omitted, but it may be present. For example: ﴿Say: Have you considered what Allah has sent down to you of provision, and you made of it lawful and unlawful? Say: Did Allah permit you?﴾ [Yunus 59]. Here the first object is present: ﴿مَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾ ("what Allah has sent down").

﴿Say: Have you considered what you invoke besides Allah? Show me what they have created of the earth﴾, and so on to the end [al-Ahqaf 4]. Here the first object is omitted. Here: ﴿Have you considered if Allah makes﴾ [al-Qasas 71]. The first object is omitted, and the estimate is: ﴿أَرَأَيْتُمْ﴾ your condition? That is: inform me about your condition, what would it be if such and such happened? So the first object is omitted, and the clause ﴿مَنْ إِلَهٌ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ﴾ [al-Qasas 71] is in the accusative position as the second object.

(﴿Have you considered if Allah makes for you the night perpetual﴾, continuing forever): ﴿جَعَلَ﴾ means "made," so its first object is ﴿اللَّيْلَ﴾ and its second object is ﴿سَرْمَدًا﴾: that Allah should make ﴿عَلَيْكُمُ اللَّيْلَ سَرْمَدًا﴾ ("the night perpetual over you").

﴿اللَّيْلَ﴾ ("the night"): from the sunset to its rising. This is the night; its meaning is that the disappearance of the sun below the horizon is the night, and its appearance is the day. The light that follows it after sunset or precedes it after dawn is from the beginnings of the day or its ends. Otherwise, the reality is that the night is from sunset to sunrise.

As for ﴿سَرْمَدًا﴾: it is said that its origin is sardan, and sard means succession, that is, consecutive. On this explanation the nun is extra, and its morphological pattern is?
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿سَرْمَدًا﴾?
* Student: (fa'malan).
* Shaykh: (fa'malan), because the nun is extra. It is also said that the nun is original and that it comes from (sarmada) when it continues. On this view its morphological pattern is (fa'lalan), because the nun is original.

What concerns us is the meaning of sarmad: it means lasting and continuous.

﴿إِلَى يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ﴾ ("until the Day of Resurrection"). If the night were perpetual until the Day of Resurrection, could anyone bring the day? No one can, indeed no one can bring the day forward before its time or delay it after its time. Now, if the whole world gathered to make the sun rise at twelve, for example, could they, if the whole world gathered to make it rise at twelve minus one minute, could they? They could not. How (...) once? Or to make it delayed until twelve and one minute, they could not; or to shift it slightly from its place? They cannot (...).

So whoever cannot change it, neither in time nor in place, cannot bring it or bring the day ever. This is why the Exalted said: (﴿Who is a god other than Allah﴾, by your claim, ﴿who would bring you light﴾, daytime in which you seek livelihood).

﴿مَنْ﴾ is the subject, ﴿إِلَهٌ﴾ is its predicate, ﴿غَيْرُ اللَّهِ﴾ is its qualifier, and ﴿يَأْتِيكُمْ﴾ is a circumstantial clause describing ﴿إِلَهٌ﴾. That is: which god ﴿would bring you light﴾.

The author's statement (by your claim) is something only a person who understands the Arabic language would notice, because ﴿مَنْ﴾ is used to ask for specification, and it accepts plurality, since specification is sought only when? When there are multiple things. When things are multiple, specification is requested. So if you say: Who stood up? you have now established by this question that a number of people stood up, but you are asking for the specification of this one who stood. When He says ﴿مَنْ إِلَهٌ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ﴾, its meaning now is that he has affirmed in the verse that there are gods, and what is sought by ﴿مَنْ﴾ is what? Specification: identify for me the god who brings you?

Is the reality that there are many gods? This is why the author said (by your claim), meaning: if you claim that there are gods, then which god brings you light? This is more forceful as a challenge. If he had said: (Is there a god other than Allah?), the question would be about the existence of a god, not the specification of the god. But asking for its specification is more forceful as a challenge; that is: even on your claim that these are gods, we challenge you: where is the god who brings this thing? If you say: By Allah, none of our gods does this, it becomes clear that their divinity is false, because a god must be capable, hearing, seeing... to the end (...).

I seem to be speaking in English now! ﴿مَنْ﴾ is used to seek what?
* Student: Specification.
* Shaykh: It seeks specification among a plurality. Here ﴿مَنْ إِلَهٌ﴾ requires that there be multiple gods, and this is not literal, but according to the claim of these polytheists, who claim that there is a god deserving worship. If that is so, by your claim that it deserves worship, then let it be capable; if it is not capable, it does not deserve worship.

﴿يَأْتِيكُمْ بِضِيَاءٍ﴾ [al-Qasas 71]: the ba' here is for transitivity; that is, it brings light to you. He said (ḍiyāʾ, light) because it is the sign of the day, indeed it is in reality the day itself, either its sign or it is the day itself.

(﴿أَفَلَا تَسْمَعُونَ﴾ ("Will you not hear?"), that is, hearing with understanding by which you turn back from association).

﴿أَفَلَا تَسْمَعُونَ﴾: meaning, have your ears been struck deaf so that you do not hear? The intended meaning of the question here is the hearing of understanding by which a person is restrained from his error, not mere hearing of perception (...).

Here someone may say: Why did He not say (Will you not see)? Because the day is the place of seeing, and seeing is clearer there (...). Rather He said ﴿أَفَلَا تَسْمَعُونَ﴾?

We say: Because it is an explanation of His saying ﴿عَلَيْكُمُ اللَّيْلَ سَرْمَدًا﴾, and is the night a place of sight or a place of hearing? A place of hearing. This is why He said ﴿أَفَلَا تَسْمَعُونَ﴾, and it is not an explanation at the end of the verse ﴿مَنْ إِلَهٌ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ يَأْتِيكُمْ بِضِيَاءٍ﴾, but rather an explanation at the beginning of the verse.

The meaning: you do not hear with the hearing from which you benefit, because the night is the place of hearing and not the place of sight (...).

Absolute monotheism belongs to Allah alone?
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ﴾.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What is the benefit?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The saying of the Exalted: ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ﴾ ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾ [al-Qasas 70].
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ﴾.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿لَهُ الْحَمْدُ﴾?
* Student: Yes (...).
* Shaykh: Upon them (...) with this?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: And what does he say?
* Student: Yes (...)?
* Shaykh: ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾?
* Student: Virtue (...).
* Shaykh: No, this (...).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿مَا تُكِنُّ صُدُورُهُمْ وَمَا يُعْلِنُونَ﴾ [al-Qasas 69].
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: So the generality: it became ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ﴾.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾. From it is derived: the affirmation of Allah's divinity.
* Second: His being singular in divinity, by His saying ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾.
* Third benefit: Allah, the Exalted, is specially deserving of absolute praise, by His saying ﴿لَهُ الْحَمْدُ﴾, absolute praise encompassing this world and the Hereafter.
* From the benefits of the verse: the manifestation of the perfection of Allah's attributes, in this world and the Hereafter, because praise describes the praised one with perfection.
* From the benefits of the verse: Allah, the Exalted, is specially the One who judges, that He alone is the Judge, by His saying ﴿وَلَهُ الْحُكْمُ﴾. What was mentioned of affirming judgment to others is a restricted matter, like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And when you judge between people, judge with justice﴾ [al-Nisa' 58]. This is restricted.
* From the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of resurrection, by His saying ﴿وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾.

﴿Say: Have you considered if Allah makes for you the night perpetual until the Day of Resurrection﴾, and so on to the end.
* From the benefits of the verse: the challenge to these polytheists that their idols should bring good or repel harm.
* Second: the demonstration of Allah's power, the Exalted, since nothing can prevent Him from making the night perpetual until the Day of Resurrection.
* Third: reminding of Allah's blessing, the Exalted, reminding the servants of Allah's blessing, since things are made evident by their opposites.
* From the benefits of the verse: no one can change Allah's sunnah in the universe; if He made it perpetual, no one could remove it.
* From the benefits of the verse: encouragement to hear what is recited of the Book of Allah with understanding and acceptance, by His saying ﴿أَفَلَا تَسْمَعُونَ﴾.
* From the benefits of the verse: the explanation of Allah's blessing upon the servants in the light of day. How much energy does this light save?
* Student: Countless.
* Shaykh: Countless. That is, if all the lighting of the night were to fall during the day, and how much energy does a nation consume to light the night? Although it is not like the light of day, in this we know the measure of Allah's blessing, the Exalted, in this light that reaches people in great quantities (...).

The last benefit? An explanation?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) the day.

﴿Say: Have you considered if Allah makes for you the day perpetual until the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Qasas 72].
* Student: The saying of the Exalted (...)?
* Shaykh: No, the intended point is the limit.

And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: Have you considered if Allah makes for you the day perpetual until the Day of Resurrection? Who is a god other than Allah who would bring you a night in which you rest? Will you not see?﴾ [al-Qasas 72].
* What is derived from this verse is what is derived from the verse before it, except that it has an addition, which is: the explanation of Allah's blessing, the Exalted. What is derived from the verse is what is derived from what precedes it in what they share.
* From it: the explanation of Allah's blessing, the Exalted, in the night, which He made a place of rest, by His saying ﴿in which you rest﴾.
* From it: that sleep at night is more beneficial to the body than sleep by day, since Allah made the night the place and time of rest, and this is an observed matter.
* From it: encouragement to reflect upon the signs of Allah, the Exalted, by His saying ﴿Will you not see?﴾, because this indicates encouragement for a person to reflect upon these signs that Allah, the Exalted, has made, so that he may take evidence from them of the perfection of the Creator's power.

As for the explanation of Allah's power and the like, it has already passed.

He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And out of His mercy﴾ [al-Qasas 73].
* Student: Doesn't this verse benefit (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, (...) we mentioned that sleep at night is more beneficial to the body than by day, because in it there is stillness. But (...) of the night; a person feels rest, but it is not like the night.
* Student: Meaning (...)?
* Shaykh: It is not equal to it in any case, taking health into consideration (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 73–75 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein﴾ [al-Qasas 73].

"﴿And out of His mercy He made﴾": the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa'l-majrur) is connected to His saying ﴿He made﴾. That is, He made for you the night and the day so that you may rest therein, out of His mercy.

As for His saying ﴿out of His mercy﴾: the ﴿min﴾ (out of) here indicates causation (lil-sababiyyah), meaning: because of His mercy, or because of the mercy with which He, glorified and exalted is He, is described. Mercy is a real attribute established for Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and it is other than will (al-irada), other than the will to bestow favour, and other than bestowing favour. The People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jama'ah) say: mercy is a real attribute established for Allah, mighty and majestic is He, which is not like the mercy of the created beings. As for the Ash'ariyyah, they distort the meaning of mercy, reducing it to bestowing favour or the will to bestow favour, so they interpret it as the act, which is bestowing favour, or its willing; because they affirm the will, which is a attribute of meaning (sifah ma'nawiyyah) that they affirm. It has already passed us that they affirm from the attributes only seven attributes, among them the will. So they explain mercy as the will to bestow favour. Why? They say: because the will is indicated by both revelation (al-sam') and reason ('aql), and we do not affirm from Allah's attributes except what reason indicates. As for what reason does not indicate, it is obligatory for us to interpret it (ta'wil); and we say: we distort it (tahrif) according to their practice. They call it ta'wil, and we say it is tahrif. They say: what reason indicates of Allah's attributes we affirm, and what it does not indicate must be interpreted, and in the more correct sense, distorted.

What is the evidence of reason for the will? They say: reason indicates the will through specification (al-takhsis): the specification of created things. Every created thing has been specified with something. Is that not so? This one Allah willed to be hard, so he became hard; that one to be soft, so he became soft; this one to be tall, so he is tall; this one short, so he is short, and so on. This [indicates]—we say (...)—this indicates what? It indicates will; that is, the matter cannot be without will.

Why have you denied mercy? They say: because mercy is a softness that afflicts the heart, necessitating tenderness toward the created being or the one shown mercy. We say to them: this mercy you mention is only the mercy of created beings, whereas we affirm for Allah a mercy that is not like the mercy of created beings. Then we also take evidence for mercy from reason just as you took evidence for the will from reason. How many blessings does Allah, glorified and exalted is He, have upon us?

* Student: They cannot be counted.

* The Shaykh: They cannot be counted or enumerated. And how many relief from distresses does Allah, glorified and exalted is He, have? They cannot be counted or enumerated. What is the matter that necessitates these things, to bring blessings and repel calamities?

* Student: Mercy.

* The Shaykh: Mercy; because the hard one who does not show mercy (...) does not bring a blessing nor repel a calamity.

So then, inference from events in which blessings are brought and calamities repelled is clearer and more evident than inference from specification to the will; because the indication of specification to the will is understood only by individuals of people, but the indication of bringing benefits and repelling calamities to mercy is understood by all people, even the common man in his market: if he sees a man harsh toward his children, for example, he says: this one has no mercy in his heart; and if he sees that he constantly brings them good and repels evil from them, he says: this is a merciful person.

So the indication of reason for mercy is stronger than its indication for the will, and yet they affirm the will and do not affirm mercy.

They say: "﴿And out of His mercy﴾" — it is not possible to affirm for Allah an attribute that is mercy; rather we say: "﴿out of His mercy﴾" [al-Qasas 73] means out of His bestowing favour. "﴿He made for you the night...﴾" to the end [al-Qasas 73].

We say: "﴿out of His mercy﴾", the ﴿min﴾ is for causation. And ﴿His mercy﴾ is His attribute with which He is described eternally and everlastingly; for this reason He opened His Book with ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [al-Fatihah 1], and joined His lordship with that: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds (2), the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [al-Fatihah 2, 3], as an indication that this lordship, all of it, is a lordship of mercy; it is not a lordship of vengeance and harshness, but a lordship of mercy. So how can we deny this great attribute of Allah's attributes and affirm what is less than it?

This indicates the contradiction of these negators (al-mu'attilah) among the Ash'ariyyah, the Mu'tazilah and others, and that they contradict themselves: they affirm for Allah from the attributes what reason indicates the affirmation of what is more worthy of it, and they deny from the attributes what reason indicates their affirmation.

"﴿out of His mercy He made for you﴾": ﴿made﴾ here means created (khalaqa), not "rendered" (sayyara); and for this reason it did not take two objects.

"﴿He made for you the night and the day﴾" [al-Qasas 73]: a night and a day alternating among you, over people.

("﴿that you may rest therein﴾" [al-Qasas 73], i.e., in the night; "﴿and that you may seek of His bounty﴾" in the day, for earning.)

His saying: ﴿that you may rest therein﴾: the lam is for causation (lil-ta'lil), meaning: for the sake of your resting therein. The existence of the effect does not necessarily entail the existence of the cause when the cause is not effective. For example: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat 56]. This is a final cause (illah gha'iyyah), and the existence of the effect does not necessarily entail the existence of the final cause; so the creation does not necessarily entail the existence of worship.

Likewise ﴿that you may rest therein﴾ is a final cause and not an effective cause, and the existence of the effect does not necessarily entail the existence of the final cause. For example, someone may say: we find some people who do not rest at night, is that correct or not? There are people who do not rest at night: one whose livelihood is at night, like guards, and one whose amusement is at night, like those idle people who sleep by day and stay up at night. We say: the existence of the effect, when the cause is final, does not necessarily entail the existence of the cause, just as if you said: I have brought you this camel so that you may ride it; perhaps you ride it, and perhaps you do not. I gave you the pen so that you may write with it; perhaps you write, and perhaps you do not.

His saying: ﴿that you may rest therein﴾: the author says: (you rest, you take comfort), since it is not from "sukna" (dwelling) but from "sukun" (rest).

Where is the nun in His saying ﴿li-taskunu﴾? The nun has been dropped.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The nun has been dropped, because the verb is in the subjunctive. Strangely, I have in my copy (litaskununahu) [you rest in it], in the explanation, and the commentator also explained it with his saying: (you take comfort in it). No, I seek Allah's forgiveness! That is the previous one.

("﴿that you may rest therein﴾", i.e., in the night) meaning you take comfort.

"﴿and that you may seek of His bounty﴾" [al-Qasas 73]: (seek) means (seek out).

His saying: "﴿of His bounty﴾" means: of His giving and provision (in the day, for earning).

In the verse here, is there a laff wa-nashr (a complex, interleaved figure) that is arranged or not arranged?

* Student: Not arranged.

* The Shaykh: ﴿He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty﴾ [al-Qasas 73]?

* Student: Not arranged.

* The Shaykh: It is arranged.

* Student: How?

* The Shaykh: Yes, it began with the night and mentioned its benefit first: rest, and this is at night; so there is an arranged laff wa-nashr: ﴿the night and the day, that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty﴾.

﴿that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty and that perhaps you may be thankful﴾.

(Perhaps) here is for causation, i.e., for the sake of your thanking Allah, glorified and exalted is He, for His blessing. Thus Allah, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned the two causes: the legal (shar'iyyah) and the divine-decreed (qadariyyah). As for the decreed cause, what is it? The decreed cause in the creation of night and day: ﴿that you may rest therein﴾.

* Student: ﴿and that you may seek of His bounty﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿and that you may seek of His bounty﴾. And the legal cause?

* Student: ﴿and that perhaps you may be thankful﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿and that perhaps you may be thankful﴾. That you thank Allah, glorified and exalted is He, for what He has bestowed upon you of the alternation of night and day; because things are made clear by their opposites. If the night were perpetual and the day perpetual, no one would rest by night, nor seek bounty by day. But Allah, glorified and exalted is He, made that for the sake of rest, although there are other benefits besides the matter of ﴿that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty﴾ [al-Qasas 73], which Allah mentioned in Surah al-Furqan: ﴿And He it is who made the night and the day to succeed one another, for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be thankful﴾ [al-Furqan 62]. And in the authentic hadith: "Indeed Allah, the Exalted, extends His hand by night so that the one who sinned by day may repent, and He extends His hand by day so that the one who sinned by night may repent."[[Recorded by Muslim (2759/31) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

So the sum is that in the alternation of night and day there are great benefits that necessitate that we thank Allah, glorified and exalted is He, for them.

Know that thanks is by the heart, the tongue and the limbs:

As for thanks by the heart: it is that a person acknowledges in his heart that these blessings are from Allah alone, acknowledging completely, so that even if these blessings came through a cause, let him believe that the cause is from whom? From Allah; it is He who brought it into being, and so this blessing was obtained through it.

As for thanks by the tongue: it is praising Allah, the Exalted, as He deserves, whether for this blessing or for other than it. So praising Allah as He deserves for this blessing or for other blessings, all of that is included in thanks.
