* The Shaykh: For causation, and it cannot be for comparison, because a person cannot be as good as Allah has been good to him; Allah's goodness to him is more perfect and greater, so comparison is impossible. Therefore the kaf here is for causation.

The kaf has come for causation in several places in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾ [al-Baqarah 198], i.e., remember Him because He guided you. And like the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "O Allah, send prayers upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad, as You sent prayers upon Ibrahim and upon the family of Ibrahim" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3370) and Muslim (406/66) from the hadith of Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah]. Here the kaf is for causation and not for comparison. This meaning we have mentioned saves us from the objection some people raised against this hadith: it is customary that the thing compared is of lesser rank than that to which it is compared, and Muhammad ﷺ is undoubtedly not less than Ibrahim, is he? So how was it said: "send prayers upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad as You sent prayers upon Ibrahim"? Some scholars answered: the intended meaning is "as You sent prayers upon Ibrahim and upon the family of Ibrahim," that it is a comparison of prayer upon one person to prayer upon a group, Ibrahim and Adam, and this is valid, that Muhammad ﷺ is given what all of these were given. But there is no need for this interpretation. Rather, we say: the meaning is, O Lord, just as You sent prayers upon Ibrahim and upon the family of Ibrahim, and this is part of Your nature and custom of generosity, so bestow likewise upon Muhammad ﷺ. Thus this clause "as You sent prayers" is for causation, and it is in reality for supplication, meaning: we seek nearness to You through what You did before with Ibrahim and his family, that You do likewise with Muhammad ﷺ and the family of Muhammad.

﴿as Allah has been good to you, and do not seek corruption in the earth﴾ [al-Qasas 77]. And His saying: ﴿as Allah has been good to you﴾: with what did Allah show goodness to him?

* Student: With wealth.

* The Shaykh: With the great wealth whose keys would weigh down a band of strong men.

﴿And do not seek corruption in the earth﴾ [al-Qasas 77]. Corruption by what? First, by oppression, as He said: ﴿So he oppressed them﴾ [al-Qasas 76]. So do not seek corruption in the earth through oppression.

Likewise, if this man were using his wealth for disobedience to Allah, this would be corruption in the earth, and this is the usual case: whoever Allah has given wealth but has no faith, his wealth becomes a means to corruption in the earth, because of His saying: ﴿corruption in the earth﴾. Does this man go about, for instance, blowing up dams and demolishing walls, or how is "corruption in the earth" to be understood?

* Student: By sins.

* The Shaykh: Sins, because sins are in reality the cause of corruption in the earth: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned, that He may let them taste part of what they have done﴾ [al-Baqarah 41]. For this reason, whatever occurs on earth of trials, wars, fighting, slaughter, and other things, is only due to sins: ﴿And if Allah were to seize mankind for what they have earned, He would not leave upon it [the earth] a single creature, but He defers them to a specified term﴾ [Fatir 45].

So this turmoil that has multiplied in this age, especially in this year, what are its causes? You can hardly turn on the radio without hearing from the beginning of the bulletin to its end: wars everywhere, assassinations, bombings, corruption, all of it due to the sins that are committed. They are a punishment for the disobedient who were struck by them, and a warning to others. You may see safe, peaceful lands to which their provision comes abundantly from everywhere, and people are brought to them from everywhere, yet you find them now destroyed: their dwellings, houses, security, and prosperity destroyed. Due to what? Due to sins. So it is a warning to others.

And this prohibition, indeed this negation, is a negation of the truth, meaning of the true object of worship, for there is no god but Allah. So the verb's object was deleted, or not?

﴿And do not grieve over them, and do not be in distress﴾ [al-Nahl 127] ("takun"): is the prohibition here effective or not?

* Student: Effective.

* The Shaykh: Undoubtedly it is effective in fact. What is it that is effective?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, the waw which is the root letter of the verb was deleted: "wa la takun." Here the waw which is the root letter was not deleted. Why? He said: "because of its being built," that it is built on fatha, while the origin of deleting the root letter of the verb is for the sake of sukun.

("Wa la takun"): how would its original form be? "Takun." If we kept the waw and made the nun sukun, two sukuns would meet, and this is not permissible in the Arabic language. When two sukuns meet and the first of them is a soft letter, it is deleted. For this reason the waw which is the root of the verb was deleted. But here: ﴿And never be among the polytheists﴾ [al-Qasas 87], it was not deleted. The author says: "because of its being built."

As for his saying: ﴿among the polytheists﴾: shirk, as we have often noted, is divided into the major type that expels from the religion, and the minor type that does not expel from the religion. The major is that one associates with Allah another in His worship or His lordship. Whoever associates with Allah in His lordship or in His worship is a polytheist. Whatever falls short of that and is called shirk is minor shirk. Usually minor shirk is either a means to major shirk, as in the matter of showing off, for showing off is shirk only because the one who performs worship and beautifies it for people may come to perform the very act of worship for people, and thereby become a major polytheist. Or minor shirk may not be a means to major shirk, but relates to other matters unconnected with shirk. But in any case, major shirk is that a person believes that Allah has a partner in His divinity or His lordship. (...)

* * *

Shall we stop here?

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: It is kufr, but the type of this kufr is shirk, because kufr is general, a genus that includes types.

* * *

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (﴿And do not invoke﴾ [al-Qasas 88]: worship).

The "la" is a prohibitive particle, and "tad'u" is a present-tense verb jussed by the prohibitive "la," its sign of jussive being the deletion of the waw, and the damma before it is evidence of it.

﴿with Allah another god﴾ is the object of ﴿tad'u﴾, and "ilah" means "ma'luh," that is, the one worshipped. ﴿Another﴾. It is impossible that there be with Allah another true god, because all the deities other than Allah are false, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood﴾ [Luqman 30].

In this verse, ﴿And do not invoke with Allah another god﴾ [al-Qasas 88], Allah the Exalted called what is worshipped a god, because "ilah" is on the pattern fi'al in the sense of maf'ul, that is, worshipped.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 77 (part 2 of 6):

﴿There is no god but Him﴾ [al-Qasas 28:88]. This sentence serves as the reason (ta'lil) for the prohibition before it, meaning: indeed, there is no god but Him. This negation is a negation of the true deity, that is, the true object of worship, so there is no god but Allah. In this case there is no contradiction between it and what precedes it, since what precedes it, as you see, affirms that there are other gods alongside Allah, but forbids that these gods be called upon. The second statement says: "There is no god but Him," which negates that there is any god at all. The way to reconcile them is to say: the true god, who is worshipped and deserves to be worshipped, is none other than Allah, whereas the false god, who is worshipped but does not deserve to be worshipped, exists for other than Allah. This is the correct understanding of the negation. It is also possible that it is a negation with the meaning of a prohibition, i.e., "Do not worship anyone but Allah." A negation carrying the meaning of a prohibition occurs in the Qur'an, as they said regarding His saying: ﴿This is the Book about which there is no doubt﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:2]. They said that its meaning, according to some exegetes (mufassirun), is: ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾, i.e., do not doubt it. Thus they made the negation carry the meaning of a prohibition. However, it is more appropriate to leave the negation on its apparent meaning and to take it as a literal negation. The negation is more emphatic than the prohibition, because a negation establishes a attribute, whereas a prohibition forbids something, which may or may not be complied with. It may occur, or it may not occur. But if it is a negation, it is greater and more fitting. Accordingly, we say: this negation does not conflict with what precedes it, because what precedes it refers to them as false gods, while this refers to them as true gods, so there is no true god but Allah.

﴿There is no god but Him﴾: the word "Him" (huwa) is a pronoun referring to Allah, and "huwa" is not an independent name, meaning that "Huwa" is not one of the names of Allah. This differs from the misguided innovating Sufis, who make "Huwa" one of the names of Allah and say "There is no god but Huwa," like "There is no god but Allah." In their false invocations they say "Huwa, Huwa, Huwa," repeating it, and they say: "This is Huwa..."

So we say: the pronoun "Huwa" is not a proper name of Allah, but rather a pronoun referring to Allah. ﴿with Allah﴾ [al-Qasas 28:88] is the noun, and ﴿there is no god but Him﴾ means: there is no god but Allah mentioned previously.

He said: ﴿Everything is perishing except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas 28:88].

﴿Everything is perishing﴾ means: passing away, ceasing, and nonexistent after having existed.

﴿Perishing except His Face﴾. The author said: "except Him" (illa iyyahu), meaning: except Allah, for He, glory be to Him, is not perishing, as Allah said: ﴿Everything upon it will perish, but there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor﴾ [al-Rahman 55:26-27].

As for His saying ﴿except His Face﴾, the author explained it as "except Him," in response to the false doctrine of those who said: "Allah will perish except His Face," God forbid, and who made "the Face" here refer only to the attribute of the face and not to the Essence. This is undoubtedly false speech. The intended meaning of "Face" here is the whole Essence, the entire exalted Being, but He expressed it with "Face," as in all other linguistic expressions, where "face" is used to refer to the whole of a thing. (...)

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: If (...) comes, that ﴿There is no god but He﴾ means: except Allah, yes. So it would be more appropriate to say: "There is no god but Allah." When a pronoun refers back to something already mentioned, it is better to mention Allah by His proper name. This is why: "Islam is built upon five: the testimony that there is no god but Allah..." [Al-Bukhari (8) and Muslim (16/20) narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Islam is built upon five: the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger, establishing the prayer, paying the zakah, pilgrimage to the House, and fasting in Ramadan."]

He said: ﴿Everything is perishing except His Face﴾. The author's statement "except Him" is correct as a rebuttal of those who say that Allah perishes except His Face, but it may give a false impression, namely the denial of the Face in reality. However, I do not think the author intends that. It is well known that the Ash'aris deny that Allah has a Face in reality. So we say: Allah undoubtedly has a real Face, and this verse is used as evidence for it. That is why He said ﴿except His Face﴾. But we say that He expressed the Essence by the Face, yes, like the other styles of the Arabic language.

It was also said: the meaning is "every thing is perishing except that which was intended by His Face," so this refers to deeds: all deeds are rejected and unaccepted, except what was done seeking the Face of Allah. Those who hold this view argue that His saying ﴿and do not call upon another god along with Allah﴾ [al-Qasas 28:88] refers to human deeds, and then He said ﴿everything is perishing except His Face,﴾ as if He said: every polytheism is perishing, ruined, and of no benefit to a person, except what is done seeking the Face of Allah, which is purely for Him, for it remains for the person.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, "perishing" means that it does not benefit the person. The meaning of ﴿perishing﴾ is that it does not benefit him, like the saying of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever does a deed that is not in accordance with our affair, it is rejected" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari with similar wording (2697), and Muslim with this wording (1718/18), from the hadith of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her].

But we say: the first meaning is stronger for the verse, namely that the intended meaning is: every thing is passing away and ruined except the Face of Allah. This is like a reason (ta'lil) for His saying: ﴿And do not call upon another god along with Allah. There is no god but Him﴾ [al-Qasas 28:88]. That is, it is as if He is saying: Will these idols worshipped besides Allah remain or not?

* Student: They will not remain.
* Shaykh: They will not remain, and Allah, exalted is He, is the One who remains, so He is the One who deserves to be worshipped.

He said: ﴿To Him belongs the judgment﴾ [al-Qasas 28:88].

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, it is not of the nature of a reason (ta'lil). This is the literal meaning, without interpretation, because "face" is always used to refer to the Essence. One says, for example: "Your noble face," meaning the noble person himself. The use of such an expression for "face" in accordance with the Arabic language involves no interpretation.

As for His saying ﴿To Him belongs the judgment﴾, this is a nominal sentence consisting of a subject and predicate. The predicate ﴿To Him﴾ is placed first, and ﴿the judgment﴾ is the delayed subject. Does placing first what should come later convey anything?

* Student: Exclusivity (al-hasr).
* Shaykh: Exclusivity. The meaning is: ﴿To Him﴾ alone ﴿belongs the judgment﴾.

The author says "judgment" means "the binding decree" (al-qada' al-nafidh), and he explained it as the universal decree (al-hukm al-kawni). The correct view is that it includes both the universal decree and the legislative ruling (al-hukm al-shar'i). So He has the binding decree over everyone, and He also has the final determination between creatures in legislative matters. Thus "judgment" includes both: the universal and the legislative ruling. We have already mentioned that an example of the legislative ruling is His saying in Surat al-Mumtahanah: ﴿That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you, and Allah is Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 60:10]. As for the universal decree, it is His saying about the brothers of Joseph: ﴿So I will not leave this land until my father permits me or Allah decides for me, and He is the best of judges﴾ [Yusuf 12:80].

As for His saying ﴿To Him belongs the judgment﴾, we mentioned that the sentence contains exclusivity: judgment belongs to Allah alone, although others also have judgment. That is why people speak of "the legal judge" (al-hakim al-shar'i), "the ruler of the country," and the like. The answer to this is to say: the judgment of these people follows the judgment of Allah, and the absolute, complete, comprehensive judgment belongs to Allah alone. Their being judges is by way of subordination, since such a judge does not rule by other than what Allah has revealed, and if he rules otherwise, his ruling is not binding.

(﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Qasas 28:88], by resurrection from your graves.)

"To Him" means to Allah, ﴿you will be returned﴾, so He will reward you for your deeds, and that will be by the resurrection when He raises you from the graves. There is no return except to Allah.

It is possible that the "return" here is more general than what the author mentioned, so that the meaning of ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ is: even in your judgments, you return only to Allah. That is why disputes among people are referred back to whom? To Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:1]. Surat al-'Ankabut is Meccan, and it has sixty-nine verses (...). Among them is a separate verse that is introduced at the beginning of surahs, except Surat Bara'ah.

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾. The author said: "Allah knows best what He means by that." This is true if we assume that this word has a meaning, but the correct view is that it has no meaning, as Mujahid and others said. In itself it has no meaning. This is because the Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language, and the composite letters of the alphabet have no meaning in themselves. "Alif, ba', ta', tha', jim" have no meaning, but these letters have an implication: they point to the fact that this noble Qur'an, which defeated you, the Arabs, and defeated others, did not come with new letters unknown to you. Rather, it came with letters you know and from which you form your speech, and yet it defeated you. That is why you will hardly find a surah beginning with these letters without mention of the Qur'an, or of something specific to the Qur'an after them. Look: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:1-2]; ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Allah, there is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer. He has sent down upon you the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:1-3]; ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad. A Book revealed to you﴾ [al-A'raf 7:1-2]; ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the wise Book﴾ [Yunus 10:1]. You will also find: ﴿Ha, Mim. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Jathiyah 45:1-2]; ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. The revelation of the Book, about which there is no doubt, is from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Sajdah 32:1-2]... and so on.

This one is: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Do people think they will be left alone because they say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:1-2]. It does not mention the Qur'an, but it mentions something that is a necessary consequence of the Qur'an, namely His saying: ﴿that they will be left alone because they say, "We believe," and they will not be tried,﴾ for whoever believes in the Qur'an must be tested.

His saying: ﴿Do people think...﴾. His saying ﴿that they will be left alone because they say...﴾ is the point of the question: Do people think that they will be left alone when they say "We believe," without being tested? This is something that will not happen. Rather, testing is necessary, and the stronger a person's faith, the greater his testing will be, for Allah, exalted is He, tests people. The most righteous are tested, the most excellent first, then those next to them, until it is seen whether his religion is strong or weak. [Ahmad (1556) narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: O Messenger of Allah, who among people suffers the greatest trials? He said: "The prophets, then the best, then the best. A servant is tested according to the measure of his religion. If his religion is firm, his trial is severe, and if there is weakness in his religion, he is tested according to that," and he said once: "his trial is severe," and [in another narration]: "according to his religion." He said: "Trials will not cease to befall the servant until he walks on the earth without any sin upon him."]

His saying ﴿Do people think...﴾: "hasiba" means "thought" (zanna).

His saying ﴿people﴾ includes whom? Believers and non-believers. This is because the statement "I am a believer" may be made by a true believer or by a hypocrite, and a hypocrite cannot properly be called a believer without qualification. Rather, one says: a believer with his tongue, a disbeliever in his heart.

﴿that they say, "We believe"﴾, that is, by their saying "We believe," meaning people think they will be left without trial when they say: ("We believe," and they will not be tested, meaning they will be examined by what makes the reality of their faith clear). Is this question for affirmation (taqrir) or for denial (inkar)?

* Student: For denial.
* Shaykh: For denial. That is, do not think that when you say "We believe," you will be left without trial. Rather, there must be trial and testing. Allah, glory be to Him, tests a person sometimes through His own acts, which He does to him, and sometimes through the acts of others, by which they are empowered over him. As for His acts, Allah may test a person with calamities by which He examines his faith: financial, family, or bodily calamities. Among people are those who, when these calamities strike them, God forbid, cannot be patient, and may apostatize after their Islam and disbelieve, God forbid. And among people are those who are patient and seek reward. Also, a person may be tested by something Allah empowers over him, which is not an act of Allah itself, such as a people who harm him with words, deeds, or both. This happened to whom? It happened to the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and his Companions. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was harmed greatly by his people and by others, and his Companions were also greatly harmed. Yet they were patient and sought reward. 'Ammar ibn Yasir and his family suffered great harm. [Among what was narrated about that: al-Hakim (5746) narrated from Ibn Ishaq, who said: 'Ammar ibn Yasir, his father, and his mother were a household of Islam, and the clan of Makhzum tortured them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Be patient, O family of Yasir, for your appointed place is Paradise."] Likewise others among the believers were harmed: some are harmed by words, some by deeds, and some by both words and deeds.

This is a trial and test from Allah, so that He, glory be to Him, may know whether this person will remain patient in his religion or will withdraw and return out of fear of the harm of these people.

Among people also are those harmed for adopting the morals of believers, such as shaving the beard, for example. He is harmed for it, either by words, mockery, and belittling, or by deeds, when he is beaten for it or imprisoned. So you find him shaving his beard out of fear of this matter. But as long as the matter is in your hands, it is not permissible for you to commit sin out of fear of people. Sins must never be committed by a person out of fear of people. He must be patient and seek reward.

So among people there is ﴿he who says, "We believe in Allah"﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:10], and ﴿We certainly tested those before them﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:3].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 28, verse 77 (part 3 of 6):

(﴿And We certainly tested those before them, so Allah will surely make known those who are truthful, and He will surely make known the liars﴾ [Al-Ankabut 3]). The knowledge meant here is ʿilm mushāhada (knowledge by observation), that is, knowledge that comes with the thing actually occurring. (Commentary on this verse is in the chapter on the Qur'an.)

﴿And We certainly tested those before them﴾: "tested" (fatannā) means "we examined" (ikhtabarnā) ﴿those before them﴾. The Prophet ﷺ informed us that among the trials of those before us was that a man would be sawn in two with iron combs, the flesh being torn from between his bone and his skin, and yet he would remain patient and seek reward (from Allah).[[Al-Bukhari (3852) narrated from Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, who said: We complained to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, while he was reclining on a cloak of his in the shade of the Kaʿba. We said to him: "Will you not seek victory for us? Will you not supplicate to Allah for us?" He said: "A man among those before you would be dug a pit in the ground and placed in it, then a saw would be brought and placed on his head, and he would be split in two, yet that would not turn him from his religion. Iron combs would be used on him to scrape what lies beneath his flesh of bone or sinew, and that would not turn him from his religion. By Allah, this affair will certainly be completed, until a rider travels from Sanaa to Hadramawt fearing none but Allah, or the wolf for his sheep. But you are being hasty."]] That is, iron combs are brought and the flesh is stripped off with them. Yes, he is sawn, and yet he remains patient in his religion and does not apostatize.

If this is the case for those before us, then this community is more deserving of patience in this great matter, especially when the situation is one of jihad, as happened to Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, during the time of the inquisition (miḥna). He was beaten with whips and dragged by mules so that he would say that the Qur'an is created, yet he refused to say that the Qur'an is created. For if he had said it, the matter would not have been confined to him alone; rather, the corruption of the entire community would have followed from it. Therefore, whoever is compelled to disbelief, when his disbelief would necessitate the disbelief of others and the corruption of the religion, it is not permissible for him to comply even if he is compelled. This is because the situation in his case is one of... what is the situation? It is a situation of jihad, and a person must strive in the way of Allah even if he is exposed to death. As for when the matter is merely personal compulsion to disbelief, this is permissible on condition that his heart is at rest in faith.

Accordingly, if a man, for example, is a model and leader among people, and he is compelled to commit a sin or to commit disbelief, his doing so is not merely to escape harm, but people would be tested through him. To such a man we say: Do not do it. Do not comply, even if you are compelled and even if you are beaten, because the situation is one of jihad in the way of Allah.

Another person, who is of no consequence and whom people do not regard or follow, is compelled to do some disbelief or something less than that. For him it is permissible to do it on condition that his heart is at rest in faith, just as Allah, glorified and exalted is He, said.

As for His saying ﴿so Allah will surely make known those who are truthful﴾ [Al-Ankabut 3]: what is the meaning of ﴿truthful﴾ (ṣadaqū)? Truthfulness is the correspondence of speech to reality, or the correspondence of action to reality.

﴿Those who are truthful﴾ [Al-Ankabut 3]: in what? In their claim that they are believers. So whoever is truthful in his faith will be saved by it, and whoever is a liar will, may Allah protect us, be deceived by this trial and turn back on his heels, losing both this world and the Hereafter.

The author's words "knowledge by observation" (ʿilm mushāhada) point to the fact that the Exalted's saying ﴿so Allah will surely make known﴾ [Al-Ankabut 3] refers to the future, as evidenced by the entry of the emphatic nūn (nūn al-tawkīd) upon it, and as evidenced by its being a sworn clause (jumla qasamiyya), and a sworn clause is in the future. So it is a present-tense verb occurring in a sworn clause and emphasized by the nūn, and therefore it refers to the future. Allah, blessed and exalted, knows that before the trial occurs. Is that not so?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: Then how do we answer His saying ﴿so Allah will surely make known﴾, which indicates that knowledge only comes after the trial?

The author said "knowledge by observation," because Allah's knowledge of things divides into two kinds: knowledge that they will occur, and knowledge that they have occurred. The first is knowledge of what has not yet existed; the second is knowledge of what has existed. The second is what such verses are addressed to, like His saying ﴿And We will surely test you until We know those among you who strive﴾ [Muhammad 31]. The meaning is knowledge by observation. As for knowing who will be a striver, that is prior knowledge, but it is knowledge that it will happen. So the object of knowledge is either a future thing that Allah knows will occur, or a present thing that Allah knows has occurred. This is one answer.

The second answer: knowledge divides into two kinds, knowledge upon which a recompense is based, and knowledge upon which no recompense is based. Allah's knowledge in eternity before a thing occurs is knowledge upon which no recompense is based, and Allah's knowledge after its occurrence is knowledge upon which recompense is based. So the knowledge that Allah makes dependent upon occurrence is meant as knowledge of requital: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

These are two answers to verses like this one. It must not be said that Allah does not know a thing until after it occurs, as the extreme Qadariyya (Qadariyya ghulāt, the extreme determinism-deniers) said. The extreme Qadariyya say that Allah did not know a thing until after it occurred, and they cite this ambiguous (mutashābih) part of the Qur'an as evidence. But we say: these people have deviation in their hearts, because they follow what is ambiguous in it. If they had returned to the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Do you not know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and the earth? Indeed, that is in a Book. Indeed, that is easy for Allah﴾ [Al-Hajj 70], it would have made clear to them that Allah knows what will be before it is.

As for His saying ﴿and He will surely make known the liars﴾ [Al-Ankabut 3]: the liars in what? In their claim that they are believers. So when Allah tests a person, the creation, He knows who is truthful in his speech and who is a liar.

In this there is a warning, a warning to a person when trials occur, that he should not apostatize from his faith and thereby become a liar.

A student: Do we say that Allah is a thing?

The Shaykh: Yes, Allah is a great thing. We mentioned in Surat al-An'am a very clear verse: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say: "Allah"﴾ [al-An'am 19]. This is clear. But note that it is not used as a name for Him, because Allah says: ﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾ [al-A'raf 180]. The names of Allah must necessarily include the most perfect and best aspects. As for what admits of this and that, it is what may be used to name Allah.

So words are of three categories: words that suggest deficiency. These cannot be said of Him or used as a name for Him, such as "oppressor" (al-zalim) and "tyrant" (al-jair), all of which suggest deficiency. These cannot be used as names for Him nor spoken of Him.

The second: what includes the most perfect matters and aspects. These are used as names for Him, yet we cannot analogize them ourselves, because the names of Allah are tawqifi (determined by revelation alone).

The third: what includes neither deficiency nor praise, but is according to what it is attached to. These are spoken of Him, but not used as names for Him.

Among words are those that are deficiency from one standpoint and perfection from another, so Allah is described by them only in the manner of perfection, such as: "cunning" (al-makr), "deception" (al-khada'), "mockery" (al-istihza') and the like. On this basis, words become four categories: pure perfection, pure deficiency, perfection from one standpoint and deficiency from another, and what includes neither.

The first (pure perfection) is used as a name for Him. The second (pure deficiency) is not spoken of Him at all, in any respect. The third (what includes both perfection and deficiency) is spoken of Him in the state in which it is perfection, such as saying: Allah the Exalted plots against the disbelievers, mocks the hypocrites, and the like. The fourth (what includes neither praise nor deficiency) is spoken of Him but not used as a name for Him, such as: "the Willer" (al-murid), "the One who comes" (al-ja'i), "the Speaker" (al-mutakallim), "the Thing" (al-shay') and "the Existent" (al-mawjud) and the like. These are spoken of Him, but not used as names for Him. This is why it is not permitted to say, for example: "O Existent, forgive me," because the word "existent" applies to what exists in a good way and to what exists in an evil way. For this reason it is not used as a name for Him. "The Speaker" speaks good and speaks evil, so it is not used as a name for Him, but it may be said that it is spoken of Him.

A student: (...) there are ways of inviting, but the goal is one?

The Shaykh: It is undoubtedly an invitation, but do we say that it is meant in reality? Because sometimes these cards are sent merely as courtesy. Even the inviter himself is not certain that this man intends to attend. Yes. Always twenty cards come to a person, and it shows you that they are not real invitations. When he wants to come, he says: "Will you come or not? Do you have a promise?" It is merely a directive for honour. So I doubt the obligation of answering these, except for a man who has a particular right upon you, such as a relative, for answering him is part of maintaining ties of kinship. Because you may not know; they may write, for example, five hundred cards and distribute them. Whoever occurs to their mind, they say: come on, let us send him a card. By Allah, I think this does not happen.

A student: (...)?

The Shaykh: In reality, if it were returned to him, he would not want from these people except a small group whose invitation is real. This is why he insists on them, saying: "The card we sent you has come," and he looks to see whether they have the intention to attend or not. So, to me, and Allah knows best, these are merely courtesies. This is why those same people sometimes say: "So-and-so, son of so-and-so, and his family," though they do not know the family and have no relation with them, neither kinship, nor companionship, nor anything.

A student: (...)?

The Shaykh: (...) may Allah keep you safe. Originally, if he specified you specifically, saying: "O so-and-so, I want you to attend at my place," as a real invitation, and you know that he has something forbidden that you cannot remove, then it is not permissible for you to attend. This is clear even if he specified you personally. But for this I think the closest is the general invitation (al-jafla). The general invitation, as you know, does not oblige answering. For example, if he says: "O people, please come," standing at the door of the mosque and saying: "O folks, please come," it is not obligatory for each one to answer. But if he specified him, then it depends on the view that it is obligatory absolutely, or obligatory only at a wedding feast.

A student: (...)?

The Shaykh: Yes, perhaps when he comes, God willing, you advise him when...

A student: (...).

The Shaykh: Yes. In any case, they prepare more, and after that, the matter of preparation: they prepare more while they are in the depth of (...).

The affirmation of the Face for Him.

Among the benefits of the verse: that the judgment belongs to Allah alone, by His saying: ﴿To Him belongs the judgment﴾ [al-Qasas 88]. It includes both the cosmic (kawni) and the legislative (shar'i) judgment.

Also among the benefits of the verse: that it is not permissible for anyone to oppose the legislative rulings of Allah, because he would be disputing with Allah over His judgment. The one who opposes is disputing with Allah, the Exalted, over His judgment, whether he opposes in legislation or opposes by disobedience, because he is contending with Allah's judgment.

Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of the Gathering (hashr) on the Day of Resurrection, by His saying: ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Qasas 88].

* * *

As for Surat al-Ankabut, it contains benefits:

Among them: the wisdom in beginning surahs with the letters of the alphabet, and we have previously explained this.

Also among the benefits of the verse: that Allah, glorified and exalted, tests the believers, so that by this He may know the truthfulness of their faith or its lack.

Among them: that this testing is not specific to this community, but applies to them and to others, by His saying: ﴿And We certainly tested those before them﴾ [al-Ankabut 3].

Among them: as it is said, "At the time of testing, a person is honoured or humiliated," and that a person's reality is not known except through his testing. When he is tested and stands firm, that is evidence of his truthfulness, and if he deviates, that is evidence of his falsehood and lack of sincerity.

Among them: the affirmation of knowledge to Allah, glorified and exalted, in His saying: ﴿So Allah will surely make evident those who are truthful﴾ [al-Ankabut 3].

Among the benefits of the verse: the division of people in faith into truthful and lying. Who is the truthful one? The one who remains steadfast in his faith at the time of testing. And the liar is the one who does not remain steadfast. Is there anything beyond this?

* * *

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds﴾, meaning shirk and sins, ﴿think that they can outrun Us?﴾ [al-Ankabut 4], that is, escape us so that we do not take vengeance upon them).

His saying: ﴿Am hasiba﴾. "Am" here is munqati'ah (disjunctive), because "am" in the Arabic language comes in two types: muttasilah (connective) and munqati'ah (disjunctive). The difference between them is that the connective means "aw" (or), comes after the hamzat al-taswiyah (interrogative of equality), and comes between two opposites. There are three signs for it: the connective comes in the sense of "aw," after the hamzat al-taswiyah, and between two opposites. An example is His saying: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah 6]. Here you find that "am" means "aw," meaning this and that are equal. Second, you find it after the hamzat al-taswiyah: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾. And you find that it is between two opposites: "you warned them" and "you did not warn them." Similarly His saying: ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Munafiqun 6]. Also: ﴿It is the same for us whether we become impatient or we endure﴾ [Ibrahim 21], and there are many examples.

As for the disjunctive, it comes in the sense of "bal" (rather), is not (...) in the sense of the waw (and), and does not occur after the hamzat al-taswiyah nor between two opposites.

So here, ﴿Am hasiba﴾ means "bal ahsabu" (rather, do I think). This transition is a transition to another topic, not a nullification. That is, after Allah, the Exalted, mentioned and rebuked those who thought ﴿that they would be left alone to say, "We believe," and they would not be tested﴾ [al-Ankabut 2], He moved, the Exalted, to mention another category of people: those who have not said "we believe" and have not believed, but who do evil deeds and think that Allah will not encompass them. ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think﴾ [al-Ankabut 4], meaning they do bad actions. The "sayyi'" (evil) is what harms its doer, and every forbidden deed is evil, because it harms its doer by what he finds of punishment, both present and future.

As for his saying: "shirk and sins": the author informs us that "sayyi'at" here includes both minor and major sins. The major ones, the highest of which is shirk, and the minor ones, which are what is below the major ones, are the sins. So it includes everything that harms its doer through disobedience to Allah, from shirk downward.

Hasiba ﴿an yasbiquna﴾ [al-Ankabut 4]: this is the object of hasiba. ("That they would outrun Us" means "that they would escape and We would not take vengeance upon them.") Sabq means escape, as you say: "I outran so-and-so," meaning: I escaped him and he did not catch me. These people, who commit evil deeds, think that Allah, glorified and exalted, will not catch them, and that Allah will not take vengeance upon them. This is undoubtedly a bad opinion of Allah, blessed and exalted. This is why He said: ﴿Evil is what they judge﴾ [al-Ankabut 4], meaning "evil is their judgment," which is their thinking that Allah, the Exalted, will not catch them.

He says: ﴿Sa'a﴾ is in the sense of "bi'sa" (evil is), and "bi'sa" is an intransitive past verb used to express blame. It requires a subject and requires an specified object (makhsus), and the specified object is always omitted, either for its being unnecessary or because the subject indicates it. This is why the author said: ﴿Sa'a﴾ in the sense of "bi'sa," ﴿ma﴾ in the sense of "alladhi" (which), so it is a relative pronoun.

(﴿Yahkumuna﴾ ... "hi"): the author supposed the pronoun "ha'" so that it refers back to the relative: ﴿sa'a﴾ "alladhi" ﴿yahkumuna﴾ "hi."

So "alladhi" is the subject. Where is the specified object? The author said: "their judgment this," this is the specified object. Every intransitive verb used for blame or praise requires a subject and requires a specified object. You say, for example: "Ni'ma dar al-muttaqin al-jannatu" (How excellent is the abode of the God-fearing: Paradise). Where is the subject?

A student: "Dar."

The Shaykh: "Dar." "Al-jannah" is the specified object of praise, and "al-jannah" here has two possible i'rab (grammatical analyses) for you: first, you make it a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), and the clause is a preposed predicate (khabar muqaddam). Second, you make it the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being "hiya al-jannah" (it is Paradise).

As for the first, "ni'ma dar al-muttaqin," this is a verb and subject according to what they did.

He says: "Bi'sa ma yahkumuna" (Evil is what they judge), "hukmuhum hadha" (their judgment this). There is no doubt that what they judged and thought, there is no doubt that it is a bad opinion that does not befit Allah, because Allah, the Exalted, says in many verses: ﴿And they will not escape Him﴾ [al-Zumar 51], ﴿And Allah is not to be rendered incapable by anything in the heavens or on the earth﴾ [Fatir 44]. Those who persisted in doing evil and thought that Allah does not have power over them and will not take vengeance upon them, these have added, may Allah protect us, evil to their evil.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting with Allah, then indeed the term of Allah is coming﴾ ("la-ati," so let him prepare for it, ﴿and He is the All-Hearing﴾ of the speech of the servants, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ [al-Ankabut 5] of their actions).

He said: ﴿man kana yarju﴾. "Man" here is conditional (shartiyyah), and the response of the condition, according to the author's view, is omitted, its estimate being "fa-l-yasta'idd lahu" (let him prepare for it). We will discuss this matter.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Man kana yarju﴾. The author, in explaining ﴿yarju﴾, said: "yakhaf" (fears). This is diverting the word from its apparent meaning. Raja' is other than fear. Raja' means hope. This is the correct view: the meaning of ﴿yarju liqa'a Allah﴾ is: he hopes to meet Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, pleased with him. ﴿Then indeed the term of Allah is coming﴾, as in His saying: ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf 110]. There is nothing that requires diverting the word from its apparent meaning. Rather, the meaning is: any person who hopes for the meeting of Allah and that he will meet Him while pleased with him, the matter is not far off.

﴿Fa-inna ajala Allah la-ati﴾, that is: the period that Allah, glorified and exalted, has placed as a barrier between you and His meeting will come, meaning: that will surely come.

It is possible that His saying ﴿fa-inna ajala Allah﴾ means the period He has determined for the meeting, and this is better: the period He has determined for His meeting must come.

(﴿fa-inna ajala Allah﴾ "bihi") meaning: with the meeting, because the meeting is deferred; everything is deferred by a known term.

﴿La-ati﴾: the lam, what is its i'rab? We have passed by it in the Alfiyyah (Ibn Malik's poem on grammar).

A student: (...)?

Shaykh: No, the lām is for emphasis, because it falls in the predicate of inna (إنَّ): ﴿Surely the term of Allah is coming﴾. So it is for emphasis. We mentioned to you, when we explained it in the Alfiyya (the grammatical poem of Ibn Malik), that its proper place is at the beginning of the sentence, but they postponed it because inna is itself an emphasizing particle. They disliked two consecutive emphasizers, so they shifted the lām to its place within the predicate.

﴿فَإِنَّ أَجَلَ اللَّهِ لَآتٍ﴾. I said that āti (آتٍ) is the predicate of inna, yet it is in the genitive (مكسورة). The known rule is that the predicate of inna is nominative (مرفوع), so how is this correct?

We say: is āti (آتٍ) a defective noun (اسم ناقص) or not? Is it a manqūṣ (منقوص)? Yes, it is manqūṣ, because nouns are either manqūṣ, maqṣūr, mamdūd, or ṣaḥīḥ al-ākhir (with a sound final letter). Here we say it is manqūṣ. Its original form was (لآتِي) with a yā', the yā' was dropped and replaced by tanwīn: ﴿لَآتٍ﴾. On this basis we say: āti (آتٍ) is the predicate of inna, nominative by it, and the sign of its nominative case is a presumed ḍammah on its final letter, on the deleted yā', because of the meeting of two sukūns.

﴿وَهُوَ﴾, that is, Allah, the Exalted, (﴿السَّمِيعُ﴾ who hears the speech of the servants, ﴿الْعَلِيمُ﴾ who knows their deeds).

Yes. ﴿As-Samī'﴾ means the One who possesses hearing, and nothing is hidden from Him. Allah perceives everything that can be heard. Hearing, as we have already gone over, is of two kinds: hearing of perception (سمع إدراك) and hearing of response (سمع إجابة). The first is like His saying: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the speech of the woman who pleads with you﴾ (al-Mujādilah 58:1). The second is like His saying: ﴿Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾ (Ibrāhīm 14:39), and like the worshipper's words: "Allah hears whoever praises Him," meaning that He answers.

We mentioned earlier that hearing of perception has several kinds: some of them imply a warning (تهديد), some imply support and assistance (نصر وتأييد), and some are meant merely as perception.

What is an example of the first, the one that is a warning?

Student: His saying: (...).

Shaykh: No, because (...). It needs regarding such-and-such, and regarding such-and-such.

Student: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of those who said, "Indeed Allah is poor and we are rich"﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 3:181).

Shaykh: Yes, this is meant as a warning. And an example of what is meant as support and assistance?

Student: ﴿Indeed I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ (Ṭā-Hā 20:46).

Shaykh: ﴿Indeed I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾, yes. And an example of what is meant merely as perception, that is, to state that Allah encompasses a thing and hears it, encompassing it?

Student: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the speech of the woman who pleads with you﴾ (al-Mujādilah 58:1).

Shaykh: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the speech of the woman who pleads with you﴾.

Does His being All-Hearing necessarily imply that He has ears? What is the answer?

Student: It does not necessarily imply that.

Shaykh: It does not necessarily imply that. Just as His being All-Seeing does not necessarily imply that He has an eye. But the eye is established by another proof. Had Allah not affirmed it for Himself by another proof, we would not affirm it. So we do not say that being All-Hearing requires that He has an ear, just as being Speaking does not require that He has a tongue, lips, or the like. We know that the earth reports its news, and it reports only after hearing. Does it have an ear?

Student: No.

Shaykh: It does not have an ear, as far as we know. Does it have a tongue?

Student: No.

Shaykh: We do not know that it has a tongue. So we say: affirming hearing does not require affirming an ear.

If someone says: it is established in the authentic ḥadīth: "Allah has never given ear (adhina) to anything as He gave ear to a Prophet with a beautiful voice who chants the Qur'an"[[Recorded by Muslim (792/233) from the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, with the wording: "Allah has never given ear to anything as He gave ear to a Prophet with a beautiful voice who chants the Qur'an aloud."]], the answer is that the meaning of "adhina lahu" is "he listened to him." This also does not necessarily imply affirming an ear, because it is not explicit. Attributes cannot be established by mere possibility. The matter must be clear and explicit.

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: No. Does "adhina" here mean "decreed" (qaddara)?

Student: Yes.

Shaykh: No, its meaning is "listened."

Student: (...).

Shaykh: No, that is not its meaning (...). Its meaning is "listened," because the matter is tied to a voice: "a Prophet with a beautiful voice who chants the Qur'an." Otherwise, Allah has given permission to people, through legislated permission for example, and has granted them concessions or allowed them things far greater than this. Tawḥīd and other things that are better than reciting the Qur'an are certainly permitted by Him far more.

As for His saying ﴿al-ʿAlīm﴾ (the All-Knowing), the author says "of their deeds." In reality, knowledge (ʿilm) relates to deeds and to speech as well. Restricting it to deeds is open to question, because what pertains only to deeds is sight (ruʾyah). Knowledge is more general: it relates to deeds, to speech, to the inner thoughts of the soul, to what is spoken aloud, and to everything.

He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And whoever strives﴾ (al-ʿAnkabūt 29:6). The author says: "striving against an enemy or striving against the self."

I forgot to mention: where is the response (jawāb) to ﴿whoever hopes for the meeting with Allah﴾? The author estimated it with his saying "let him prepare for it" and considered it omitted. In my view, there is no harm in saying that the response of the condition is His saying ﴿for indeed the term of Allah is coming﴾, and the meaning is that whoever hopes to meet Allah will surely attain it. There is no need to estimate something omitted, because the original state is not to omit.

What the author estimated here is similar to what he estimated in His saying: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Jibrīl – for indeed it is he who brought it down upon your heart﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:97). It has already been mentioned that the author estimated it with his saying "let him die of rage," and we mentioned there that there is no need for this estimation.

Student: Would it not be (...)?

Shaykh: It is feminine.

Student: It is feminine (...).

Shaykh: Yes, but hope (al-amal) is based on love. You do not hope for something unless you love it. So the hope for a thing, meaning expectation of its occurrence, is based on that.

He says: "﴿And whoever strives﴾, striving against an enemy or striving against the self."

The author has informed us from this phrase that striving (jihād) is of two kinds: striving in war, which is fighting the enemies, and striving against the self, by striving against your own soul in performing acts of obedience and abstaining from what is forbidden.

﴿And whoever strives, he strives only for himself﴾. He said about its meaning: "the benefit of his striving is for himself, not for Allah." The one who strives, and striving (jihād) means exerting effort in something, does not strive for Allah but works for himself, as in His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self﴾ (Fuṣṣilat 41:46).

The author's words "the benefit of his striving is for himself, not for Allah." Yes, "for himself," because he is rewarded, whether he strives against his own self or against others. Even when he strives against others, the benefit may also go to them, since such a person may enter the religion of Allah, and then he gains benefit.

The point is that Allah, the Exalted, does not benefit from this striving. For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed Allah is free of need from the worlds﴾ (al-ʿAnkabūt 29:6). This is like a reason for His saying ﴿he strives only for himself﴾. Allah is independent of it: He does not benefit from obedience and is not harmed by disobedience.

As for His saying "free of need from them." What is the meaning of al-Ghanī (the Self-Sufficient)? It means the One who does not need them, because of what He has of generosity, abundance, and management of affairs. He does not need all the worlds. The author said: "﴿al-ʿĀlamīn﴾ (the worlds) are mankind, jinn, and angels." What comes after that?

Student: "And from their worship."

Shaykh: "And from their worship." Yes. He is free of need from them, He does not need them. ﴿I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me. I do not want provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me﴾ (al-Dhāriyāt 51:56–57). Likewise, He is free of need of their worship, because their worship is for their own benefit. As for Allah, the Exalted, He does not benefit from the obedience of the obedient, nor is He harmed by the disobedience of the disobedient.

As for His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is free of need﴾, is the sentence here emphasized with how many emphasizers?

Student: Two.

Shaykh: Two: inna and the lām. ﴿Indeed Allah is free of need from the worlds﴾.

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds – We will surely remove from them their misdeeds, by the doing of righteous deeds, and We will surely reward them with the best of what they used to do﴾ (al-ʿAnkabūt 29:7). "Ḥasan" (good): "aḥsan" here means "ḥasan" (good), and it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition "bi" (ب). The righteous deeds: that is, the righteous deeds.

His saying ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ is in contrast to ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they can outrun Us?﴾ (al-ʿAnkabūt 29:4). Here He says ﴿those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. Faith, as has been established many times, is affirmation together with acceptance and submission, not mere affirmation.

His saying ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ refers to deeds of the limbs. So faith is in the heart, and doing righteous deeds is in the limbs. Action (ʿamal) includes both deed and speech. For this reason, it is not the counterpart of speech, as some people assume, saying "speech and action." Rather, the counterpart of speech is deed, while action includes both speech and deed. So ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ includes deeds, such as bowing, prostration, prayer, standing and sitting in it, and includes speech, such as reciting the Qur'an, glorifying Allah (tasbīḥ), praising Allah (taḥmīd), and so on.

His saying ﴿righteous﴾ means righteous deeds. It is an adjective of an omitted noun, and its estimate is "righteous deeds." The righteous deed is that which combines what? The righteous deed is that which combines how many conditions?

Student: Sincerity and following the Sunnah.

Shaykh: Yes, it combines two conditions: sincerity (ikhlāṣ) and following the Sunnah (mutābaʿah). Sincerity means that you intend by your deed the face of Allah, the Exalted, and the Last Abode. Following means that in it you follow the Prophet ﷺ. The opposite of the first is associating partners with Allah (shirk), and the opposite of the second is innovation (bidʿah). So you are neither a polytheist nor an innovator.

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds – We will surely remove from them their misdeeds﴾ (al-ʿAnkabūt 29:7). Here He said ﴿We will surely remove﴾, and the clause is the response to an implied oath, as if it were: "By Allah, we will surely remove." It is therefore emphasized with three emphasizers: the oath, the lām, and the nūn.

His saying ﴿We will surely remove from them their misdeeds﴾. Takfīr means covering, from which comes "al-kufrā," which is the membrane that covers the spathe of a date palm. So the meaning of ﴿We will surely remove from them their misdeeds﴾ is that We will cover them. The intended covering entails its consequence, which is pardon.

But by what does ﴿We will surely remove from them their misdeeds﴾ happen? By their faith and their righteous deeds, because faith demolishes what came before it, and about righteous deeds Allah says: ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will remove from you your minor misdeeds﴾ (al-Nisāʾ 4:31).

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: Yes, this is its covering. It derives from disbelief (kufr) and covering (satr).

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: Yes, that is correct. And from it: ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds﴾, because it derives from concealment, and concealing misdeeds means removing them and not being held accountable for them.

His saying ﴿We will surely remove from them their misdeeds﴾. The author said: "by doing righteous deeds." So their righteous deeds cover the misdeeds. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The five prayers, and Friday to Friday, and Ramaḍān to Ramaḍān are expiations for what is between them, so long as major sins are avoided"[[Recorded by Muslim (233/16) and Aḥmad (9197), with this wording, from the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, except that he said: "expiations for what is between them."]]. He also said ﷺ: "The ʿumrah to the ʿumrah is an expiation for what is between them"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (1773) and Muslim (1349/437) from the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. So righteous deeds act like a covering over misdeeds, so that their effect does not appear.

He said: ﴿We will surely remove from them their misdeeds and We will surely reward them with the best﴾ (al-ʿAnkabūt 29:7).

﴿And We will surely reward them﴾. Reward (jazāʾ) means recompense for a thing. What was said about the emphasis in His saying ﴿We will surely remove﴾ applies to ﴿We will surely reward them﴾.

His saying ﴿the best﴾. The author said: "in the sense of good (ḥasan)." It seems he wanted to escape an objection that might be raised, namely that the verse indicates they are rewarded with the best of what they used to do. Then, is "good" (ḥasan) something rewarded or not?

Student: They are not rewarded for it.

Shaykh: They are not rewarded for it. Therefore the author interpreted "aḥsan" as meaning "ḥasan," the good of what they used to do. But we see that there is no need for this interpretation. What the verse indicates is more correct than what the author estimated. Allah says: ﴿and We will surely reward them with the best﴾ of reward ﴿of what they used to do﴾. Yes, so it is by an omitted estimate: ﴿and We will surely reward them with the best of reward﴾. The best reward is explained by Allah in His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ (al-Anʿām 6:160), and He said: ﴿The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven spikes, in each spike a hundred grains, and Allah multiplies for whom He wills, and Allah is all-encompassing﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:261). Is this reward the best reward? Yes, it is the best reward, because the most a reward can be is equal to what the doer did, but here one is rewarded with what is better and greater.

On this basis, aḥsan is not in the accusative by removal of the preposition, as the author said ("in the accusative by removal of the preposition bi"). Rather, it is a second object of "najzī" (We reward), and the first object is the pronoun (hā') in ﴿We will surely reward them﴾. The mīm in ﴿them﴾ is for emphasis. This is the meaning of the noble verse: Allah promised them two things: the removal of their misdeeds through righteous deeds, and reward for these deeds with the best reward they can receive. That is, a good deed is multiplied to ten times its like, up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples.

His saying ﴿the best of what they used to do﴾. Where does "what" come from? The author said: "and it is the righteous deeds." So these righteous deeds that they do, Allah rewards them for them with the best reward they can be rewarded with.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And We have enjoined upon mankind kindness to his parents﴾ (al-ʿAnkabūt 29:8).

When He mentioned the general outline of His right, what He threatens the violators with, and what He promises the hypocrites, He said: ﴿And We have enjoined upon mankind to his parents﴾.

"We enjoined him with them," meaning We made a covenant with him regarding them. Enjoining (wiṣāyah) is only in important matters.

His saying ﴿to his parents﴾ means his mother and father.

﴿ḥusnan﴾ (kindness). The author said: "meaning, enjoining one of goodness." So according to his view, His saying ﴿ḥusnan﴾ is an attribute of an omitted noun, meaning an enjoining of goodness. Ḥusn, as you know, is a verbal noun (maṣdar), not an adjective ḥasan. Since it is a verbal noun, it must have an omitted modifying noun, namely "one of goodness" (dhā ḥusn). This is what the author said.

But there is a strong possibility that this ḥusnan is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, meaning "We made a covenant with him regarding goodness," and that ḥusn here means iḥsān (excellence in conduct), as Allah says in another verse: ﴿And We have enjoined upon mankind kindness to his parents﴾ (al-Aḥqāf 46:15). This is closer than the author's estimate, and Allah knows best. (...)

Shaykh: [This warning is] for whoever thinks that Allah, the Exalted, cannot take vengeance on him for doing misdeeds, based on His saying: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they can outrun Us?﴾ (al-ʿAnkabūt 29:4).

It is also derived from it: a warning to those who commit misdeeds that Allah will seize them, and that they have not escaped Allah.

It is derived from this: the prohibition of thinking ill of Allah, based on His saying: ﴿Evil is what they judge﴾ [al-'Ankabut 4], for whoever thinks that Allah (...).
